items.title: The torus of §1

milnor.label: §1, pp. 1–3
milnor.statement: A torus $M$ stands on a plane $V$ to which it is tangent (Diagram 1), $f : M \to \mathbb R$ is the height above $V$, and $M^a = \{x \in M : f(x) \le a\}$. Milnor lists five stages as $a$ increases: $M^a$ is vacuous below $f(p)$, homeomorphic to a 2-cell for $f(p) < a < f(q)$, to a cylinder for $f(q) < a < f(r)$, to a compact genus-one surface bounded by a circle for $f(r) < a < f(s)$, and is the full torus above $f(s)$. Up to homotopy type, passing $f(p)$, $f(q)$, $f(r)$, $f(s)$ attaches a 0-cell, a 1-cell, a 1-cell and a 2-cell. The four points are the critical points of $f$, and in suitable coordinates $f = x^2 + y^2$ at $p$, $f = \text{const} + x^2 - y^2$ at $q$ and $r$, and $f = \text{const} - x^2 - y^2$ at $s$: the number of minus signs is the dimension of the cell attached.
milnor.note: No equations are given and nothing is checked: the example is offered as an illustration of the theorems to come.

lean.statement: For $0 < \rho < R$ let $T \subseteq \mathbb R^3$ be the torus $(\sqrt{x_1^2 + x_2^2} - R)^2 + x_3^2 = \rho^2$, a compact surface (V3.22), and $f(x) = x_1 + R + \rho$ its height above the plane $x_1 = -(R + \rho)$, which touches $T$ at $p = (-(R + \rho), 0, 0)$. Then $f|T$ has exactly four critical points, $p$, $q = (-(R - \rho), 0, 0)$, $r = (R - \rho, 0, 0)$ and $s = (R + \rho, 0, 0)$, at the heights $0$, $2\rho$, $2R$ and $2R + 2\rho$; all four are non-degenerate, of indices $0, 1, 1, 2$. $T^a = \emptyset$ for $a < 0$ and $T^a = T$ for $a \ge 2R + 2\rho$. If $a \le b$ and $[a, b]$ contains none of the four heights, a $C^\infty$ diffeomorphism of $T$ carries $T^a$ onto $T^b$, $T^a$ is a strong deformation retract of $T^b$, and the inclusion $T^a \to T^b$ is a homotopy equivalence.

diff: Of the five stages only (1) and (5) are proved. That the intermediate sublevel sets are a disk, a cylinder and a torus with a disk removed is not, and neither are the cell attachments of p. 2; between critical heights only Theorem 3.1 is applied.
The torus is fixed: the torus of revolution with $0 < \rho < R$, standing upright on its tangent plane. Lying flat, its height function would have two circles of degenerate critical points.
The critical points, their indices and the four critical values are proved, where Milnor asserts them; the normal forms are not restated, but follow from the lemma of Morse (V1.8) and the indices.
Case (1) is printed $a < 0 < f(p)$ in the scan, whereas $f(p) = 0$; the hypothesis is $a < 0$. The details, whose Lean files sit with Chapter 3, are V3.22–V3.25.

items.title: Attaching a cell

milnor.label: §1, pp. 2–3
milnor.statement: With $e^k$ the $k$-cell of vectors of length at most $1$ in $\mathbb R^k$, $\dot e^k$ its boundary sphere $S^{k-1}$, and $g : S^{k-1} \to Y$ continuous, the space $Y \cup_g e^k$, $Y$ with a $k$-cell attached by $g$, is obtained from the topological sum of $Y$ and $e^k$ by identifying each $x \in S^{k-1}$ with $g(x) \in Y$. For $k = 0$, $e^0$ is a point and $\dot e^0 = S^{-1}$ is empty, so that attaching a 0-cell adds a disjoint point.

lean.statement: For a topological space $X$, an integer $n \ge 0$ and a continuous map $\varphi : S^{n-1} \to X$, the space $X \cup_\varphi e^n$ is the pushout, in the category of topological spaces, of $\varphi$ and the inclusion of the unit sphere $S^{n-1}$ in the closed unit ball $D^n$ of $\mathbb R^n$: the quotient of $X \sqcup D^n$ by the identification of each $u \in S^{n-1}$ with $\varphi(u)$, so that a map out of it is a pair of maps on $X$ and on $D^n$ which agree along $\varphi$. For $n = 0$ the sphere is empty and $D^0$ is a point. The disk and the sphere are Mathlib's, those of its CW complexes.

items.title: Critical points, the Hessian, index and nullity in coordinates

milnor.label: §2, pp. 4–5
milnor.statement: A point $p$ is a critical point of a smooth $f : M \to \mathbb R$ when the induced map $f_* : TM_p \to T\mathbb R_{f(p)}$ is zero, which in local coordinates means that the first partial derivatives vanish at $p$; $f(p)$ is then a critical value. A critical point is non-degenerate when the matrix $(\partial^2 f/\partial x^i \partial x^j(p))$ is non-singular, a condition which can be checked directly not to depend on the coordinates. The index of a bilinear functional $H$ on a vector space is the maximal dimension of a subspace on which $H$ is negative definite, and its nullity is the dimension of the null space $\{v : H(v, w) = 0 \text{ for all } w\}$; a critical point is non-degenerate exactly when $f_{**}$ has nullity $0$.
milnor.note: The coordinate condition for a critical point is displayed in the book, but the display is lost in the scan.

lean.statement: Let $E$ be a real normed space and $f : E \to \mathbb R$. A point $p$ is a critical point of $f$ if $f$ is differentiable at $p$ with derivative $0$. The Hessian of $f$ at $p$ is the second derivative $d^2 f_p$, a continuous bilinear form on $E$, symmetric when $f$ is $C^2$ at $p$; it is defined at every point but only used at critical points. For a continuous bilinear form $H$ on $E$ the null space is $\{v : H(v, w) = 0 \text{ for all } w\}$, the nullity is its dimension, $H$ is non-degenerate if its null space is $0$, and the index of $H$ is the negative index of inertia of $v \mapsto H(v, v)$. For finite-dimensional $E$ the index is the largest dimension of a subspace on which $H(v, v) < 0$ for all $v \ne 0$, and non-degenerate means nullity $0$; for $E = \mathbb R^n$ and $f$ of class $C^2$ at $p$, it means that the matrix $(\partial^2 f/\partial x^i\partial x^j(p))$ is non-singular.

chips: index: the negative index of inertia
diff: The index is defined as Mathlib's negative index of inertia, and Milnor's definition, the maximal dimension of a negative definite subspace, is a theorem.
Non-degeneracy is defined by a zero null space; Milnor's definition by a non-singular matrix of second partial derivatives is a theorem, for $f$ of class $C^2$ at $p$.
The nullity is a dimension in Mathlib's sense, which is $0$ for an infinite-dimensional null space; the counts are meaningful in finite dimension, where they are used.

items.title: The same notions on a manifold; Morse functions

milnor.label: §2, pp. 4–5
milnor.statement: At a critical point $p$ of $f$ on a manifold $M$, the Hessian is the symmetric bilinear functional $f_{**}$ on $TM_p$ given by $f_{**}(v, w) = \tilde v_p(\tilde w(f))$, where $\tilde v$ and $\tilde w$ are vector fields extending $v$ and $w$; it is symmetric because the Poisson bracket term $[\tilde v, \tilde w]_p(f)$ vanishes at a critical point, and hence independent of both extensions. In local coordinates its matrix in the basis $\partial/\partial x^i|_p$ is $(\partial^2 f/\partial x^i\partial x^j(p))$. The index of $f$ at $p$ is the index of $f_{**}$. Differentiable functions with no degenerate critical points are the subject of Theorem 3.5 (p. 20).

lean.statement: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold without boundary modelled on a real normed space $E$, with no Hausdorff or countability hypothesis, $f : M \to \mathbb R$ and $p \in M$. The point $p$ is a critical point of $f$ if $df_p : T_pM \to \mathbb R$ is $0$; equivalently, $df_p$ is not surjective, which is the companion project's definition. The Hessian $f_{**}$ at $p$ is the second derivative at $\kappa(p)$ of $f \circ \kappa^{-1}$, $\kappa$ the preferred chart at $p$: a bilinear form on $E$, which Mathlib identifies with $T_pM$ through the same chart. The index and the nullity of $f$ at $p$ are those of $f_{**}$, and $p$ is a non-degenerate critical point if it is critical and $f_{**}$ is non-degenerate. A Morse function is a $C^\infty$ function on $M$ all of whose critical points are non-degenerate.

chips: the Hessian read in the preferred chart
diff: Milnor's intrinsic formula $\tilde v_p(\tilde w(f))$, and its independence of the extensions, are not formalized. The formal Hessian is his coordinate expression, the matrix of second partial derivatives (his formula for extensions with constant coefficients), read in the preferred chart; its independence of the chart is proved instead (V1.5).
Mathlib's derivative is $0$ at a point where $f$ is not differentiable, so such a point counts as critical; for smooth $f$ this never matters.

items.title: Independence of the coordinate system

milnor.label: §2, pp. 4–5
milnor.statement: Milnor remarks that non-degeneracy does not depend on the coordinate system, which can be checked directly and will also follow from the intrinsic definition of the Hessian; on p. 5 he computes that the matrix $(\partial^2 f/\partial x^i\partial x^j(p))$ represents $f_{**}$ with respect to the basis $\partial/\partial x^1|_p, \dots, \partial/\partial x^n|_p$.

lean.statement: On normed spaces: if $\psi$ is $C^2$ at $q$, $f$ is $C^2$ at $\psi(q)$ and $df_{\psi(q)} = 0$, then $d^2(f\circ\psi)_q(v, w) = d^2 f_{\psi(q)}(d\psi_q v, d\psi_q w)$. On a manifold $M$ as in V1.4, a smooth coordinate system is a homeomorphism $y$ of an open subset of $M$ onto an open subset of a real normed space $E'$, $C^\infty$ with $C^\infty$ inverse (for $E' = E$ these are exactly the charts of the maximal atlas); let $p$ lie in its domain. If $f$ is differentiable at $p$, then $p$ is critical iff $y(p)$ is a critical point of $f \circ y^{-1}$, that is, for $E' = \mathbb R^n$, iff all the $\partial f/\partial y^i(p)$ vanish. If $f$ is $C^2$ at $p$ and $p$ is critical, the Hessian of $f \circ y^{-1}$ at $y(p)$ is $f_{**}$ composed in both arguments with the derivative of $y^{-1}$ at $y(p)$; hence non-degeneracy, index and nullity are those of $f \circ y^{-1}$ at $y(p)$, and for $E' = \mathbb R^n$, $p$ is non-degenerate iff $\det(\partial^2 f/\partial y^i\partial y^j(p)) \ne 0$.

diff: Milnor works with smooth functions and coordinates in $\mathbb R^n$; the formal statements need $f$ only $C^2$ at $p$ and allow coordinates with values in any real normed space.
Criticality enters exactly once, to kill the first-order term $df(d^2\psi)$ of the chain rule: away from a critical point the matrix of second partial derivatives is not a tensor.

items.title: Functions on a slice submanifold

milnor.label: §6, pp. 35–36
milnor.statement: The book has no separate setting for functions on a submanifold. §2 is written for an abstract manifold, and from §6 on Milnor computes on $M \subset \mathbb R^n$ in local coordinates $u \mapsto \vec x(u)$ without comment. For $L_{\vec p}(\vec q) = \|\vec q - \vec p\|^2$ he notes that $\vec q$ is critical iff $\vec q - \vec p$ is normal to $M$ at $\vec q$ (p. 35), and that at a critical point the second partial derivatives are $2(\partial\vec x/\partial u^i \cdot \partial\vec x/\partial u^j + \partial^2\vec x/\partial u^i\partial u^j \cdot (\vec x - \vec p))$ (p. 36).

lean.statement: Let $V$ be a real normed space and $N \subseteq V$ a slice submanifold modelled on $Z$ in the sense of the companion project: every point of $N$ lies in the domain of a slice chart $\sigma$, a $C^\infty$ diffeomorphism of an open subset of $V$ onto an open subset of $Z \times W$ carrying the points of $N$ in its domain exactly onto $Z \times \{0\}$. $N$ need not be closed; it is a smooth manifold modelled on $Z$, with the parametrizations $x(z) = \sigma^{-1}(z, 0)$. Let $T_qN \subseteq V$ be the range of the derivative of the inclusion, $F : V \to \mathbb R$, and $q \in N$ in the domain of $\sigma$. If $F$ is differentiable at $q$, then $q$ is a critical point of $F|N$ iff $\sigma(q)_1$ is a critical point of $F \circ x$, iff $dF_q$ vanishes on $T_qN$, and, for a complete inner product space $V$, iff $\nabla F(q) \perp T_qN$. If $F$ is $C^2$ at a critical point $q$ of $f = F|N$, the Hessian of $F \circ x$ at $\sigma(q)_1$ is the Hessian $f_{**}$ of V1.4 composed with the derivative of the parametrization, so non-degeneracy, index and nullity of $F|N$ at $q$ are those of $F \circ x$. For $V$ an inner product space and $L_p(y) = \|y - p\|^2$: $q$ is a critical point of $L_p|N$ iff $q - p \perp T_qN$; for any $x$ of class $C^2$ at $u$, the second derivative of $L_p \circ x$ at $u$ is $2(\langle \partial x/\partial v, \partial x/\partial w\rangle + \langle \partial^2 x/\partial v\,\partial w, x(u) - p\rangle)$; and at a critical point the index and the nullity of $L_p|N$ are those of this form.

diff: No counterpart as a statement: these identifications are what Milnor uses silently whenever he computes on a submanifold in a parametrization, and every later statement about a submanifold of Euclidean space rests on them.

The Hessian of $F \circ x$ is not the restriction of the ambient Hessian of $F$: the chain rule adds $dF_q(\partial^2 x/\partial v\,\partial w)$, which does not vanish at a critical point of $F|N$ and which, for $L_p$, is the second-fundamental-form term of Milnor's formula.

items.title: Lemma 2.1 (Hadamard)

milnor.label: §2, Lemma 2.1
milnor.statement: A $C^\infty$ function $f$ on a convex neighbourhood $V$ of $0$ in $\mathbb R^n$ with $f(0) = 0$ can be written $f(x) = \sum_i x_i g_i(x)$, the $g_i$ being $C^\infty$ on $V$ with $g_i(0) = \partial f/\partial x_i(0)$. The proof writes $f(x)$ as $\int_0^1 \frac{d}{dt} f(tx)\,dt$ and takes $g_i(x) = \int_0^1 \partial f/\partial x_i(tx)\,dt$.

lean.statement: Let $V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and convex with $0 \in V$, and $f$ smooth on $V$ with $f(0) = 0$. Then $f(x) = \sum_i x_i g_i(x)$ on $V$ for functions $g_i$ smooth on $V$ with $g_i(0) = \partial f/\partial x_i(0)$. More generally, let $V$ be open and star-shaped about $0$ in a real normed space $E$ and $f$ smooth on $V$, with values in a complete normed space and $f(0) = 0$. Then $f(x) = L(x)\,x$ on $V$ for a family of linear maps $L$ smooth on $V$ with $L(0) = df_0$; and if moreover $df_0 = 0$, then $f(x) = B(x)(x, x)$ on $V$ for a family of bilinear maps $B$ smooth on $V$, with $B(x)$ symmetric for each $x \in V$ and $B(0) = \frac12 d^2 f_0$. Along the way: if $h$ is $C^n$ on an open $U \subseteq E \times \mathbb R$ containing $V \times [0, 1]$, $V$ open, then $x \mapsto \int_0^1 h(x, t)\,dt$ is $C^n$ on $V$.

diff: Convexity is weakened to star-shapedness, $\mathbb R^n$ to any real normed space, and the values may lie in any complete normed space; $V$ must be open, which the book leaves implicit.
The smoothness of the $g_i$, which Milnor does not argue, is differentiation under the integral sign on an open set, proved here.

On p. 7 Milnor applies the lemma twice, symmetrizes, and asserts without proof that the coefficients at $0$ are $\frac12\,\partial^2 f/\partial x^i\partial x^j(0)$. That second-order form is proved directly, by Taylor's formula with integral remainder, with $B(x) = \int_0^1 (1 - t)\,d^2 f_{tx}\,dt$.

items.title: Lemma 2.2 (the lemma of Morse)

milnor.label: §2, Lemma 2.2
milnor.statement: Near a non-degenerate critical point $p$ of $f$ there are local coordinates $(y^1, \dots, y^n)$, all vanishing at $p$, on a neighbourhood $U$ of $p$, in which $f = f(p) - (y^1)^2 - \dots - (y^\lambda)^2 + (y^{\lambda+1})^2 + \dots + (y^n)^2$ on all of $U$, $\lambda$ being the index of $f$ at $p$. The proof writes $f = \sum x_ix_jh_{ij}$ by Lemma 2.1 and completes one square at a time by induction, after a linear change of the last $n - r + 1$ coordinates making $H_{rr}(0) \ne 0$.

lean.statement: Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real normed space, $n = \dim E$, $f$ smooth on an open set $U \ni p$, and $p$ a critical point at which $d^2 f_p$ is non-degenerate, of index $\lambda$. Then there is a homeomorphism $y$ of an open neighbourhood $U' \subseteq U$ of $p$ onto an open subset of $\mathbb R^n$, $C^\infty$ with $C^\infty$ inverse, such that $y(p) = 0$ and $f = f(p) - (y^1)^2 - \dots - (y^\lambda)^2 + (y^{\lambda+1})^2 + \dots + (y^n)^2$ throughout $U'$. In coordinate-free form, there is such a $\varphi$ onto an open subset of $E$ with $\varphi(p) = 0$, $d\varphi_p = \mathrm{id}$ and $f = f(p) + \frac12 d^2 f_p(\varphi, \varphi)$ on its domain. On a smooth manifold without boundary modelled on $E$, with no Hausdorff hypothesis, for $f$ smooth on an open $U \ni p$ and $p$ a non-degenerate critical point of index $\lambda$: there is a smooth coordinate system $y$ with values in $\mathbb R^n$, domain an open neighbourhood of $p$ inside $U$, $y(p) = 0$ and the same normal form on its domain; and there is a chart $\varphi$ of the maximal atlas with domain inside $U$, $\varphi(p) = 0$ and $f = f(p) + \frac12 f_{**}(\varphi, \varphi)$.

diff: Milnor's $f$ is smooth on $M$; the formal $f$ need only be smooth on an open set containing $p$, and on a manifold no Hausdorff or countability hypothesis enters.

The proof is not Milnor's induction, which completes one square at a time and does not justify the linear change making $H_{rr}(0) \ne 0$. One application of the inverse function theorem, to a map on linear operators whose derivative at the identity is $H \mapsto 2B_0(H\cdot, \cdot)$, gives linear maps $C(x)$, smooth in $x$, with $C(0) = \mathrm{id}$ and $f(p + x) = f(p) + \frac12 d^2 f_p(C(x)x, C(x)x)$.
Sylvester's law of inertia, from Mathlib, then diagonalizes $\frac12 d^2 f_p$ with the negative squares first.

items.title: The index is forced by the normal form

milnor.label: §2, proof of Lemma 2.2
milnor.statement: The proof of Lemma 2.2 begins by showing that if $f(q) = f(p) - (z^1(q))^2 - \dots - (z^\lambda(q))^2 + (z^{\lambda+1}(q))^2 + \dots + (z^n(q))^2$ in some coordinate system $z$ around $p$, then $\lambda$ must be the index of $f$ at $p$: the matrix of $f_{**}$ in the basis $\partial/\partial z^i|_p$ is diagonal with $\lambda$ entries $-2$ and $n - \lambda$ entries $2$, so $f_{**}$ is negative definite on a subspace of dimension $\lambda$ and positive definite on one of dimension $n - \lambda$, and no larger negative definite subspace exists.

lean.statement: On a real normed space $E$ with $n = \dim E$: if $f$ is $C^2$ at a critical point $p$ and $z$ is a homeomorphism of an open neighbourhood of $p$ onto an open subset of $\mathbb R^n$, $C^\infty$ with $C^\infty$ inverse, with $z(p) = 0$ and $f = f(p) - \sum_{i \le k}(z^i)^2 + \sum_{i > k}(z^i)^2$ on its domain, $k \le n$, then $k$ is the index of $f$ at $p$. On a manifold as in V1.4, with no hypothesis on $f$: if $z$ is a smooth coordinate system around $p$ with values in $\mathbb R^n$, $z(p) = 0$, $k \le n$, and $f$ has this form on its domain, then $p$ is a non-degenerate critical point of $f$ of index $k$.

diff: On a manifold the formal statement assumes nothing about $f$ beyond the normal form, and concludes that $p$ is a non-degenerate critical point, of index $k$.
The proof is Milnor's, with the independence of coordinates (V1.5) that he uses without comment.

items.title: Corollary 2.3: non-degenerate critical points are isolated

milnor.label: §2, Corollary 2.3
milnor.statement: A non-degenerate critical point is isolated: no other critical point comes arbitrarily close to it. The corollary is stated directly after the proof of Lemma 2.2, with no proof of its own.

lean.statement: Let $E$ be finite-dimensional. If $f : E \to \mathbb R$ is $C^2$ at $p$ and $p$ is a non-degenerate critical point, then $p$ has a neighbourhood in which it is the only critical point of $f$. The same holds on a manifold without boundary modelled on $E$, for $f$ of class $C^2$ at $p$.

chips: not through the lemma of Morse
diff: Milnor's functions are smooth; the formal statement needs only $C^2$ at the point, where the lemma of Morse is not available.
The proof does not use the normal form: $x \mapsto df_x$ has the injective derivative $d^2 f_p$ at $p$, so it does not vanish at the points $x \ne p$ near $p$.

items.title: Finitely many critical points in a compact set

milnor.label: §3, proof of Theorem 3.5
milnor.statement: The book does not state this. In the proof of Theorem 3.5 Milnor lists the critical values $c_1 < c_2 < c_3 < \dots$ and says that the sequence has no cluster point since each $M^a$ is compact, which needs each compact set to contain only finitely many critical points, a consequence of Corollary 2.3 left to the reader.

lean.statement: Let $M$ be as in V1.4. The critical set of a $C^1$ function on $M$ is closed. If $E$ is finite-dimensional and $f$ is $C^2$ with all its critical points non-degenerate, the critical points of $f$ form a discrete set and every compact set contains only finitely many of them; in particular a Morse function on a compact $M$ has finitely many critical points. Hausdorffness is not needed.

diff: A consequence of Corollary 2.3 that the book uses without stating. Theorem 3.5, the Morse inequalities and the Euler characteristic formula all count critical points, and this is what makes the counts finite.

items.title: Examples of degenerate critical points

milnor.label: §2, pp. 8–9
milnor.statement: Milnor pictures five degenerate critical points: (a) $f(x) = x^3$ at the origin; (b) $e^{-1/x^2}\sin^2(1/x)$, whose origin is a degenerate and non-isolated critical point; (c) the monkey saddle $x^3 - 3xy^2$, the real part of $(x + iy)^3$, at $(0, 0)$; (d) $f(x, y) = x^2$, whose critical points, all degenerate, form the $x$ axis, a submanifold of $\mathbb R^2$; (e) $x^2y^2$, whose degenerate critical points fill the union of the $x$ and $y$ axes, not even a submanifold of $\mathbb R^2$.

lean.statement: (a) The only critical point of $x^3$ on $\mathbb R$ is $0$, where the Hessian is $0$, so it is degenerate. (c) The only critical point of $x^3 - 3xy^2$ on $\mathbb R^2$ is the origin, where the Hessian is $0$. (d) The critical points of $x^2$ on $\mathbb R^2$ are the points of the line $x = 0$, and all are degenerate. (e) The critical points of $x^2y^2$ are the points of the two coordinate axes, and all are degenerate. In (d) and (e) degeneracy is the contrapositive of Corollary 2.3: a critical point that is a limit of other critical points, of a function $C^2$ there, is degenerate.

diff: In (d) the book says the critical set is the $x$ axis; since $\partial f/\partial x = 2x$ and $\partial f/\partial y = 0$, it is the $y$ axis. The formalization noticed this.
In (a) and (c) the formal statements add that the origin is the only critical point.
Example (b) is not formalized: its smoothness at $0$ needs the flatness of $e^{-1/x^2}$ against the growth of the derivatives of $\sin^2(1/x)$. Nor are the submanifold claims of (d) and (e).

items.title: One-parameter groups of diffeomorphisms

milnor.label: §2, pp. 9–10
milnor.statement: Milnor's 1-parameter group of diffeomorphisms of $M$ is a $C^\infty$ map $\varphi : \mathbb R \times M \to M$ whose maps $\varphi_t$ are diffeomorphisms of $M$ with $\varphi_{t+s} = \varphi_t \circ \varphi_s$. It determines the vector field $X_q(f) = \lim_{h \to 0} (f(\varphi_h(q)) - f(q))/h$, which is said to generate $\varphi$, and each orbit $t \mapsto \varphi_t(q)$ solves $d\varphi_t(q)/dt = X_{\varphi_t(q)}$ with $\varphi_0(q) = q$.

lean.statement: On a real normed space $E$, a one-parameter group of diffeomorphisms is a map $\varphi : \mathbb R \times E \to E$, $C^\infty$ in $(t, x)$, such that each $\varphi_t$ is a $C^\infty$ diffeomorphism of $E$ and $\varphi_{t+s} = \varphi_t\circ\varphi_s$ for all $t$, $s$. A vector field $X : E \to E$ generates $\varphi$ if for every $x$ the curve $h \mapsto \varphi_h(x)$ has derivative $X(x)$ at $h = 0$. Then $\varphi_0 = \mathrm{id}$, and if $X$ generates $\varphi$, every orbit $t \mapsto \varphi_t(x)$ is an integral curve of $X$.

diff: Only for $M = E$, where a tangent vector is a vector and Milnor's limit defining $X_q(f)$ becomes the derivative of $h \mapsto \varphi_h(q)$.
That $\varphi_0 = \mathrm{id}$, used on p. 10 as the initial condition, follows from the group law because $\varphi_0$ is injective.

items.title: Global flows, and smooth dependence on the initial point

milnor.label: §2, pp. 10–11
milnor.statement: In the proof of Lemma 2.4 Milnor quotes as well known, citing Graves, that the equation $d\varphi_t(q)/dt = X_{\varphi_t(q)}$, $\varphi_0(q) = q$, has locally a unique solution which depends smoothly on the initial conditions. Covering the compact support $K$ by finitely many such neighbourhoods gives $\epsilon_0 > 0$ and solutions for $|t| < \epsilon_0$, smooth in both variables; for larger $t$ he iterates $\varphi_{\epsilon_0/2}$, and says it is not difficult to verify that the result is well defined, smooth, and satisfies $\varphi_{t+s} = \varphi_t\circ\varphi_s$.

lean.statement: Let $E$ be a complete real normed space and $X : E \to E$ bounded and globally Lipschitz, for instance $C^1$ with compact support. Through every point there is an integral curve of $X$ defined on all of $\mathbb R$, every integral curve is a flow line, and the flow satisfies $\varphi_0 = \mathrm{id}$ and $\varphi_{s+t} = \varphi_s\circ\varphi_t$, is jointly continuous in $(t, x)$, and each $\varphi_t$ is a homeomorphism with inverse $\varphi_{-t}$. If $X$ is $C^n$, $1 \le n \le \infty$, with compact support, then $(t, x) \mapsto \varphi_t(x)$ is $C^n$ on $\mathbb R \times E$ and each $\varphi_t$ is a $C^n$ diffeomorphism.

diff: Milnor quotes the local theory and iterates it; the formal statements are global, for bounded Lipschitz or compactly supported fields on a Banach space, so no consistency of the splitting of $t$ into multiples of $\epsilon_0/2$ has to be checked.

Smooth dependence on the initial point, which Mathlib lacks, is proved rather than quoted: on $[0, 1]$ the flow line through $x$ solves $\Psi(\gamma) = x$ in the Banach space $C([0, 1], E)$, with $\Psi(\gamma) = \gamma - \int_0^{\cdot} X(\gamma)$ a homeomorphism with everywhere invertible derivative for a small Lipschitz constant, so the time-one map is as smooth as $X$.
Only vector spaces are treated; on submanifolds of $\mathbb R^K$ Chapter 2 uses the ambient flow of a field tangent to the submanifold instead.

items.title: Lemma 2.4: compactly supported fields generate flows

milnor.label: §2, Lemma 2.4
milnor.statement: If a smooth vector field on $M$ vanishes outside some compact set $K \subset M$, then it generates exactly one 1-parameter group of diffeomorphisms of $M$.
milnor.note: The Remark on p. 11 shows that compact support cannot be omitted: $d/dt$ on the open interval $(0, 1)$ generates no 1-parameter group.

lean.statement: Let $E$ be a complete real normed space and $X : E \to E$ a $C^\infty$ vector field which vanishes outside a compact set. Then there is exactly one one-parameter group of diffeomorphisms of $E$ (V1.13) generated by $X$, namely its flow (V1.14).

diff: Only for $M = E$. If $E$ is infinite-dimensional the hypothesis forces $X = 0$, so the content is the case $E = \mathbb R^n$; on a manifold that is not a vector space the lemma is not formalized.
The uniqueness, implicit in the book, holds among all one-parameter groups generated by $X$, because uniqueness of integral curves is global in time; on a manifold it would need $M$ Hausdorff.

items.title: Sublevel sets and strong deformation retracts

milnor.label: §3, pp. 12–13
milnor.statement: Throughout §3, $M^a = f^{-1}(-\infty, a] = \{p \in M : f(p) \le a\}$. Milnor uses “deformation retract” without a definition: in the proof of Theorem 3.1 he builds a 1-parameter family of maps $r_t : M^b \to M^b$ with $r_0$ the identity and $r_1$ a retraction onto $M^a$, concludes that $M^a$ is a deformation retract of $M^b$, and so that the inclusion is a homotopy equivalence.

lean.statement: For a real function $f$ on a set and $c \in \mathbb R$, $M^c = \{x : f(x) \le c\}$. A subset $A$ of a topological space $X$ is a strong deformation retract of $X$ if there are a continuous map $r : X \to X$ with values in $A$ and a homotopy $r_t$, $0 \le t \le 1$, from $r_0 = \mathrm{id}_X$ to $r_1 = r$ with $r_t(a) = a$ for all $t$ and all $a \in A$. If $A \subseteq B$ are subsets of a space and $A$ is a strong deformation retract of $B$, the inclusion $A \to B$ is a homotopy equivalence, with $r_1$ as homotopy inverse.

diff: Every deformation Milnor constructs fixes the smaller set at all times, and every formal statement asserts this strong form, which implies the weaker ones; the strong form is also what the homology of pairs needs in Chapter 3 (V3.33).

items.title: Theorem 3.1 on a Euclidean space

milnor.label: §3, Theorem 3.1
milnor.statement: For a smooth real function $f$ on a manifold $M$ and $a < b$, if the set $f^{-1}[a, b]$ of points where $a \le f \le b$ is compact and free of critical points of $f$, then $M^a$ and $M^b$ are diffeomorphic; moreover $M^a$ is a deformation retract of $M^b$, so the inclusion $M^a \to M^b$ is a homotopy equivalence. The proof chooses a Riemannian metric, takes $\rho$ equal to $1/\langle \mathrm{grad} f, \mathrm{grad} f\rangle$ on $f^{-1}[a, b]$ and vanishing outside a compact neighbourhood of it, and pushes $M^b$ down to $M^a$ along the flow $\varphi_t$ of $\rho\,\mathrm{grad} f$; then $\varphi_{b-a}$ carries $M^a$ diffeomorphically onto $M^b$.

lean.statement: Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space, $f : E \to \mathbb R$ of class $C^\infty$, $a \le b$, and suppose that $f^{-1}[a, b]$ is compact and contains no critical point of $f$. Then there is a $C^\infty$ diffeomorphism $\Phi$ of $E$ with $\Phi(M^a) = M^b$; $M^a$ is a strong deformation retract of $M^b$; the inclusion $M^a \to M^b$ is a homotopy equivalence; and $M^a$ and $M^b$ are homeomorphic.

diff: Only on $\mathbb R^n$, whose inner product plays the part of Milnor's Riemannian metric; submanifolds of Euclidean space are V2.3, compact manifolds V2.4, and non-compact abstract manifolds are not covered.
“$M^a$ is diffeomorphic to $M^b$” is formalized as what the proof gives, a diffeomorphism of the whole space carrying $M^a$ onto $M^b$, Milnor's $\varphi_{b-a}$.

The cut-off $\rho$ is constructed. Milnor's “clearly” needs that each trajectory crosses the slab $f^{-1}[a, b]$ once, at unit speed, which is proved for any continuous flow along which $f$ has derivative $1$ in the slab; his two-case $r_t$ becomes the single continuous formula $r_t(q) = \varphi_{t\min(0,\, a - f(q))}(q)$.

items.title: Theorem 3.1 on a submanifold of Euclidean space

milnor.label: §3, Theorem 3.1
milnor.statement: For a smooth real function $f$ on a manifold $M$ and $a < b$, if $f^{-1}[a, b]$ is compact and contains no critical points of $f$, then $M^a$ is diffeomorphic to $M^b$, and $M^a$ is a deformation retract of $M^b$, so that the inclusion is a homotopy equivalence.

lean.statement: Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real normed space, $N \subseteq V$ a slice submanifold modelled on a finite-dimensional $Z$ (V1.6; $N$ need not be closed), $F : V \to \mathbb R$ of class $C^\infty$ and $f = F|N$. Let $a \le b$, and suppose that $f^{-1}[a, b] \subseteq N$ is compact and contains no critical point of $f$, as a function on the manifold $N$. Then there is a $C^\infty$ diffeomorphism $\Phi$ of $N$ with $\Phi(N^a) = N^b$, $N^a$ is a strong deformation retract of $N^b$, and the inclusion $N^a \to N^b$ is a homotopy equivalence. When $N$ is compact, the compactness of $f^{-1}[a, b]$ need not be assumed.

diff: $M$ is a submanifold of a Euclidean space, Hausdorff and second countable as a subset, and $f$ must be the restriction of a smooth function on the ambient space.

No metric is used. Slice charts and bump functions give a smooth field $Y$ on $V$, tangent to $N$ along $N$, with $dF(Y) > 0$ on $f^{-1}[a, b]$; the field $\rho Y$, with $\rho\,dF(Y) = 1$ there, replaces $\rho\,\mathrm{grad} f$, and its flow on $V$ preserves $N$.

items.title: Theorem 3.1 on a compact manifold

milnor.label: §3, Theorem 3.1
milnor.statement: For a smooth real function $f$ on a manifold $M$ and $a < b$, if $f^{-1}[a, b]$ is compact and contains no critical points of $f$, then $M^a$ is diffeomorphic to $M^b$, and $M^a$ is a deformation retract of $M^b$, so that the inclusion is a homotopy equivalence.

lean.statement: Let $M$ be a compact Hausdorff smooth manifold without boundary modelled on a finite-dimensional real normed space, $f : M \to \mathbb R$ of class $C^\infty$, $a \le b$, and suppose that $f^{-1}[a, b]$ contains no critical point of $f$. Then a $C^\infty$ diffeomorphism of $M$ carries $M^a$ onto $M^b$, $M^a$ is a strong deformation retract of $M^b$, and the inclusion $M^a \to M^b$ is a homotopy equivalence.

diff: Only compact $M$, Hausdorff as Milnor's manifolds tacitly are. Mathlib's Whitney embedding for compact manifolds makes $M$ diffeomorphic to a compact slice submanifold $N \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}$, on which $f$ is the restriction of a smooth function on $\mathbb R^{K+1}$, so V2.3 applies, and its conclusions are carried back to $M$.
For a non-compact $M$ with $f^{-1}[a, b]$ compact the transfer would need a closed embedding into Euclidean space, which Mathlib does not have.

items.title: Compactness cannot be omitted

milnor.label: §3, Remark after Theorem 3.1
milnor.statement: The compactness of $f^{-1}[a, b]$ is essential. Diagram 3 pictures a surface with a point $p$ between the levels $a$ and $b$ removed, where, Milnor says, $M^a$ is clearly not a deformation retract of $M^b$.
milnor.note: The Remark is unnumbered; Remark 3.3 is the statement of p. 19.

lean.statement: Let $M = \mathbb C \setminus \{i\}$, $f(z) = |z|^2$ on $M$, $a = \frac14$ and $b = 4$. No $z \in \mathbb C$ with $\frac14 \le |z|^2 \le 4$ is a critical point of $|z|^2$, but $f^{-1}[\frac14, 4] \subseteq M$ is not compact; $M^{1/4}$, the closed disc of radius $\frac12$, and $M^4$, the closed disc of radius $2$ without $i$, are not homotopy equivalent, so $M^{1/4}$ is not a strong deformation retract of $M^4$, and the two are not homeomorphic. With $i$ put back, Theorem 3.1 applies: in $\mathbb C$ the disc of radius $\frac12$ is a strong deformation retract of the disc of radius $2$.

diff: The pictured surface is replaced by the punctured plane, and the conclusion is the stronger one that the two sublevel sets are not even homotopy equivalent. $M$ is open in $\mathbb C$, so the critical points of $f$ are those of $|z|^2$.
The “clearly” is the non-contractibility of the punctured disc, proved by lifting a null-homotopy of $z \mapsto z - i$ through the covering $\exp : \mathbb C \to \mathbb C \setminus \{0\}$.

items.title: Theorem 3.2 on a Euclidean space

milnor.label: §3, Theorem 3.2
milnor.statement: Take a smooth $f : M \to \mathbb R$ and a non-degenerate critical point $p$ of index $\lambda$, with $c = f(p)$, and assume that for some $\epsilon > 0$ the set $f^{-1}[c - \epsilon, c + \epsilon]$ is compact with $p$ its only critical point. Then, once $\epsilon$ is small enough, $M^{c+\epsilon}$ is homotopy equivalent to $M^{c-\epsilon}$ with a $\lambda$-cell attached. In the proof a function $\mu$ modifies $f$ near $p$ to a smooth $F$ with $F^{-1}(-\infty, c - \epsilon] = M^{c-\epsilon} \cup H$, and four Assertions show that $M^{c-\epsilon} \cup e^\lambda$ is a deformation retract of $M^{c+\epsilon}$.
milnor.note: The scan prints “a k-cell” and renders the index as “A”; both are read as $\lambda$, as the proof requires.

lean.statement: Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space, $f : E \to \mathbb R$ of class $C^\infty$, $p$ a critical point at which $d^2 f_p$ is non-degenerate, $\lambda$ its index and $c = f(p)$, and suppose that for some $\epsilon_0 > 0$ the set $f^{-1}[c - \epsilon_0, c + \epsilon_0]$ is compact and contains no critical point other than $p$. Then there is $\epsilon_1 > 0$ such that for every $\epsilon$ with $0 < \epsilon \le \epsilon_1$ there is a map $\chi$ from the closed unit ball $D^\lambda$ of $\mathbb R^\lambda$ to $E$, continuous and injective on $D^\lambda$, with $\chi(z) \in M^{c-\epsilon}$ exactly when $|z| = 1$ and $\chi(D^\lambda) \subseteq M^{c+\epsilon}$, such that $M^{c-\epsilon} \cup \chi(D^\lambda)$ is a strong deformation retract of $M^{c+\epsilon}$. Hence the inclusion of $M^{c-\epsilon} \cup \chi(D^\lambda)$ in $M^{c+\epsilon}$ is a homotopy equivalence, and there is an injective continuous $\varphi : S^{\lambda-1} \to M^{c-\epsilon}$ such that $M^{c+\epsilon}$ is homotopy equivalent to $M^{c-\epsilon} \cup_\varphi e^\lambda$.

diff: Only on $\mathbb R^n$ with an inner product; on submanifolds of Euclidean space it is V2.8, and on abstract manifolds it is not formalized.

The conclusion is stronger than a homotopy type: a strong deformation retraction of $M^{c+\epsilon}$ onto $M^{c-\epsilon}$ together with an embedded cell meeting it exactly in its boundary sphere, which is what the proof produces. “For all sufficiently small $\epsilon$” is read as “for every $\epsilon$ in some $(0, \epsilon_1]$”.

Milnor's $\mu$ ($C^\infty$, $\mu(0) > \epsilon$, $\mu = 0$ on $[2\epsilon, \infty)$, $-1 < \mu' \le 0$), whose existence he does not show, is $\mu(r) = \frac34\int_r^{2\epsilon}\beta$ for a smooth plateau $\beta$. Assertion 2 uses $\partial F/\partial\eta \ge 1$; the scan shows $> 1$, which fails where $\mu' = 0$.

The three cases of $r_t$ in Assertion 4 are one formula, $(x, y) \mapsto (x, \sigma_t(x, y)\,y)$, continuous on the whole patch; it pastes with the identity because it moves only points of the compact ellipsoid $\xi + 2\eta \le 2\epsilon$ and keeps them there.

items.title: A cell meeting a closed set in its boundary is attached to it

milnor.label: §3, proof of Theorem 3.2
milnor.statement: With $e^\lambda$ the set of points of the coordinate patch with $(u^1)^2 + \dots + (u^\lambda)^2 \le \epsilon$ and $u^{\lambda+1} = \dots = u^n = 0$, Milnor notes that $e^\lambda \cap M^{c-\epsilon}$ is precisely the boundary $\dot e^\lambda$, so that $e^\lambda$ is attached to $M^{c-\epsilon}$ as required. That the subspace $M^{c-\epsilon} \cup e^\lambda$ is then the space $M^{c-\epsilon} \cup_\varphi e^\lambda$ defined in §1 is not argued.

lean.statement: Let $A$ be a closed subset of a Hausdorff space $M$ and $\chi : \mathbb R^n \to M$ continuous and injective on $D^n$, with $\chi(z) \in A$ exactly when $|z| = 1$, for $z \in D^n$. Then the subspace $A \cup \chi(D^n)$ of $M$ is the pushout of $\varphi = \chi|S^{n-1} : S^{n-1} \to A$ and the inclusion $S^{n-1} \to D^n$, that is, $A \cup_\varphi e^n$ (V1.2), and $\varphi$ is injective. Consequently, if $f : M \to \mathbb R$ is continuous, $a \le b$, $\chi$ is as above for $A = M^a$, $\chi(D^n) \subseteq M^b$, and $M^a \cup \chi(D^n)$ is a strong deformation retract of $M^b$, then $M^b$ is homotopy equivalent to $M^a \cup_\varphi e^n$.

chips: the subspace is the adjunction space
diff: The identification of the subspace with the adjunction space is a lemma that Milnor does not state (Lemma D of the exposition). It needs $M$ Hausdorff and $A$ closed, so that the cell is closed and $\chi$ is a homeomorphism onto it.
The proof checks the universal property of the pushout directly, by the pasting lemma for the closed cover of $A \cup \chi(D^n)$ by $A$ and $\chi(D^n)$.

items.title: Theorem 3.2 in a Morse patch, and on a submanifold

milnor.label: §3, Theorem 3.2
milnor.statement: For a non-degenerate critical point $p$ of index $\lambda$, $c = f(p)$, with $f^{-1}[c - \epsilon, c + \epsilon]$ compact and free of other critical points, $M^{c+\epsilon}$ has the homotopy type of $M^{c-\epsilon}$ with a $\lambda$-cell attached, for all sufficiently small $\epsilon$. The proof works in a coordinate neighbourhood $U$ of $p$ in which $f = c - \xi + \eta$; Assertion 3, that $F^{-1}(-\infty, c - \epsilon]$ is a deformation retract of $M^{c+\epsilon}$, is Theorem 3.1 applied to $F$, and the rest of the argument takes place in the patch.

lean.statement: (i) The topological half, in any Hausdorff space $M$. Let $X$, $Y$ be finite-dimensional real inner product spaces with $\dim X = \lambda$, $f : M \to \mathbb R$, $p \in M$, and $\varphi$ a homeomorphism of an open neighbourhood of $p$ onto an open subset of $X \times Y$ with $\varphi(p) = 0$, $f = f(p) - |x|^2 + |y|^2$ on its domain, and image containing the ball $|x|^2 + |y|^2 \le 2\epsilon$, $\epsilon > 0$. Let $\mu$ satisfy Milnor's four conditions, and let $F = f - \mu(|x|^2 + 2|y|^2)$ on the domain of $\varphi$ and $F = f$ elsewhere. If $F^{-1}(-\infty, f(p) - \epsilon]$ is a strong deformation retract of $M^{f(p)+\epsilon}$, the conclusion of V2.6 about the cell holds in $M$ for this $\epsilon$. (ii) Let $V$, $Z$ be finite-dimensional, $N \subseteq V$ a slice submanifold modelled on $Z$, $F : V \to \mathbb R$ of class $C^\infty$, $f = F|N$, $p \in N$ a non-degenerate critical point of $f$ of index $\lambda$, $c = f(p)$, and suppose that for some $\epsilon_0 > 0$ the set $f^{-1}[c - \epsilon_0, c + \epsilon_0]$ is compact and contains no critical point of $f$ other than $p$. Then there is $\epsilon_1 > 0$ such that for every $\epsilon \in (0, \epsilon_1]$ there is a cell $\chi(D^\lambda) \subseteq N^{c+\epsilon}$, $\chi$ continuous and injective on $D^\lambda$, meeting $N^{c-\epsilon}$ exactly in $\chi(S^{\lambda-1})$, with $N^{c-\epsilon} \cup \chi(D^\lambda)$ a strong deformation retract of $N^{c+\epsilon}$; and $N^{c+\epsilon}$ is homotopy equivalent to $N^{c-\epsilon} \cup_\varphi e^\lambda$ for an injective $\varphi$.

chips: the patch half in any Hausdorff space
diff: On a manifold, Theorem 3.2 is proved for $f = F|N$ on a slice submanifold of a Euclidean space; abstract manifolds, compact or not, are not covered.

Hausdorffness, used silently by Milnor, is needed for the ellipsoid $\xi + 2\eta \le 2\epsilon$ to be closed in $M$, for the smoothness of $F$ and the continuity of $r_t$, and for the cell to be attached (V2.7); it is automatic for $N \subseteq V$.

The Morse coordinates are the lemma of Morse on the manifold $N$, taken inside one slice chart. Assertion 3 is V2.3 applied to $F$, which first requires extending $F$ to a smooth function on $V$, a step that Milnor's intrinsic Theorem 3.1 does not need.

items.title: Remark 3.3: several critical points on one level

milnor.label: §3, Remark 3.3
milnor.statement: When the level $f^{-1}(c)$ contains $k$ non-degenerate critical points $p_1, \dots, p_k$, of indices $\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k$, the same kind of proof gives that $M^{c+\epsilon}$ is homotopy equivalent to $M^{c-\epsilon} \cup e^{\lambda_1} \cup \dots \cup e^{\lambda_k}$.

lean.statement: Let $N \subseteq V$, $F$ and $f = F|N$ be as in V2.8 (ii), $S$ a finite set of non-degenerate critical points of $f$, all with value $c$, and suppose that for some $\epsilon_0 > 0$ the set $f^{-1}[c - \epsilon_0, c + \epsilon_0]$ is compact and all its critical points lie in $S$. Then there is $\epsilon_1 > 0$ such that for every $\epsilon \in (0, \epsilon_1]$ there are cells $e_p = \chi_p(D^{\lambda_p})$, $p \in S$, $\lambda_p$ the index of $p$, each $\chi_p$ continuous and injective on $D^{\lambda_p}$, meeting $N^{c-\epsilon}$ exactly in $\chi_p(S^{\lambda_p - 1})$, contained in $N^{c+\epsilon}$ and pairwise disjoint, such that $N^{c-\epsilon} \cup \bigcup_{p \in S} e_p$ is a strong deformation retract of $N^{c+\epsilon}$.

chips: cells attached one at a time
diff: Only on slice submanifolds, for $f$ the restriction of an ambient smooth function.

The hypotheses left to “a similar proof” are written out: a compact $f^{-1}[c - \epsilon_0, c + \epsilon_0]$ whose critical points all lie on the level, and Morse charts with pairwise disjoint domains, which needs Hausdorffness.
That the union is $N^{c-\epsilon}$ with the cells attached one at a time is part of the proof of Theorem 3.5 (V2.12).

items.title: Remark 3.4: the critical level

milnor.label: §3, Remark 3.4
milnor.statement: With a small change in the proof of 3.2, $M^c$ too is a deformation retract of $M^{c+\epsilon}$, being one of $F^{-1}(-\infty, c]$, which is one of $M^{c+\epsilon}$ (Diagram 8). Together with 3.2, Milnor says, one sees easily that $M^{c-\epsilon} \cup e^\lambda$ is a deformation retract of $M^c$.
milnor.note: The scan prints it as “Remark 2.4”; p. 24 cites it as Remark 3.4.

lean.statement: Under the hypotheses of V2.6, $E$ a finite-dimensional real inner product space, there is $\epsilon_1 > 0$ such that for every $\epsilon \in (0, \epsilon_1]$: $M^c$ is a strong deformation retract of $M^{c+\epsilon}$; and there is a map $\chi$ from $D^\lambda$ to $E$, continuous and injective on $D^\lambda$, with $\chi(z) \in M^{c-\epsilon}$ exactly when $|z| = 1$, such that the part of $M^{c-\epsilon} \cup \chi(D^\lambda)$ lying in $M^c$ is a strong deformation retract of $M^c$.

diff: Only on $\mathbb R^n$ with an inner product, not on submanifolds; so the Remark of p. 24 at a critical value is not reached there (V2.15).

The “easily” uses a lemma Milnor does not state: if $A \subseteq B \subseteq C$ and both $A$ and $B$ are strong deformation retracts of $C$, then $A$ is a strong deformation retract of $B$; only the retraction of $C$ onto $B$ is used.
The whole cell lies in $M^c$, since $f = c - \epsilon|z|^2$ on it; the proof uses this, but the formal statement does not record it.

items.title: Iterated adjunction spaces in place of CW-complexes

milnor.label: §3, Theorem 3.5
milnor.statement: Theorem 3.5 asserts the homotopy type of a CW-complex, for whose definition Milnor refers to J. H. C. Whitehead. In the proof (p. 23) each attaching map is replaced, by cellular approximation, by a map into the $(\lambda_j - 1)$-skeleton, so that attaching the new cells to a CW-complex gives a CW-complex again.

lean.statement: A space $K$ is an iterated adjunction space with cells $(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k)$ if it is obtained from the empty space by attaching a $\lambda_1$-cell, then a $\lambda_2$-cell, and so on, each along an arbitrary continuous map of its boundary sphere into the space built so far (V1.2). A space $X$ has the homotopy type of a finite cell complex with cells $(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k)$ if it is homotopy equivalent to such a $K$.

diff: Weaker than a CW-complex with these cells: the attaching maps need not be cellular, and the cells are attached in the listed order rather than by dimension.

Milnor makes the attaching maps cellular by the cellular approximation theorem, which Mathlib does not have; with it and Lemma 3.6 such a space would be homotopy equivalent to a CW-complex with the same number of cells in each dimension, a step that is not formalized.

items.title: Theorem 3.5 for a compact submanifold of Euclidean space

milnor.label: §3, Theorem 3.5
milnor.statement: A manifold $M$ carrying a differentiable function without degenerate critical points, all of whose sublevel sets $M^a$ are compact, is homotopy equivalent to a CW-complex with one cell of dimension $\lambda$ for each critical point of index $\lambda$. The proof (pp. 23–24) lists the critical values $c_1 < c_2 < \dots$, notes that $M^a$ is vacuous for $a < c_1$, passes each critical level by Theorems 3.1 and 3.2 and Remark 3.3, and carries the cells along homotopy equivalences by Lemmas 3.6 and 3.7; the non-compact case uses a direct limit and Whitehead's theorem.

lean.statement: Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real normed space, $N \subseteq V$ a compact slice submanifold modelled on a finite-dimensional $Z$, $F : V \to \mathbb R$ of class $C^\infty$, and suppose that every critical point of $f = F|N$ is non-degenerate. Then the critical points of $f$ can be listed without repetition as $p_1, \dots, p_k$, with $f(p_1) \le \dots \le f(p_k)$, so that $N$ has the homotopy type of a finite cell complex with cells $(\lambda(p_1), \dots, \lambda(p_k))$ in the sense of V2.11, $\lambda(p)$ the index of $p$. In particular $N$ has the homotopy type of such a complex whose number of cells of dimension $\lambda$ is, for every $\lambda$, the number $C_\lambda$ of critical points of index $\lambda$. If the critical values are distinct, the list is strictly increasing.

diff: $N$ is a compact submanifold of a Euclidean space and $f$ the restriction of an ambient smooth function; the non-compact case, with its direct limit and Whitehead's theorem, is not formalized.
The conclusion is an iterated adjunction space (V2.11), not a CW-complex; Lemma 3.6 is not needed, since the attaching maps are not made cellular.
Hidden steps made explicit: that $M^a$ is empty below the first critical value needs the global minimum to be a critical point, and that the critical values do not accumulate is V1.11.

items.title: Lemma 3.6 (Whitehead)

milnor.label: §3, Lemma 3.6
milnor.statement: If two maps $\varphi_0$, $\varphi_1$ of the sphere $\dot e^\lambda$ into $X$ are homotopic, the identity of $X$ extends to a homotopy equivalence $k$ from $X \cup_{\varphi_0} e^\lambda$ to $X \cup_{\varphi_1} e^\lambda$. The proof gives explicit formulas for $k$ and for a map $\ell$ the other way, and says it is not difficult to verify that $k\ell$ and $\ell k$ are homotopic to the identities.

lean.statement: Let $X$ be a topological space, $n \ge 0$, and $\varphi_0, \varphi_1 : S^{n-1} \to X$ homotopic maps. Then there is a homotopy equivalence $k : X \cup_{\varphi_0} e^n \to X \cup_{\varphi_1} e^n$ which is the identity on $X$. The proof uses Milnor's formulas for $k$ and $\ell$; the homotopies he leaves to the reader are written down, built through the exponential law for the locally compact $[0, 1]$, which is the fact, used silently, that $[0, 1] \times$ (a quotient map) is a quotient map.

items.title: Lemma 3.7, and the Assertion of p. 22

milnor.label: §3, Lemma 3.7
milnor.statement: For an attaching map $\varphi : \dot e^\lambda \to X$, every homotopy equivalence $f : X \to Y$ extends to a homotopy equivalence $F$ from $X \cup_\varphi e^\lambda$ to $Y \cup_{f\varphi} e^\lambda$. The proof, after an unpublished paper of Hilton, takes $F = f$ on $X$ and the identity on the cell, and rests on an Assertion (p. 22): if a map $F$ has a left homotopy inverse $L$ and a right homotopy inverse $R$, then $F$ is a homotopy equivalence, and $R$ (or $L$) is a two-sided homotopy inverse.

lean.statement: Let $X$, $Y$ be topological spaces, $\varphi : S^{n-1} \to X$ continuous and $f : X \to Y$ a homotopy equivalence. Then the map $F : X \cup_\varphi e^n \to Y \cup_{f\varphi} e^n$ equal to $f$ on $X$ and to the identity on the cell is a homotopy equivalence. And for maps $F$, $L$, $R$: if $LF \simeq \mathrm{id}$ and $FR \simeq \mathrm{id}$, then $RF \simeq \mathrm{id}$.

chips: uses the formula for $k$ of Lemma 3.6
diff: Milnor's statement says only that $f$ extends to some homotopy equivalence; the formal statement names the extension, $f$ on $X$ and the identity on the cell, as his proof does.
The proof is Milnor's, and it uses the formula for $k$ from the proof of Lemma 3.6, not only its statement.

items.title: The Remark of p. 24: sublevel sets at regular values

milnor.label: §3, Remark after Theorem 3.5
milnor.statement: The proof of Theorem 3.5 also gives, for every $a$, that $M^a$ is homotopy equivalent to a finite CW-complex with one $\lambda$-cell for each critical point of index $\lambda$ in $M^a$, and this holds even when $a$ is a critical value (compare Remark 3.4).

lean.statement: Let $N \subseteq V$, $F$ and $f = F|N$ be as in V2.12, and let $a$ be a real number which is not a critical value of $f$. Then the critical points $p$ with $f(p) < a$ can be listed without repetition as $p_1, \dots, p_j$, with $f(p_1) \le \dots \le f(p_j)$, so that $N^a$ has the homotopy type of a finite cell complex with cells $(\lambda(p_1), \dots, \lambda(p_j))$ (V2.11).

diff: Only for $a$ not a critical value: at a critical value Remark 3.4 would be needed on submanifolds, where it is not formalized.
As in V2.12, the setting is a compact submanifold of a Euclidean space and the conclusion an iterated adjunction space rather than a CW-complex.

items.title: Small sublevel sets at the extrema are closed cells

milnor.label: §4, proof of Theorem 4.1
milnor.statement: In the proof of Reeb's theorem, with $f(p) = 0$ the minimum and $f(q) = 1$ the maximum, Milnor says that if $\epsilon$ is small enough the sets $M^\epsilon = f^{-1}[0, \epsilon]$ and $f^{-1}[1 - \epsilon, 1]$ are closed $n$-cells, by the lemma of Morse (2.2).

lean.statement: (i) On a manifold $M$ modelled on a real normed space $E$, a local minimum or local maximum of any $f : M \to \mathbb R$ is a critical point. If moreover $M$ is a smooth manifold without boundary, $E$ has finite dimension $n$, $f$ is smooth on an open $U \ni p$ and $p$ is a non-degenerate local minimum (maximum), then the index of $f$ at $p$ is $0$ (resp. $n$), and there are smooth coordinates $y$ on an open subset of $U$ containing $p$, with values in $\mathbb R^n$ with its Euclidean norm, such that $y(p) = 0$ and $f = f(p) + \|y\|^2$ (resp. $f = f(p) - \|y\|^2$) on the domain of $y$. (ii) Let $X$ be a compact topological space, $f : X \to \mathbb R$ continuous with a strict global minimum at $p$ ($f(p) < f(x)$ for all $x \ne p$), and $y$ a homeomorphism from an open neighbourhood of $p$ onto an open subset of a real normed space $F$, with $y(p) = 0$ and $f = f(p) + \|y\|^2$ on its domain. Then there is $\delta > 0$ such that for every $0 < \varepsilon < \delta$ the map $v \mapsto y^{-1}(\sqrt\varepsilon\, v)$ is continuous and injective on the closed unit ball of $F$, maps it onto $\{f \le f(p) + \varepsilon\}$, and maps the unit sphere onto the level set $\{f = f(p) + \varepsilon\}$. Applied to $-f$, the same holds at a strict maximum.

chips: a ball, its sphere onto the level set
index $0$ at a minimum, $n$ at a maximum
diff: The closed cell is produced as the image of the closed unit ball under a continuous injective map, with its boundary sphere going onto the level set, which the gluing at the end of the proof needs and “closed $n$-cell” does not say.

The lemma of Morse describes $f$ only near $p$. That the whole sublevel set lies in the Morse chart needs compactness and the uniqueness of the minimum: off a small coordinate ball, $f \ge f(p) + \eta$ for some $\eta > 0$.
That the minimum has index $0$ and the maximum index $n$, used without comment, is proved first: in a Morse chart $f$ decreases along an axis carrying a minus sign, so a minimum has none.

items.title: The two critical points are the minimum and the maximum

milnor.label: §4, proof of Theorem 4.1
milnor.statement: The two critical points must be the minimum and the maximum points of $f$; Milnor normalizes $f(p) = 0$ at the minimum and $f(q) = 1$ at the maximum.

lean.statement: Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold without boundary modelled on a finite-dimensional real normed space $E$ with $n = \dim E \ge 1$, and $f : M \to \mathbb R$ smooth with exactly two critical points, both non-degenerate. Then there are points $p$, $q$ with $f(p) < f(q)$ such that the critical points are exactly $p$ and $q$, $f(p) < f(x)$ for every $x \ne p$, $f(x) < f(q)$ for every $x \ne q$, and the index of $f$ is $0$ at $p$ and $n$ at $q$. Hausdorffness is not needed.

diff: In dimension $0$ every point is critical and $f$ may be constant, so $n \ge 1$ is needed. Non-degeneracy is what shows that $f$ is not constant: a constant $f$ would make its minimum point also a maximum, of index $n \ne 0$.
That no other point takes an extreme value, which the cells of V3.2 need, is part of the conclusion.

items.title: Theorem 3.1 also carries the boundary level

milnor.label: §4, proof of Theorem 4.1
milnor.statement: In the proof of Reeb's theorem, $M^\epsilon$ is homeomorphic to $M^{1-\epsilon}$ by Theorem 3.1, and $M$ is then the union of the two closed $n$-cells $M^{1-\epsilon}$ and $f^{-1}[1 - \epsilon, 1]$, matched along their common boundary.

lean.statement: Let $N$ be a slice submanifold of a finite-dimensional real normed space $V$, modelled on a finite-dimensional $Z$, $F : V \to \mathbb R$ smooth, $f = F|N$, and $a \le b$ with $f^{-1}[a, b]$ compact and containing no critical point of $f$. Then there is a smooth diffeomorphism $\Phi$ of $N$ with $\Phi(N^a) = N^b$ and $\Phi(f^{-1}(a)) = f^{-1}(b)$.

diff: The gluing needs a homeomorphism that also carries the level $f^{-1}(\epsilon)$ onto $f^{-1}(1 - \epsilon)$. The statement of Theorem 3.1 does not give this; its proof does, since the flow moves the levels of the slab at unit speed, and $\Phi$ is the time-$(b - a)$ map of that flow.

items.title: Two closed balls glued along their boundary form a sphere

milnor.label: §4, proof of Theorem 4.1
milnor.statement: Thus $M$ is the union of two closed $n$-cells matched along their common boundary, and Milnor says that it is now easy to construct a homeomorphism between $M$ and $S^n$. None is constructed.

lean.statement: (i) Alexander's trick: if $g$ is a homeomorphism of the unit sphere of a real normed space $E$, the cone $x \mapsto \|x\|\,g(x/\|x\|)$, $0 \mapsto 0$, is a homeomorphism of $E$ that preserves norms and extends $g$. (ii) Let $X$ be a Hausdorff space, $n \ge 0$, $D^n$ and $S^{n-1}$ the closed unit ball and unit sphere of $\mathbb R^n$, and $h_1, h_2 : D^n \to X$ continuous and injective, with $h_1(D^n) \cup h_2(D^n) = X$, $h_1(D^n) \cap h_2(D^n) = h_1(S^{n-1})$ and $h_2(S^{n-1}) = h_1(S^{n-1})$. Then $X$ is homeomorphic to the unit sphere $S^n \subseteq \mathbb R^{n+1}$.

diff: The identification $h_2^{-1} \circ h_1$ of the two boundary spheres is in general not the identity and must be extended over a ball, which is Alexander's trick; the inverse is continuous because a continuous bijection from a compact space onto a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism.
The cone is in general not differentiable at $0$: this is where smoothness is lost, as Milnor's Remark 2 says it must be.

items.title: Theorem 4.1 (Reeb)

milnor.label: §4, Theorem 4.1 (Reeb)
milnor.statement: A compact manifold $M$ carrying a differentiable function with only two critical points, both non-degenerate, is homeomorphic to a sphere. The proof: the two critical points are the minimum and the maximum; small sublevel and superlevel sets are closed $n$-cells by Lemma 2.2; $M^\epsilon$ is homeomorphic to $M^{1-\epsilon}$ by Theorem 3.1; so $M$ is two closed $n$-cells matched along their boundary.
milnor.note: Remark 1 adds that the theorem remains true for degenerate critical points, with a more difficult proof, and Remark 2 that $M$ need not be diffeomorphic to $S^n$.

lean.statement: Let $N$ be a compact slice submanifold of a finite-dimensional real normed space $V$, modelled on a finite-dimensional space of dimension $n$, and $f = F|N$ with $F : V \to \mathbb R$ smooth. If $f$ has exactly two critical points, both non-degenerate, then $N$ is homeomorphic to the unit sphere $S^n \subseteq \mathbb R^{n+1}$. For a compact $N \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}$ modelled on $\mathbb R^n$, $n \ge 1$, the same holds for every smooth $f : N \to \mathbb R$, which is always the restriction of a smooth function on $\mathbb R^{K+1}$. In dimension $0$, where every point is critical, $N$ has exactly two points.

diff: $N$ is a compact submanifold of a vector space; the abstract compact Hausdorff case is V4.24, proved through the Whitney embedding.
“Only two” is read as exactly two: on a non-empty compact manifold of positive dimension the extrema already give two. The sphere is $S^n$ with $n = \dim N$, and $N$ has no boundary.
In dimension $0$ Milnor's proof does not apply, since $f$ may be constant, but every point is critical, so $N$ has two points.
The proof is Milnor's, made complete by V3.2–V3.5; the normalization $f(p) = 0$, $f(q) = 1$ is not needed.

items.title: Subadditive and additive functions

milnor.label: §5, Definition
milnor.statement: An integer-valued function $S$, defined on certain pairs of spaces, is subadditive if $S(X, Z) \le S(X, Y) + S(Y, Z)$ for every $X \supset Y \supset Z$, and additive if equality always holds.

lean.statement: Spaces are replaced by the elements of a preordered set $\iota$, $a \le b$ standing for $X_a \subseteq X_b$. A function on pairs is an integer-valued function $S(a, b)$ of two indices, used only for $a \le b$, where $S(a, b)$ stands for Milnor's $S(X_b, X_a)$, the smaller space written first. $S$ is subadditive if $S(a, c) \le S(a, b) + S(b, c)$ whenever $a \le b \le c$, and additive if equality always holds.

chips: indices of a preorder for spaces
diff: Milnor does not say on which pairs $S$ is defined; the class must be closed under the passage from $(X, Y)$ and $(Y, Z)$ to $(X, Z)$. Here every pair $a \le b$ of the index set is allowed.

items.title: Lemma 5.1

milnor.label: §5, Lemma 5.1
milnor.statement: For a subadditive $S$ and spaces $X_0 \subset X_1 \subset \dots \subset X_n$, $S(X_n, X_0) \le \sum_{i=1}^n S(X_i, X_{i-1})$, with equality when $S$ is additive. The proof is by induction on $n$, and taking $X_0 = \emptyset$ gives inequality (1), $S(X_n) \le \sum_i S(X_i, X_{i-1})$.

lean.statement: If $S$ is subadditive and $X_0 \le X_1 \le \dots \le X_n$ with $n \ge 1$, then $S(X_0, X_n) \le \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} S(X_k, X_{k+1})$, that is, in Milnor's notation, $S(X_n, X_0) \le \sum_{i=1}^n S(X_i, X_{i-1})$; if $S$ is additive, equality holds. One form assumes subadditivity only on the triples $X_0 \le X_m \le X_{m+1}$, which is all the induction uses.

diff: For $n = 0$ the statement would be $S(X_0, X_0) \le 0$, which subadditivity does not give: it gives $S(X, X) \ge 0$. Milnor's induction starts at $n = 1$, and the hypothesis is written out.

items.title: The homology of a filtration, and its Morse numbers

milnor.label: §5, pp. 28–30
milnor.statement: Milnor works with singular homology with coefficients in a field $F$: $R_\lambda(X, Y)$, the $\lambda$-th Betti number of $(X, Y)$, is the rank over $F$ of $H_\lambda(X, Y; F)$, for any pair for which this rank is finite. He uses the exact sequence of a triple $X \supset Y \supset Z$, with its final $\to 0$ (p. 29), and $C_\lambda$ counts the critical points of index $\lambda$.

lean.statement: Fix a field $F$ and a preordered set $\iota$. A homology of a filtration assigns to every degree $i \ge 0$ and indices $a$, $b$ a vector space $H_i(a, b)$ over $F$, to be read as $H_i(X_b, X_a; F)$, finite-dimensional for $a \le b$, and to every triple $a \le b \le c$ a long exact sequence of $F$-linear maps $\cdots \to H_i(a,b) \to H_i(a,c) \to H_i(b,c) \to H_{i-1}(a,b) \to \cdots \to H_0(a,b) \to H_0(a,c) \to H_0(b,c) \to 0$, exact at every term. Nothing else is assumed: no functoriality, no compatibility between the sequences of different triples, no vanishing of $H_*(a, a)$, no excision. For a chain $X_0 \le X_1 \le \dots \le X_n$ the Betti numbers are $R_i = \dim H_i(X_0, X_n)$ and the Morse numbers are $C_i = \sum_{k<n} \dim H_i(X_k, X_{k+1})$. On a chain indexed by $\mathbb N$ the structure can be built from the exact sequences and the finiteness of the steps alone, so that the finiteness of the total homology is a consequence.

diff: Every algebraic statement of §5 (V3.10–V3.15) is proved for every such structure; singular homology over a field is an instance (V3.32), and the slab computation that applies it to a manifold is V3.33–V3.34.
The final $\to 0$ of the sequence of a triple is the surjectivity of $H_0(X, Z) \to H_0(X, Y)$, which Milnor uses on p. 29.

items.title: The Betti numbers are subadditive, and the Euler characteristic additive

milnor.label: §5, p. 28
milnor.statement: $R_\lambda$ is subadditive, as is easily seen from the portion $H_\lambda(Y, Z) \to H_\lambda(X, Z) \to H_\lambda(X, Y)$ of the exact sequence of the triple; and the Euler characteristic $\chi(X, Y) = \sum (-1)^\lambda R_\lambda(X, Y)$ is additive, which is asserted without argument.

lean.statement: For a homology of a filtration: (i) for every $\lambda$, $(a, b) \mapsto \dim H_\lambda(a, b)$ is subadditive, and in a segment $H_\lambda(a, b) \to H_\lambda(a, c) \to H_\lambda(b, c)$ of a long exact sequence the middle term is finite-dimensional when the outer two are; (ii) the alternating sum of the dimensions in a finite exact sequence $0 \to V_n \to \dots \to V_0 \to 0$ of finite-dimensional spaces is $0$; (iii) if $H_{N+1}(a, b) = 0$ for all $a \le b$, the truncated Euler characteristic $\chi_N(a, b) = \sum_{i \le N} (-1)^i \dim H_i(a, b)$ is additive.

diff: Additivity of $\chi$ needs the total homology to be finite; here $\chi$ is truncated at a degree $N$, with vanishing in degree $N + 1$, and is Milnor's $\chi$ when the homology vanishes above $N$.
That the pairs with finite-dimensional homology are closed under triples, which subadditivity presupposes, is the second half of (i).

items.title: Theorem 5.2 (weak Morse inequalities), abstractly

milnor.label: §5, Theorem 5.2
milnor.statement: On a compact manifold $M$, with $C_\lambda$ the number of critical points of index $\lambda$: (2) $R_\lambda(M) \le C_\lambda$, and (3) $\sum (-1)^\lambda R_\lambda(M) = \sum (-1)^\lambda C_\lambda$. The proof chooses $a_1 < \dots < a_k$ with exactly $i$ critical points in $M^{a_i}$ and $M^{a_k} = M$, computes $H_*(M^{a_i}, M^{a_{i-1}})$ as the coefficient group in dimension $\lambda_i$ and $0$ otherwise, by excision, and applies Lemma 5.1 to $R_\lambda$ and to $\chi$.

lean.statement: For a homology of a filtration and a chain $X_0 \le \dots \le X_n$ with $n \ge 1$: (2) $R_\lambda \le C_\lambda$ for every $\lambda$; (3) if no slab $H_{N+1}(X_k, X_{k+1})$ is non-zero, then $\sum_{i \le N} (-1)^i R_i = \sum_{i \le N} (-1)^i C_i$. In terms of critical points: let $P$ be a finite set, each $p \in P$ carrying an index $\mathrm{ind}(p)$ and a step $\mathrm{step}(p) < n$, and assume the cell hypothesis $\dim H_i(X_k, X_{k+1}) = \#\{p \in P : \mathrm{step}(p) = k,\ \mathrm{ind}(p) = i\}$ for all $k < n$ and all $i$. Then $C_i$ is the number of $p \in P$ of index $i$, and (2) reads $R_\lambda \le \#\{p \in P : \mathrm{ind}(p) = \lambda\}$; with one critical point per slab this is Milnor's count.

chips: any number of points per slab
diff: The topological input, the slab computation of p. 29 (Theorems 3.1 and 3.2, homotopy invariance, excision and the homology of a cell modulo its boundary), is the cell hypothesis here, not a theorem; and $R_\lambda$ is a dimension in the abstract structure of V3.9. Both are supplied for singular homology in V3.32–V3.35.

Milnor's choice of the $a_i$, one critical point per slab, needs distinct critical values; the cell hypothesis allows any number of critical points per slab. His chain starts at $\emptyset = M^{a_0}$, with $a_0$ never introduced; here $X_0$ is arbitrary and $R_i$ is the homology of the pair.

items.title: Lemma 5.3

milnor.label: §5, Lemma 5.3
milnor.statement: The function $S_\lambda(X, Y) = R_\lambda(X, Y) - R_{\lambda-1}(X, Y) + \dots \pm R_0(X, Y)$ is subadditive. The proof computes, for an exact sequence of vector spaces $\to A \to B \to C \to \dots \to D \to 0$, that the rank of the map $h$ into $A$ is $\operatorname{rank} A - \operatorname{rank} B + \operatorname{rank} C - \dots \pm \operatorname{rank} D$, hence $\ge 0$, and applies this to the boundary $\partial : H_{\lambda+1}(X, Y) \to H_\lambda(Y, Z)$ of the sequence of the triple $X \supset Y \supset Z$.

lean.statement: (i) If $V_{n+1} \xrightarrow{h} V_n \to \dots \to V_0 \to 0$ is exact at $V_0, \dots, V_n$ and all $V_k$ are finite-dimensional, then $\operatorname{rank} h = \dim V_n - \dim V_{n-1} + \dots \pm \dim V_0$. (ii) For the sequence of a triple $a \le b \le c$ in a homology of a filtration, $\operatorname{rank}(\partial : H_{\lambda+1}(b, c) \to H_\lambda(a, b)) = S_\lambda(a, b) - S_\lambda(a, c) + S_\lambda(b, c)$, where $S_\lambda = R_\lambda - R_{\lambda-1} + \dots \pm R_0$ of the pair; hence $S_\lambda(a, c) \le S_\lambda(a, b) + S_\lambda(b, c)$. (iii) So $S_\lambda$ is subadditive.

chips: in the abstract structure of V3.9
diff: Milnor's rank computation is proved as he makes it, with the finite dimensions that rank–nullity needs, and the identity for the rank of $\partial$ is a lemma of its own.

items.title: The strong Morse inequalities, abstractly

milnor.label: §5, the Morse inequalities
milnor.statement: Applying Lemma 5.1 to the subadditive function $S_\lambda$ and the spaces $\emptyset \subset M^{a_1} \subset \dots \subset M^{a_k}$ gives the Morse inequalities $(4_\lambda)$: $R_\lambda(M) - R_{\lambda-1}(M) + \dots \pm R_0(M) \le C_\lambda - C_{\lambda-1} + \dots \pm C_0$.

lean.statement: For a homology of a filtration and a chain with $n \ge 1$: $R_\lambda - R_{\lambda-1} + \dots \pm R_0 \le C_\lambda - C_{\lambda-1} + \dots \pm C_0$ for every $\lambda$; under the cell hypothesis of V3.11, with $C_i$ the number of critical points of index $i$.

diff: As for V3.11: the slab computation is an assumption here, and $R_\lambda$ a dimension in the abstract structure. In singular homology, with every hypothesis proved, the inequalities are V3.36.

items.title: Consequences of the strong inequalities

milnor.label: §5, p. 30
milnor.statement: The strong inequalities contain the weak ones: the sum of $(4_\lambda)$ and $(4_{\lambda-1})$ is $(2_\lambda)$, and comparing $(4_\lambda)$ with $(4_{\lambda-1})$ for $\lambda > n$ yields the equality (3). As an illustration Milnor shows that $C_{\lambda+1} = 0$ forces $R_{\lambda+1} = 0$, and then $(4_\lambda)$, compared with $(4_{\lambda+1})$, becomes an equality.

lean.statement: Let $b$, $c$ be integer sequences with $S_\lambda(b) \le S_\lambda(c)$ for every $\lambda$, where $S_\lambda(d) = d_\lambda - d_{\lambda-1} + \dots \pm d_0$. Then $b_\lambda \le c_\lambda$ for every $\lambda$; if $c_{\lambda+1} = 0$ and $b_{\lambda+1} \ge 0$, then $S_\lambda(b) = S_\lambda(c)$; if $b \ge 0$ and $c_{N+1} = 0$, then $\sum_{i \le N} (-1)^i b_i = \sum_{i \le N} (-1)^i c_i$. For a filtration with the cell hypothesis, $R_l = 0$ if no critical point has index $l$, and, if every index is at most $N$, $\sum_{i \le N} (-1)^i R_i = \sum_{p \in P} (-1)^{\mathrm{ind}(p)}$, the left side being the whole alternating sum.

diff: Only $\lambda = n + 1$ matters in the comparison for $\lambda > n$, and it uses $C_{n+1} = 0$ and $R_{n+1} \ge 0$; that the left side of (3) is the whole alternating sum uses $R_i = 0$ for $i > n$, which is (2).
Milnor's intermediate step $R_{\lambda+1} = 0$ is not needed: $R_{\lambda+1} \ge 0$ suffices.

items.title: Corollary 5.4, and the lacunary principle

milnor.label: §5, Corollary 5.4
milnor.statement: If $C_{\lambda+1} = C_{\lambda-1} = 0$ then $R_\lambda = C_\lambda$ and $R_{\lambda+1} = R_{\lambda-1} = 0$. Milnor adds that this would also follow from Theorem 3.5, and that the corollary gives the homology groups of complex projective space (§4) without Theorem 3.5.

lean.statement: For integer sequences $b \ge 0$ and $c$ satisfying every $(4_\lambda)$, and so for the Betti and Morse numbers of a chain: if $\lambda \ge 1$ and $c_{\lambda+1} = c_{\lambda-1} = 0$, then $b_\lambda = c_\lambda$ and $b_{\lambda+1} = b_{\lambda-1} = 0$; if $c_1 = 0$, then $b_0 = c_0$ and $b_1 = 0$; and if no two consecutive $c_i$ are non-zero (for instance, if every odd $c_i$ vanishes), then $b_i = c_i$ for every $i$.

diff: The lacunary form, $b_i = c_i$ for every $i$ when no two consecutive $c_i$ are non-zero, is added; it is what Milnor's remark about complex projective space needs.
For $\lambda = 0$ the condition $C_{\lambda-1} = 0$ is empty, and the case is stated separately.
The corollary yields Betti numbers over a field, not integral homology groups; for a compact manifold it is V3.37 and V3.39, and $\mathbb CP^n$ is not constructed.

items.title: The numbers $C_\lambda$ of a function

milnor.label: §5, p. 29
milnor.statement: $C_\lambda$ denotes the number of critical points of index $\lambda$ of the function on the compact manifold $M$, a function with isolated, non-degenerate critical points; the alternating sums of Theorem 5.2 end with $\pm C_n$.

lean.statement: For $f : M \to \mathbb R$ on a manifold modelled on a real normed space $E$, $C_\lambda(f)$ is the number of critical points of $f$ of index $\lambda$, set to $0$ if there are infinitely many. If $E$ is finite-dimensional and $f$ has finitely many critical points, $\sum_{p \text{ critical}} (-1)^{\mathrm{index}_p f} = \sum_{\lambda=0}^{\dim E} (-1)^\lambda C_\lambda(f)$.

diff: The convention for infinitely many critical points never applies in the theorems that use $C_\lambda$: a Morse function on a compact manifold has finitely many (V1.11).
$C_\lambda = 0$ for $\lambda > \dim M$, which is why Milnor's sums stop at $\pm C_n$ with $n = \dim M$.

items.title: The Poincaré–Hopf integer

milnor.label: §5, p. 28, and §6, Application 2
milnor.statement: Milnor's $\chi$ is the Euler characteristic $\sum (-1)^\lambda R_\lambda$ of singular homology over a field (p. 28). In Application 2 (pp. 36–37) he uses that the sum of the indices of any vector field on a compact $M$ is a topological invariant, citing Steenrod (§39.7), so that it equals $\chi(M)$.

lean.statement: Let $N \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}$ be a compact non-empty slice submanifold modelled on $\mathbb R^{d+1}$. An integer $\chi$ is an Euler number of $N$ if every smooth tangent vector field on $N$ whose zeros are finitely many distinct points has index sum $\chi$, the index being that of the Milnor project: the index at a zero of the extension $x \mapsto v(r(x)) + (x - r(x))$ of $v$ to a tubular neighbourhood, $r$ the nearest-point retraction. For $K \ge 1$ an Euler number exists: this is the Poincaré–Hopf theorem of the Milnor project, where it is the degree of the Gauss map of the boundary of a tubular neighbourhood. It is unique, and is written $\chi(N)$.

chips: defined by vector fields, not homology
diff: $\chi(N)$ is defined through vector fields, as the Poincaré–Hopf integer; its identification with $\sum_i (-1)^i \dim H_i(N; F)$ is V3.38.
Uniqueness comes from Morse theory: every Euler number equals the alternating count of the critical points of any Morse function (V3.20), and $N$ carries one (V4.13).
The ambient dimension must be at least $2$, as the Milnor project's Poincaré–Hopf theorem requires.

items.title: The index of the gradient field is $(-1)^\lambda$

milnor.label: §6, Application 2
milnor.statement: In Application 2 Milnor asserts, without proof, that $(-1)^\lambda$ is the index of the vector field $\mathrm{grad} f$ at a point where $f$ has index $\lambda$.

lean.statement: Let $N \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}$, $K \ge 1$, be a compact non-empty slice submanifold modelled on $\mathbb R^{d+1}$, $F : \mathbb R^{K+1} \to \mathbb R$ smooth and $f = F|N$. The tangential gradient $v(q) = P_q\nabla F(q)$, $P_q$ the orthogonal projection onto $T_qN$, is the gradient of $f$ for the metric induced from $\mathbb R^{K+1}$; its zeros are exactly the critical points of $f$, and it is a smooth tangent field. If $q$ is a non-degenerate critical point of $f$ of index $\lambda$, the derivative of $v$ at $q$ is an invertible endomorphism of $T_qN$ whose determinant has sign $(-1)^\lambda$, and the index of $v$ at $q$ is $(-1)^\lambda$. Along the way: for a non-degenerate symmetric form $H(v, w) = \langle Av, w\rangle$ on a finite-dimensional inner product space, $\operatorname{sgn}\det A = (-1)^{\mathrm{index}\,H}$.

diff: A metric must be chosen; here it is the one induced from $\mathbb R^{K+1}$, and $M$ is a compact submanifold of a Euclidean space, since vector fields and their indices are defined in the Milnor project only there.

The Hessian of $F|N$ is not the restriction of the Hessian of $F$, since at a critical point $\nabla F(q)$ is normal to $N$, not zero. The proof replaces $F$ by $F \circ r$, $r$ the nearest-point retraction, which agrees with $F$ on $N$ and is critical at $q$ as a function on $\mathbb R^{K+1}$; the derivative of $v$ at $q$ is an endomorphism of $T_qN$ only because $v(q) = 0$.
The sign of the determinant is $(-1)^{\mathrm{index}}$ by the spectral theorem and Sylvester's law of inertia, and it does not depend on the inner product.

items.title: Formula (3) without homology

milnor.label: §5, formula (3), and §6, Application 2
milnor.statement: For a compact manifold $M$ and a function with isolated, non-degenerate critical points, Lemma 5.1 applied to the additive $\chi$ gives $\chi(M) = C_0 - C_1 + C_2 - \dots \pm C_n$, recorded as (3) of Theorem 5.2. In Application 2 (pp. 36–37) Milnor deduces that on a compact $M$ the vector field $\mathrm{grad} f$ has index sum $\chi(M)$, and so, the index sum being a topological invariant, every vector field does.

lean.statement: Let $N \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}$, $K \ge 1$, be a compact non-empty slice submanifold of dimension $d + 1 \ge 1$. There is an integer $\chi(N)$, an Euler number of $N$ in the sense of V3.17, such that every Morse function $f$ on $N$ (smooth, with only non-degenerate critical points) satisfies $\sum_{\lambda=0}^{d+1} (-1)^\lambda C_\lambda(f) = \sum_{q \text{ critical}} (-1)^{\mathrm{index}_q f} = \chi(N)$. Consequently the alternating count is the same for all Morse functions on $N$, and every Euler number of $N$ equals the alternating count of any one Morse function. Every smooth $f : N \to \mathbb R$ is the restriction of a smooth function on $\mathbb R^{K+1}$.

diff: What is verified here is the topological invariance of $\sum (-1)^\lambda C_\lambda$, by running Application 2 in the direction that needs no homology: the gradient field of $f$ (V3.19) has index sum $\sum (-1)^\lambda C_\lambda(f)$, and every tangent field has the index sum $\chi(N)$.

Its equality with $\sum (-1)^i R_i(N)$, formula (3) as Milnor states it, is V3.35; the identification of $\chi(N)$ with the homological Euler characteristic is V3.38; abstract compact manifolds are V4.19.

“Isolated” is redundant for non-degenerate critical points, and distinct critical values are not needed. In Application 2, “any differentiable function” must be one with only non-degenerate critical points, and the critical points of a vector field are its zeros.

items.title: The torus of Diagram 1 is a compact surface

milnor.label: §1, p. 1
milnor.statement: Milnor takes a torus $M$ tangent to a plane $V$, drawn standing upright in Diagram 1. No equations are given, and nothing is said about why $M$ is a smooth compact surface.

lean.statement: For $0 < \rho < R$ let $T = \{x \in \mathbb R^3 : (\sqrt{x_1^2 + x_2^2} - R)^2 + x_3^2 = \rho^2\}$, the torus of revolution about the $x_3$-axis with core radius $R$ and tube radius $\rho$. $T$ is the zero set of $g(x) = (\|x\|^2 + R^2 - \rho^2)^2 - 4R^2(x_1^2 + x_2^2)$, and $dg$ does not vanish on $T$; hence $T$ is a $2$-dimensional slice submanifold of $\mathbb R^3$, compact and non-empty, and its tangent plane at $q$ is $\ker dg_q$, of dimension $2$.

chips: the regular zero set of a quartic
diff: The surface is fixed as the torus of revolution. $\rho < R$ makes it a smooth ring torus, and also makes the four critical values of V3.23 distinct, which cases (3) and (4) of p. 1 presuppose.

items.title: The height function: four critical points, of indices 0, 1, 1, 2

milnor.label: §1, p. 3
milnor.statement: The points $p$, $q$, $r$, $s$ at which the homotopy type of $M^a$ changes are the critical points of $f$: in any coordinates $(x, y)$ near them both partial derivatives of $f$ vanish, and one can choose coordinates with $f = x^2 + y^2$ at $p$, $f = \text{const} - x^2 - y^2$ at $s$, and $f = \text{const} + x^2 - y^2$ at $q$ and $r$. The number of minus signs is the dimension of the cell attached in passing the point.

lean.statement: Let $f = x_1 + R + \rho$ on $T$, the height above the plane $\{x_1 = -(R + \rho)\}$, which touches $T$ at $p = (-(R + \rho), 0, 0)$; the axis of revolution is parallel to the plane, so the torus stands upright. The critical points of $f$ are exactly $p$, $q = (-(R - \rho), 0, 0)$, $r = (R - \rho, 0, 0)$ and $s = (R + \rho, 0, 0)$, with critical values $0$, $2\rho$, $2R$, $2R + 2\rho$. All four are non-degenerate, of indices $0, 1, 1, 2$; $f$ is a Morse function on $T$, with $C_0 = 1$, $C_1 = 2$, $C_2 = 1$ and $C_\lambda = 0$ for $\lambda \ge 3$.

chips: indices proved, normal forms not restated
