diff: Milnor asserts the critical points and the normal forms without verification. The formal statement proves that there are exactly four critical points, non-degenerate, with the indices the normal forms imply; the normal forms follow from the lemma of Morse (V1.8) and are not restated.
The upright position is essential: lying flat, the height function has two circles of degenerate critical points.

The proof is Lagrange's rule. At a point $(a, 0, 0)$ of $T$, $dg = \kappa\,dx_1$ with $\kappa \ne 0$, so $G = f - \kappa^{-1}g$ agrees with $f$ on $T$ and is critical at the point as a function on $\mathbb R^3$; the Hessian of $f|T$ is then $d^2G$ on the tangent plane, a diagonal form whose entries are, up to sign, the principal curvatures.

items.title: Milnor's cases (1) and (5), and Theorem 3.1 on the torus

milnor.label: §1, p. 1
milnor.statement: (1) If $a < 0 < f(p)$, as the scan prints it, then $M^a$ is vacuous; (5) if $f(s) < a$, then $M^a$ is the full torus; and for $a$ between consecutive critical values, cases (2)–(4), $M^a$ is homeomorphic to a 2-cell, to a cylinder, and to a compact genus-one surface bounded by a circle.

lean.statement: $T^a = \emptyset$ for $a < 0$, and $T^a = T$ for $a \ge 2R + 2\rho = f(s)$. If $a \le b$ and $[a, b]$ contains none of the critical values $0$, $2\rho$, $2R$, $2R + 2\rho$, then a smooth diffeomorphism of $T$ carries $T^a$ onto $T^b$, $T^a$ is a strong deformation retract of $T^b$, and the inclusion $T^a \to T^b$ is a homotopy equivalence; in particular the $T^a$ with $a$ in any one of $(0, 2\rho)$, $(2\rho, 2R)$, $(2R, 2R + 2\rho)$ are diffeomorphic to one another.

diff: Of cases (2)–(4) only what Theorem 3.1 gives is verified; the homeomorphism types, a disk, a cylinder and a torus with a disk removed, are not, and would need explicit homeomorphisms.
$f(p) = 0$ because the plane touches $M$ at $p$, so the hypothesis of (1) must be read as $a < 0 = f(p)$; and (5) holds for $a = f(s)$ as well.

items.title: The Euler number of the torus is 0

milnor.label: §1, p. 2
milnor.statement: The book computes no Euler characteristic for the torus. On p. 2 Milnor describes the passage from (1) to (5) as attaching a 0-cell, a 1-cell, another 1-cell and a 2-cell, which gives the count $1 - 2 + 1$.

lean.statement: $0$ is an Euler number of $T$ in the sense of V3.17, and every Euler number of $T$ is $0$: by V3.20 from $C_0 - C_1 + C_2 = 1 - 2 + 1$, and independently of Morse theory, because the rotation field $(-x_2, x_1, 0)$ is a smooth tangent field on $T$ without zeros. Hence every Morse function on $T$ has $C_0 - C_1 + C_2 = 0$.

diff: A check of V3.20 on the book's own example: the count from the height function agrees with the index sum of a nowhere-vanishing rotation field. By V3.38 the value is also the homological Euler characteristic of $T$; the Betti numbers $1, 2, 1$ themselves are not derived.

items.title: Relative singular homology and the exact sequence of a pair

milnor.label: §5, pp. 28–29
milnor.statement: Milnor quotes the homology of pairs with coefficients in a field, and its exact sequences, as standard (p. 28); on p. 29 he replaces a pair by a homotopy equivalent one without comment.

lean.statement: Coefficients are an object $R$ of an abelian category with coproducts, for instance a field or any commutative ring; pairs $(X, A)$ are embeddings $A \hookrightarrow X$. The relative chain complex $C(X, A)$ is the cokernel of the chain map $C(A) \to C(X)$ of singular chains, which is injective, so that $0 \to C(A) \to C(X) \to C(X, A) \to 0$ is exact; $H_n(X, A)$ is its homology, and both are functorial in maps of pairs. The sequence $\cdots \to H_{n+1}(X, A) \to H_n(A) \to H_n(X) \to H_n(X, A) \to H_{n-1}(A) \to \cdots \to H_0(X) \to H_0(X, A) \to 0$ is exact at every place, and its boundary is natural. $H_n(X, \emptyset) \cong H_n(X)$ naturally, and $H_n(X, X) = 0$. A map of pairs inducing isomorphisms in the homology of both spaces induces isomorphisms in relative homology; maps of pairs homotopic through maps of pairs induce the same maps. If $A \subseteq B \subseteq X$ and $B$ is a strong deformation retract of $X$, then $H_n(B, A) \to H_n(X, A)$ is an isomorphism and $H_n(X, B) = 0$. With these data singular homology is a homotopy-invariant homology pretheory in the sense of Mathlib's formulation of the Eilenberg–Steenrod axioms.

diff: Mathlib has the singular chain complex, absolute singular homology and its homotopy invariance, but no relative homology; everything Milnor quotes about pairs is built here.

The first equality of p. 29 needs homotopy equivalences of pairs; what is proved and used is the version for strong deformation retracts. Homotopy invariance for pairs comes from the absolute one, through the cylinder $(X \times I, A \times I)$ and the five lemma.

items.title: The exact sequence of a triple

milnor.label: §5, pp. 28–30
milnor.statement: Milnor quotes the homology exact sequence of a triple $X \supset Y \supset Z$: its portion $H_\lambda(Y, Z) \to H_\lambda(X, Z) \to H_\lambda(X, Y)$ for subadditivity (p. 28), its final $\to 0$ (p. 29), and its boundary $H_{\lambda+1}(X, Y) \to H_\lambda(Y, Z)$ in Lemma 5.3 (p. 30).

lean.statement: For a triple $Z \subseteq Y \subseteq X$ (two composable embeddings, for instance subsets $A \subseteq B \subseteq D$ of a space), the inclusions of pairs give a short exact sequence $0 \to C(Y, Z) \to C(X, Z) \to C(X, Y) \to 0$, hence the sequence $\cdots \to H_{n+1}(X, Y) \to H_n(Y, Z) \to H_n(X, Z) \to H_n(X, Y) \to H_{n-1}(Y, Z) \to \cdots \to H_0(X, Z) \to H_0(X, Y) \to 0$, exact at every place, whose boundary is the boundary of the pair $(X, Y)$ followed by $H_n(Y) \to H_n(Y, Z)$.

diff: The short exact sequence of relative chains is the third isomorphism theorem $(C(X)/C(Z))/(C(Y)/C(Z)) \cong C(X)/C(Y)$, proved in any abelian category; the sequence of the triple is the long exact sequence of that short exact sequence of complexes.

items.title: Excision

milnor.label: §5, p. 29
milnor.statement: In the computation of $H_*(M^{a_i}, M^{a_{i-1}})$ one equality is justified simply by excision, which Milnor quotes.

lean.statement: (i) If the interiors of a family of subsets of a space $X$ cover $X$, the inclusion of the chains made of simplices each lying in one member of the family into all singular chains is a chain homotopy equivalence, for any coefficients. With coefficients in a commutative ring: (ii) if $A, B \subseteq X$ have interiors covering $X$, then $(B, A \cap B) \to (X, A)$ induces isomorphisms $H_n(B, A \cap B) \cong H_n(X, A)$ for all $n$; (iii) if $Z \subseteq A \subseteq X$ and the closure of $Z$ lies in the interior of $A$, then $(X \setminus Z, A \setminus Z) \to (X, A)$ induces isomorphisms in all degrees.

chips: not literally the step of p. 29
diff: Proved as in Hatcher (Proposition 2.21 and Theorem 2.20), by barycentric subdivision with the diameter bound $(n/(n+1))^k$.
The step Milnor calls excision is not literally an instance of (iii): the closure of the set to be excised does not lie in the interior of $M^{a_{i-1}}$. How the step is made is V3.31.

items.title: The homology of disks, spheres and cells

milnor.label: §5, p. 29
milnor.statement: Milnor quotes that $H_*(e^\lambda, \dot e^\lambda)$ is the coefficient group in dimension $\lambda$ and $0$ otherwise.

lean.statement: Coefficients in a commutative ring $R$; $D^n$ and $S^{n-1}$ are the closed unit ball and unit sphere of $\mathbb R^n$, with $S^{-1} = \emptyset$. $H_i(D^n, S^{n-1}) \cong R$ for $i = n$ and $H_i(D^n, S^{n-1}) = 0$ for $i \ne n$. For $n \ge 1$, $H_0(S^n) \cong R$, $H_n(S^n) \cong R$ and $H_i(S^n) = 0$ for $i \ne 0, n$; $H_0(S^0) \cong R \oplus R$. Over a field, $\dim H_i(D^n, S^{n-1}) = [i = n]$ and $\dim H_i(S^n) = [i = 0] + [i = n]$. More generally, if $E$ is Hausdorff and $\chi : \mathbb R^k \to E$ is continuous and injective on $D^k$, the pair $(\chi(D^k), \chi(S^{k-1}))$ has the homology of $(D^k, S^{k-1})$, and an image of $S^n$ under a map continuous and injective on it has the homology of $S^n$.

diff: Computed by induction on the dimension, through the boundary of the triple $\{q\} \subseteq \chi(S^k) \subseteq \chi(D^{k+1})$, $q$ a point onto which the cell contracts, and excision for the upper hemisphere of $S^k$ attached to the lower one.

items.title: Attaching cells to a closed set: the step “by excision”

milnor.label: §5, p. 29
milnor.statement: For $M^{a_i}$, which has the homotopy type of $M^{a_{i-1}} \cup e^{\lambda_i}$, Milnor writes $H_*(M^{a_{i-1}} \cup e^{\lambda_i}, M^{a_{i-1}}) = H_*(e^{\lambda_i}, \dot e^{\lambda_i})$, by excision, which is the coefficient group in dimension $\lambda_i$ and $0$ otherwise.

lean.statement: Let $E$ be a Hausdorff space, $Y \subseteq X \subseteq E$ with $Y$ closed, and $\chi_j : \mathbb R^{k_j} \to E$, $j = 1, \dots, m$, maps continuous and injective on the closed unit balls $D^{k_j}$, whose cells $e_j = \chi_j(D^{k_j})$ are pairwise disjoint, such that $\chi_j(z) \in Y$ exactly when $\|z\| = 1$, and $X = Y \cup e_1 \cup \dots \cup e_m$. Coefficients in a commutative ring $R$. For one cell of dimension $k$, the inclusion $(e_1, \chi_1(S^{k-1})) \to (X, Y)$ and the characteristic map $(D^k, S^{k-1}) \to (X, Y)$ induce isomorphisms in all degrees: $H_k(X, Y) \cong R$ and $H_i(X, Y) = 0$ for $i \ne k$. For several cells, $H_i(X, Y) \cong R^{c_i}$, $c_i$ the number of cells of dimension $i$; over a field $\dim H_i(X, Y) = c_i$.

diff: The step is not literally excision: the closure of the set to be excised is not inside the interior of $M^{a_{i-1}}$. One first deforms $X$ minus the centre of the cell onto $Y$, pushing the punctured cell radially onto its boundary, and then excises; $Y$ must be closed.

Any number of disjoint cells is allowed, as Remark 3.3 needs: with several cells on one level the exact sequence of a triple gives only an inequality of dimensions, and additivity uses the disjointness of the cells. This is the exposition's Lemma E.

items.title: The Morse inequalities for any filtration of a space

milnor.label: §5, pp. 28–30
milnor.statement: Milnor applies Lemma 5.1 to $R_\lambda$, to $\chi$ and to $S_\lambda$ on the chain $\emptyset = M^{a_0} \subset M^{a_1} \subset \dots \subset M^{a_k} = M$, which gives Theorem 5.2 and the inequalities $(4_\lambda)$.

lean.statement: Let $X_0 \subseteq X_1 \subseteq \cdots$ be subsets of a space and $\Bbbk$ a field. With $H_i(a, b) = H_i(X_b, X_a; \Bbbk)$ for $a \le b$ and the exact sequences of triples of V3.27, singular homology is a homology of a filtration in the sense of V3.9, provided every step $(X_{k+1}, X_k)$ has finite-dimensional homology. Consequently, for $n \ge 1$, if the steps $k < n$ have finite-dimensional homology, so has $(X_n, X_0)$, and with $b_i = \dim H_i(X_n, X_0; \Bbbk)$ and $C_i = \sum_{k < n} \dim H_i(X_{k+1}, X_k; \Bbbk)$: $b_l \le C_l$; $b_l - b_{l-1} + \dots \pm b_0 \le C_l - C_{l-1} + \dots \pm C_0$ for every $l$; and $\sum_{i \le N} (-1)^i b_i = \sum_{i \le N} (-1)^i C_i$ if no step has homology in degree $N + 1$. Under the cell hypothesis of V3.11, $C_i$ is the number of critical points of index $i$, and the alternating sum is $\sum_{p \in P} (-1)^{\mathrm{ind}\,p}$ when every index is at most $N$.

chips: finiteness of the total a consequence
diff: This is the instance of the abstract structure of V3.9 that V3.10–V3.15 lacked. It applies to any filtration of any space whose steps have finite-dimensional homology, not only to sublevel sets, and the finiteness of the homology of $(X_n, X_0)$ is a consequence, not an assumption.

items.title: Betti numbers, and the homology of a slab

milnor.label: §5, pp. 28–29
milnor.statement: $R_\lambda(X, Y)$ is the rank over $F$ of $H_\lambda(X, Y; F)$ (p. 28). On p. 29, $H_*(M^{a_i}, M^{a_{i-1}}) = H_*(M^{a_{i-1}} \cup e^{\lambda_i}, M^{a_{i-1}})$, the pair being replaced, by Theorems 3.1 and 3.2, by one in which $M^{a_i}$ becomes $M^{a_{i-1}}$ with a cell attached.

lean.statement: For a space $X$, $b_i(X) = \dim_\Bbbk H_i(X; \Bbbk)$, Mathlib's singular homology, is Milnor's $R_i(X)$; it is $0$ by convention if $H_i(X; \Bbbk)$ is infinite-dimensional, which never happens for the spaces below. Homeomorphic spaces have the same Betti numbers. If $A \subseteq B \subseteq D$ and $A$ is a strong deformation retract of $B$, then $H_i(D, A) \cong H_i(D, B)$, by the sequence of the triple, in which $H_*(B, A) = 0$. The slab lemma: let $A \subseteq B \subseteq X' \subseteq X$ be subsets of a Hausdorff space, $B$ closed, and $e_1, \dots, e_m$ pairwise disjoint cells attached to $B$ as in V3.31, with $B \cup e_1 \cup \dots \cup e_m \subseteq X'$; if $A$ is a strong deformation retract of $B$, $B \cup e_1 \cup \dots \cup e_m$ one of $X'$, and $X'$ one of $X$, then $H_i(X, A; \Bbbk)$ is finite-dimensional, of dimension the number of cells of dimension $i$.

chips: the bottom moves by a triple
diff: The first equality of p. 29 is about pairs, not spaces: the top of a pair moves along deformations that fix the bottom, but the bottom moves only through the sequence of a triple. This needs strong deformation retracts, whereas Milnor states Theorem 3.2 only up to homotopy type.
With $A = M^{a_{i-1}}$, $B = M^{c-\epsilon}$, $X' = M^{c+\epsilon}$, $X = M^{a_i}$ and $c$ the critical value, this is the slab computation; V3.34 supplies the hypotheses.

items.title: The Morse filtration of a compact submanifold

milnor.label: §5, p. 29
milnor.statement: For a compact $M$ and a differentiable $f$ with isolated, non-degenerate critical points, Milnor takes $a_1 < \dots < a_k$ with exactly $i$ critical points in $M^{a_i}$ and $M^{a_k} = M$, and finds $H_*(M^{a_i}, M^{a_{i-1}})$ to be the coefficient group in dimension $\lambda_i$, the index of the $i$-th critical point, and $0$ in every other dimension.

lean.statement: Let $N$ be a compact slice submanifold of a finite-dimensional real normed space $V$, modelled on a finite-dimensional space, and $F : V \to \mathbb R$ smooth such that every critical point of $f = F|N$ is non-degenerate. (i) If $a' \le a$ are not critical values and all critical values in $(a', a)$ are equal, then $H_i(N^a, N^{a'}; \Bbbk)$ is finite-dimensional, of dimension the number of critical points of index $i$ in $f^{-1}(a', a)$. (ii) There are $n \ge 1$ and non-critical values $a_0 \le a_1 \le \dots$ with $N^{a_0} = \emptyset$, $N^{a_n} = N$ and at most one critical value in each $(a_k, a_{k+1})$; by (i) each step $(N^{a_{k+1}}, N^{a_k})$ has finite-dimensional homology over every field. (iii) Hence $H_i(N; \Bbbk)$ is finite-dimensional for every $i$. These statements hold for every space homeomorphic to $N$, homology being carried along the homeomorphism.

diff: Milnor's choice of the $a_i$ needs distinct critical values; here each slab contains at most one critical value, with any number of critical points on it, handled by Remark 3.3 (V2.9).

$M^{a_0} = \emptyset$ and $M^{a_k} = M$ rest on the minimum and the maximum of $f$ being critical values; the finiteness of $R_\lambda(M)$ is a consequence, not an assumption; and “isolated” is redundant.
The setting is a compact submanifold of a Euclidean space with $f$ the restriction of an ambient function; abstract compact manifolds are reached in V3.39.

items.title: Theorem 5.2 in singular homology

milnor.label: §5, Theorem 5.2
milnor.statement: (The weak Morse inequalities.) On a compact manifold $M$, with $C_\lambda$ the number of critical points of index $\lambda$ and Betti numbers taken over a field $F$: $R_\lambda(M) \le C_\lambda$ and $\sum (-1)^\lambda R_\lambda(M) = \sum (-1)^\lambda C_\lambda$.

lean.statement: In the setting of V3.34, with $n = \dim N$, $b_i = \dim H_i(N; \Bbbk)$ for any field $\Bbbk$, and $C_\lambda = C_\lambda(f)$: (2) $b_\lambda \le C_\lambda$ for every $\lambda$; (3) $\sum_{i=0}^n (-1)^i b_i = \sum_{\lambda=0}^n (-1)^\lambda C_\lambda$; and $H_i(N; \Bbbk) = 0$ for $i > n$, so that the left side of (3) is the whole alternating sum. The same holds for every space homeomorphic to $N$.

diff: $M$ is a compact submanifold of a Euclidean space and $f$ the restriction of a smooth function on the ambient space; abstract compact manifolds are V3.39.

Every topological input of p. 29 is proved: the homology of pairs and triples (V3.26, V3.27), the cell computation (V3.31) and the slab homology (V3.34). $R_\lambda(M) = 0$ for $\lambda > n$, which makes $\sum (-1)^\lambda R_\lambda(M)$ a finite sum, follows from (2).

items.title: The strong Morse inequalities in singular homology

milnor.label: §5, the Morse inequalities
milnor.statement: For every $\lambda$, $R_\lambda(M) - R_{\lambda-1}(M) + \dots \pm R_0(M) \le C_\lambda - C_{\lambda-1} + \dots \pm C_0$, from Lemma 5.1 applied to the subadditive $S_\lambda$ on $\emptyset \subset M^{a_1} \subset \dots \subset M^{a_k}$.

lean.statement: In the setting of V3.35, over every field: $b_\lambda - b_{\lambda-1} + \dots \pm b_0 \le C_\lambda - C_{\lambda-1} + \dots \pm C_0$ for every $\lambda$.

diff: As for V3.35: proved for compact submanifolds of a Euclidean space, with every topological input proved; abstract compact manifolds are V3.39.

items.title: Corollary 5.4 and the lacunary principle in singular homology

milnor.label: §5, Corollary 5.4
milnor.statement: If $C_{\lambda+1} = C_{\lambda-1} = 0$ then $R_\lambda = C_\lambda$ and $R_{\lambda+1} = R_{\lambda-1} = 0$. Milnor notes that the corollary finds the homology groups of complex projective space (§4) without Theorem 3.5.

lean.statement: In the setting of V3.35, over every field: if $\lambda \ge 1$ and $C_{\lambda+1} = C_{\lambda-1} = 0$, then $b_\lambda = C_\lambda$ and $b_{\lambda+1} = b_{\lambda-1} = 0$; if $C_1 = 0$, then $b_0 = C_0$ and $b_1 = 0$; and if no two consecutive $C_i$ are non-zero, then $b_i = C_i$ for every $i$.

diff: Proved for compact submanifolds of a Euclidean space; abstract compact manifolds are V3.39.
The lacunary form is added. Integral homology groups are not derived and $\mathbb CP^n$ is not constructed, so Milnor's application is not reached.

items.title: The Euler characteristic, three ways

milnor.label: §5, p. 28, and formula (3)
milnor.statement: Milnor's Euler characteristic is $\chi(X, Y) = \sum (-1)^\lambda R_\lambda(X, Y)$ (p. 28); formula (3) gives $\chi(M) = C_0 - C_1 + \dots \pm C_n$ (p. 29), and in Application 2 (pp. 36–37) $\chi(M)$ is the index sum of every vector field. That $\chi(M)$ is the same over every field is never stated.

lean.statement: (i) Let $N \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}$, $K \ge 1$, be a compact non-empty slice submanifold of dimension $d + 1 \ge 1$. Every Euler number $\chi$ of $N$ (V3.17, the Poincaré–Hopf integer) satisfies $\chi = \sum_{i=0}^{d+1} (-1)^i \dim H_i(N; \Bbbk)$ for every field $\Bbbk$; the same holds for every space homeomorphic to $N$. (ii) For a compact Hausdorff smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, modelled on a finite-dimensional real normed space, the integer $\chi(M)$ of V4.18 ($\sum_\lambda (-1)^\lambda C_\lambda$ for any Morse function) equals $\sum_{i=0}^{\dim M} (-1)^i \dim H_i(M; \Bbbk)$ for every field $\Bbbk$. In particular this alternating sum does not depend on the field.

diff: The three descriptions of $\chi$, by homology, by critical points and by index sums of vector fields, are identified, which closes the circle left open in V3.20 and V4.19.

Passing from $M$ to an embedded copy uses the invariance of homology under homeomorphisms, which the book never states. The proof applies (3) of V3.35 to a Morse function $L_p = \|\cdot - p\|^2$ (Theorem 6.6, V4.12) and compares with V3.20, resp. V4.19, through a Whitney embedding.

items.title: The Morse inequalities on a compact manifold

milnor.label: §5, Theorem 5.2 and Corollary 5.4
milnor.statement: §5 is stated for a compact manifold $M$ and a function with isolated, non-degenerate critical points: $R_\lambda(M) \le C_\lambda$, $\sum (-1)^\lambda R_\lambda(M) = \sum (-1)^\lambda C_\lambda$, the inequalities $(4_\lambda)$ and Corollary 5.4, for Betti numbers over a field.

lean.statement: The homology over any field of a compact $k$-dimensional slice submanifold of $\mathbb R^n$, or of a space homeomorphic to one, is finite-dimensional and vanishes above degree $k$. Let $M$ be a compact Hausdorff smooth manifold without boundary, modelled on a finite-dimensional real normed space, of dimension $n$. Then $H_i(M; \Bbbk)$ is finite-dimensional and is $0$ for $i > n$, and for every Morse function $g$ on $M$, with $b_i = \dim H_i(M; \Bbbk)$ and $C_\lambda = C_\lambda(g)$: $b_\lambda \le C_\lambda$; $(4_\lambda)$; $\sum_{i \le n} (-1)^i b_i = \sum_{\lambda \le n} (-1)^\lambda C_\lambda$; and $b_i = C_i$ for every $i$ if no two consecutive $C_i$ are non-zero.

diff: Hausdorffness is assumed, for the embedding; Milnor's manifolds are tacitly Hausdorff.

The proof passes through a Whitney embedding $M \cong N \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}$ (V4.16), on which $g$ becomes the restriction of a smooth ambient function with the same numbers $C_\lambda$ (V4.15), and homology is carried back along the homeomorphism; dimension $0$ is done directly from (3).
Non-compact manifolds and integral homology are not covered.

items.title: The normal bundle and the endpoint map

milnor.label: §6, p. 32
milnor.statement: For a $k$-dimensional manifold $M$ differentiably embedded in $\mathbb R^n$, $k < n$, Milnor takes the set $N \subset M \times \mathbb R^n$ of pairs $(q, v)$ with $v$ perpendicular to $M$ at $q$, the total space of the normal vector bundle, which, he says, is not difficult to show to be an $n$-manifold differentiably embedded in $\mathbb R^{2n}$; and the endpoint map $E : N \to \mathbb R^n$, $E(q, v) = q + v$.

lean.statement: Throughout, $M \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ is a slice submanifold modelled on $\mathbb R^k$ with complement $\mathbb R^w$; if $M$ is non-empty, $k + w = n$. The normal bundle is $N = \{(q, v) \in M \times \mathbb R^n : v \perp T_qM\}$; when $k + w = n$ it is a slice submanifold of $\mathbb R^n \times \mathbb R^n$ of dimension $n$ (the Milnor project's construction). The endpoint map is $E(q, v) = q + v$; more generally, for a map $\Gamma : \mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R^n$, $E_\Gamma(q, v) = \Gamma(q) + v$, smooth over every open set on which $\Gamma$ is smooth, with $E_{\mathrm{id}} = E$.

diff: “Differentiably embedded” must mean a submanifold, which a slice submanifold is: an injectively immersed manifold need not be one (V4.14).

$k = n$ is allowed and $M$ need not be closed or compact. That $N$ is an $n$-manifold, which Milnor calls not difficult, is the Milnor project's construction of the normal bundle as a slice submanifold; for slice charts, $k + w = n$ needs $M \ne \emptyset$.
The twisted endpoint map $E_\Gamma$ is not in the book; it serves the perturbation argument of V4.20.

items.title: Focal points and their multiplicity

milnor.label: §6, Definition
milnor.statement: A point $e = q + v$, $(q, v) \in N$, is a focal point of $(M, q)$, of multiplicity $\mu$, when the Jacobian of $E$ at $(q, v)$ has nullity $\mu > 0$, and a focal point of $M$ when it is one of $(M, q)$ for some $q \in M$; intuitively, focal points are where nearby normals meet. The proof of Corollary 6.2 uses that the focal points are exactly the images under $E$ of its critical points.

lean.statement: Assume $k + w = n$. The nullity of $E$ at $x \in N$ is the dimension of the kernel of $dE_x$, the tangent space of $N$ at $x$ being identified with $\mathbb R^n$ by the chart of $N$ at $x$. A point $e \in \mathbb R^n$ is a focal point of $(M, q)$ with multiplicity $\mu$ if $(q, e - q) \in N$ and the nullity of $E$ at $(q, e - q)$ is $\mu > 0$; a focal point of $(M, q)$ if this holds for some $\mu$; and a focal point of $M$ if it is a focal point of $(M, q)$ for some $q \in M$. The nullity is positive exactly at the critical points of $E$, the points where $dE$ is not onto; so the set of focal points of $M$ is the set of critical values of $E$.

chips: nullity read in a chart of $N$
diff: The nullity is computed in a chart of $N$; it does not depend on the chart, two charts differing by an isomorphism of $\mathbb R^n$.
The characterization used in the proof of Corollary 6.2 is proved as an equality of sets.

items.title: Theorem 6.1 (Sard)

milnor.label: §6, Theorem 6.1 (Sard)
milnor.statement: For a $C^1$ map $f : M_1 \to M_2$ between differentiable manifolds of the same dimension, each with a countable basis, the critical points, where the Jacobian of $f$ is singular, have an image of measure $0$ in $M_2$. Milnor gives no proof, referring to de Rham.

lean.statement: Let $M$ be a second countable smooth manifold without boundary modelled on a finite-dimensional real normed space $E$, $F$ a finite-dimensional real normed space with a Haar measure $\mu$, $U \subseteq M$ open and $f : M \to F$ smooth on $U$. Then the image under $f$ of the points of $U$ where $df$ is not onto is $\mu$-null; in particular, for $f$ smooth on $M$, the set of critical values is null. $E$ and $F$ are required to lie in the same universe of Lean's type theory, a formality with no mathematical content.

diff: $f$ is smooth, not merely $C^1$, and the target is a vector space; on the other hand the dimensions are arbitrary. Every use in §6 is for a smooth map into $\mathbb R^n$.
“Measure $0$” in the target needs a measure class; only $\mathbb R^n$ is used, where all Haar measures have the same null sets.
The proof uses countably many charts and the Euclidean Sard theorem of the Milnor project, which is proved for smooth maps only.

items.title: Corollary 6.2: almost no point is focal

milnor.label: §6, Corollary 6.2
milnor.statement: Almost every point of $\mathbb R^n$ is not a focal point of $M$. Proof: $N$ is an $n$-manifold and the focal points are the images of the critical points of $E : N \to \mathbb R^n$, so they form a set of measure $0$ by Sard's theorem.

lean.statement: If $k + w = n$, the set of focal points of $M$ is null for every Haar measure on $\mathbb R^n$.

diff: Sard's theorem needs $N$ to have a countable basis, automatic for a subset of $\mathbb R^{2n}$; $M$ need not be closed or compact.

items.title: The first and second fundamental forms

milnor.label: §6, pp. 33–34
milnor.statement: In local coordinates $u^1, \dots, u^k$ on $M \subset \mathbb R^n$, with $\vec x(u)$ the inclusion, the first fundamental form is the matrix $g_{ij} = \partial\vec x/\partial u^i \cdot \partial\vec x/\partial u^j$, and the second fundamental form is the symmetric matrix $(\vec\ell_{ij})$ of vector-valued functions, $\vec\ell_{ij}$ the normal component of $\partial^2\vec x/\partial u^i\partial u^j$. For a unit vector $\vec v$ normal to $M$ at $q$, the matrix $(\vec v \cdot \vec\ell_{ij})$ is the second fundamental form of $M$ at $q$ in the direction $\vec v$. Milnor gives no invariant definition and works in a fixed coordinate system.

lean.statement: For $q \in M$, the coordinates $u \mapsto x(u)$ are the inverse of the slice chart of $M$ chosen at $q$, with $x(u_q) = q$; $dx$ and $d^2x$ are its first and second derivatives at $u_q$. The first fundamental form is the bilinear form $g(\xi, \eta) = \langle dx\,\xi, dx\,\eta\rangle$ on $\mathbb R^k$; the second fundamental form in a direction $v \in \mathbb R^n$ is $\ell_v(\xi, \eta) = \langle v, d^2x(\xi, \eta)\rangle$; and for a linear map $T$ of $\mathbb R^n$ the form $(\xi, \eta) \mapsto \langle T\,dx\,\xi, dx\,\eta\rangle - \ell_v(\xi, \eta)$ is the one attached to $E_\Gamma$ with $T = d\Gamma_q$, equal to $g - \ell_v$ for $T = \mathrm{id}$.

chips: the coordinates of a slice chart
diff: $\ell_v$ is defined for every $v$ by the inner product with $d^2x$; for $v$ normal at $q$ it is Milnor's $(\vec v \cdot \vec\ell_{ij})$, the tangential part of $d^2x$ being orthogonal to $v$.
The coordinates are those of the chosen slice chart, where Milnor allows any coordinates.

items.title: Principal curvatures

milnor.label: §6, p. 34
milnor.statement: In coordinates for which $(g_{ij})$ is the identity matrix at $q$, the principal curvatures $K_1, \dots, K_n$ of $M$ at $q$ in the normal direction $\vec v$ are the eigenvalues of $(\vec v \cdot \vec\ell_{ij})$; the reciprocals of those that are non-zero are the principal radii of curvature.

lean.statement: The shape operator $S_v$ of $M$ at $q$ in the direction $v$ is the endomorphism of the tangent space $T_qM = \operatorname{range} dx$ with $\langle S_v a, b\rangle = \ell_v(dx^{-1}a, dx^{-1}b)$; it is self-adjoint. The principal curvatures of $M$ at $q$ in the direction $v$ are its $k$ eigenvalues, with multiplicity, in decreasing order; the multiplicity of $K$ is the dimension of the eigenspace of $K$.

diff: No normalization: the eigenvalues of $S_v$ are those of $g^{-1}(v \cdot \ell)$, which are Milnor's $K_i$ when $g$ is the identity. That coordinates with $g_{ij}(q) = \delta_{ij}$ exist, and that the eigenvalues do not depend on them, the book leaves implicit.
That $S_v$ does not depend on the parametrization is not proved, and nothing uses it.
The scan lists the curvatures as $K_1, \dots, K_n$; there are $k$ of them, and Lemma 6.3 itself uses $1 \le i \le k$.

items.title: Lemma 6.3: focal points along a normal line

milnor.label: §6, Lemma 6.3
milnor.statement: Let $\vec v$ be a unit normal to $M$ at $\vec q$. On the normal line $\ell = \{\vec q + t\vec v\}$ the focal points of $(M, q)$ are exactly the points $\vec q + K_i^{-1}\vec v$ with $1 \le i \le k$ and $K_i \ne 0$; counted with their multiplicities, there are therefore at most $k$ of them on $\ell$.

lean.statement: Assume $k + w = n$, and let $\mathrm{mult}_q(e)$ be the multiplicity of $e$ as a focal point of $(M, q)$, $0$ if it is not one. For $q \in M$, $v \perp T_qM$ and $t \in \mathbb R$: $\mathrm{mult}_q(q + tv) = 0$ if $t = 0$, and otherwise it is the multiplicity of $1/t$ as an eigenvalue of $S_v$. Hence $q + tv$ is a focal point of $(M, q)$ iff $t = K^{-1}$ for a non-zero principal curvature $K$ in the direction $v$, the multiplicity of $q + K^{-1}v$ is that of $K$, and for any finitely many values of $t$ the multiplicities of the points $q + tv$ add up to at most $k$.

chips: any normal $v$, not only unit ones
diff: $v$ is any normal vector, not necessarily a unit vector.

$t = 0$ must be set aside in “$1/t$ is an eigenvalue”: $q$ is never a focal point of $(M, q)$ (V4.9). The multiplicity of an eigenvalue of a symmetric matrix as a root of the characteristic polynomial equals the dimension of its eigenspace, which is what the proof produces.
In place of Milnor's normalized coordinates, for $t \ne 0$ the map $dx$ carries the null space of $g - t\ell_v$ onto the eigenspace of $S_v$ for $1/t$.

items.title: The Jacobian of the endpoint map

milnor.label: §6, proof of Lemma 6.3
milnor.statement: Milnor chooses unit normal fields $\vec w_1, \dots, \vec w_{n-k}$, orthogonal to each other, coordinates $(u, t)$ on $N$ given by $(u, t) \mapsto (\vec x(u), \sum_\alpha t^\alpha\vec w_\alpha(u))$, and takes inner products of the partial derivatives of $E$ with $\partial\vec x/\partial u^1, \dots, \partial\vec x/\partial u^k, \vec w_1, \dots, \vec w_{n-k}$. This gives an $n \times n$ matrix whose rank equals that of the Jacobian of $E$, with an identity block below; he says its rank is the rank of the upper left block, which is $(g_{ij} - \sum_\alpha t^\alpha \vec w_\alpha \cdot \vec\ell_{ij})$.

lean.statement: Assume $k + w = n$ and let $(q, v) \in N$. A pair $(a, b) \in \mathbb R^n \times \mathbb R^n$ is tangent to $N$ at $(q, v)$ iff $a = dx\,\xi$ for some $\xi \in \mathbb R^k$ and $\langle b, dx\,\eta\rangle + \langle v, d^2x(\xi, \eta)\rangle = 0$ for every $\eta \in \mathbb R^k$. For $\Gamma$ differentiable at $q$, the derivative of $E_\Gamma$ at $(q, v)$ is $(a, b) \mapsto d\Gamma_q(a) + b$ on this tangent space, and its nullity equals the nullity of the form $(\xi, \eta) \mapsto \langle d\Gamma_q\,dx\,\xi, dx\,\eta\rangle - \langle v, d^2x(\xi, \eta)\rangle$ on $\mathbb R^k$. For $\Gamma = \mathrm{id}$: the nullity of $E$ at $(q, v)$ is the nullity of $g - \ell_v$.

diff: No normal frame is used: the tangent space of $N$ is the kernel of the derivative of the local defining function of $N$, and its second condition is the derivative of Milnor's identity $\vec w_\alpha \cdot \partial\vec x/\partial u^j = 0$. The fields $\vec w_\alpha$ exist only locally, and the book does not say why they exist.
The sentence that the rank of the matrix equals the rank of the upper left block does not hold as written, the two ranks differing by $n - k$; what holds, and is needed, is that the nullities agree.

items.title: Assertion 6.4

milnor.label: §6, Assertion 6.4
milnor.statement: For a unit normal $\vec v$, $\vec q + t\vec v$ is a focal point of $(M, q)$ of multiplicity $\mu$ exactly when the matrix $(g_{ij} - t\,\vec v \cdot \vec\ell_{ij})$ is singular of nullity $\mu$.

lean.statement: Assume $k + w = n$. For $q \in M$, $v \perp T_qM$, $t \in \mathbb R$ and $\mu \in \mathbb N$: $q + tv$ is a focal point of $(M, q)$ with multiplicity $\mu$ iff the form $g - t\ell_v$ (in the coordinates of V4.5) has nullity $\mu > 0$. In particular $q$ is never a focal point of $(M, q)$, $g$ being non-degenerate.

diff: $v$ need not be a unit vector, and the case $t = 0$, left implicit, is part of the statement: $q$ is never a focal point of $(M, q)$.

items.title: The critical points and the Hessian of $L_p$

milnor.label: §6, pp. 35–36
milnor.statement: For fixed $\vec p \in \mathbb R^n$, $f = L_{\vec p}$ satisfies $f(\vec x(u)) = \|\vec x(u) - \vec p\|^2$ and $\partial f/\partial u^i = 2\,\partial\vec x/\partial u^i \cdot (\vec x - \vec p)$, so $f$ has a critical point at $\vec q$ iff $\vec q - \vec p$ is normal to $M$ at $\vec q$. At a critical point the second partial derivatives are $2(\partial\vec x/\partial u^i \cdot \partial\vec x/\partial u^j + \partial^2\vec x/\partial u^i\partial u^j \cdot (\vec x - \vec p))$, which on setting $\vec p = \vec x + t\vec v$ becomes $2(g_{ij} - t\,\vec v \cdot \vec\ell_{ij})$.
milnor.note: The second display is cut off in the scan; its value is the one used on p. 38.

lean.statement: For $p \in \mathbb R^n$ let $L_p(q) = \|q - p\|^2$ on $M$. Then $q$ is a critical point of $L_p$ iff $p - q \perp T_qM$, that is, iff $(q, p - q) \in N$; and at every $q \in M$ the Hessian of $L_p \circ x$ at $u_q$ is $2(g - \ell_{p - q})$.

chips: at every point, not only critical ones
no unit vector, no case $p = q$
diff: Setting $\vec p = \vec q + t\vec v$ with $\vec v$ a unit normal presupposes that $p - q$ is normal, that is, that $q$ is critical, and that $p \ne q$. The formula is proved at every point, in the direction $p - q$ itself, so neither is needed.

items.title: Lemma 6.5

milnor.label: §6, Lemma 6.5
milnor.statement: A point $\vec q \in M$ is a degenerate critical point of $L_{\vec p}$ exactly when $\vec p$ is a focal point of $(M, \vec q)$, and the nullity of the critical point is then the multiplicity of the focal point.

lean.statement: Assume $k + w = n$, and let $p \in \mathbb R^n$, $q \in M$. If $q$ is a critical point of $L_p$, the nullity of $L_p$ at $q$ (the nullity of its Hessian) equals the nullity of $E$ at $(q, p - q)$. Hence $p$ is a focal point of $(M, q)$ with multiplicity $\mu$ iff $q$ is a critical point of $L_p$ of nullity $\mu > 0$, and $q$ is a degenerate critical point of $L_p$ iff $p$ is a focal point of $(M, q)$.

diff: The case of a non-critical $q$, left implicit, is covered: then $p - q$ is not normal at $q$ and $p$ is not a focal point of $(M, q)$.

items.title: Theorem 6.6

milnor.label: §6, Theorem 6.6
milnor.statement: Outside a set of measure $0$ of points $\vec p \in \mathbb R^n$, the function $L_{\vec p} : M \to \mathbb R$ has no degenerate critical point; Milnor obtains this at once from Lemma 6.5 and Corollary 6.2.

lean.statement: For every slice submanifold $M \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ and every Haar measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R^n$ (in particular Lebesgue measure), for $\mu$-almost every $p$ the function $L_p$ is a Morse function on $M$, smooth with only non-degenerate critical points. If $L_p$ is not a Morse function, $p$ is a focal point of $M$. Every non-empty open subset of $\mathbb R^n$ contains a $p$ for which $L_p$ is a Morse function.

diff: $M$ need not be closed or compact, $k = n$ is allowed, and any Haar measure may be used. $M = \emptyset$ is trivial, and is the only case in which $k + w = n$ may fail.

items.title: Corollary 6.7 for closed submanifolds of $\mathbb R^n$

milnor.label: §6, Corollary 6.7
milnor.statement: Every manifold $M$ carries a differentiable function without degenerate critical points all of whose sublevel sets $M^a$ are compact. The proof applies Theorem 6.6 to $M$ embedded differentiably as a closed subset of $\mathbb R^{2n+1}$, which Whitney's theorem provides.

lean.statement: If the slice submanifold $M \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ is a closed subset, then for every $p$ and every $a$ the sublevel set $\{q \in M : L_p(q) \le a\}$ is compact; so for almost every $p$, $L_p$ is a Morse function on $M$ with compact sublevel sets, and $M$ carries a Morse function $f$ each of whose sublevel sets $M^a$ is compact and contains only finitely many critical points. If $M$ is compact, for almost every $p$, $L_p$ is a Morse function with finitely many critical points.

diff: Proved for closed submanifolds of $\mathbb R^n$; abstract compact manifolds are V4.17, and non-compact abstract manifolds are not covered, Mathlib's Whitney embedding being for compact manifolds only.

The embedding must be closed: for the open interval in $\mathbb R$, every $L_p$ has a non-compact sublevel set. And “any manifold” must be read as Hausdorff with a countable basis: on the long line every continuous real function is eventually constant, so some sublevel set is not compact.

items.title: The image of an embedding is a submanifold

milnor.label: §6, proof of Corollary 6.7
milnor.statement: Not stated. In the proof of Corollary 6.7 Milnor applies Theorem 6.6, a statement about manifolds in $\mathbb R^n$, to the image of Whitney's embedding, taking for granted that the image is a submanifold diffeomorphic to $M$.

lean.statement: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold without boundary modelled on a finite-dimensional real normed space $E$, $F$ a finite-dimensional real normed space, and $e : M \to F$ smooth, a topological embedding (a homeomorphism onto its image), with injective derivative at every point. For finite-dimensional $Z$, $W$ with $\dim Z = \dim E$ and $\dim Z + \dim W = \dim F$, the image $e(M)$ is a slice submanifold of $F$ modelled on $Z$ with complement $W$, and $e : M \to e(M)$ is a smooth diffeomorphism.

chips: the inverse smooth by slice charts
diff: $e$ must be a homeomorphism onto its image: the figure eight, an injectively immersed line, is not a submanifold. The inverse of $e$ is smooth because of the slice charts, not merely because $e$ is a smooth bijection, as $x \mapsto x^3$ on $\mathbb R$ shows.

The proof is the local immersion theorem, from the Milnor project's inverse function theorem on manifolds, applied to $(z, w) \mapsto e(\varphi^{-1}(Tz)) + Lw$, with $\varphi$ a chart of $M$, $T : Z \cong E$, and $L$ completing $de_x$ to an isomorphism.

items.title: The Morse notions are invariant under diffeomorphisms

milnor.label: §6, p. 36
milnor.statement: Not stated; used without comment wherever a manifold is replaced by its image under an embedding, as in the proof of Corollary 6.7.

lean.statement: Let $g : M \to M'$ be a smooth diffeomorphism of smooth manifolds without boundary modelled on real normed spaces $E$, $E'$, and $f : M \to \mathbb R$. For every $f$, $q$ is a critical point of $f \circ g^{-1}$ iff $g^{-1}(q)$ is a critical point of $f$, and the numbers of critical points agree. If $f$ is $C^2$ at a critical point $g^{-1}(q)$, the Hessian of $f \circ g^{-1}$ at $q$ is the Hessian of $f$ at $g^{-1}(q)$ pulled back by $d(g^{-1})_q$, so non-degeneracy, index and nullity agree there. $f$ is a Morse function iff $f \circ g^{-1}$ is, and for $f$ of class $C^2$ the numbers $C_\lambda$ of $f$ and $f \circ g^{-1}$ agree.

diff: Every result of this edition about an abstract compact manifold (V2.4, V3.39, V4.17, V4.19, V4.22, V4.24) is proved on an embedded copy and carried back by these invariances.

items.title: Whitney's embedding, for compact manifolds

milnor.label: §6, proof of Corollary 6.7
milnor.statement: An $n$-dimensional manifold can be embedded differentiably as a closed subset of $\mathbb R^{2n+1}$; Milnor quotes Whitney, Geometric Integration Theory, p. 113.

lean.statement: Let $M$ be a compact Hausdorff smooth manifold without boundary modelled on a finite-dimensional real normed space $E$, $n = \dim E$. Then $M$ has a smooth closed embedding with injective derivative into some $\mathbb R^m$ (Mathlib's Whitney embedding), whose image is a slice submanifold modelled on $E$; such an embedding exists into $\mathbb R^{K+1}$ with $K \ge 1$ and $K + 1$ as large as desired; and $M$ is diffeomorphic to a compact, closed slice submanifold $N \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}$, $K \ge 1$, modelled on $\mathbb R^n$.

diff: Compact manifolds only, Hausdorff as Milnor's tacitly are: Mathlib's Whitney embedding is for compact manifolds.
The ambient dimension is not $2n + 1$, which plays no role; $K \ge 1$ is arranged by two extra zero coordinates, for the Poincaré–Hopf theorem.

items.title: Corollary 6.7 for a compact manifold

milnor.label: §6, Corollary 6.7
milnor.statement: Every manifold $M$ carries a differentiable function without degenerate critical points all of whose sublevel sets $M^a$ are compact.

lean.statement: Every compact Hausdorff smooth manifold without boundary, modelled on a finite-dimensional real normed space, carries a Morse function, and it has finitely many critical points.

diff: Only compact $M$, where every $M^a$ is compact anyway; the function is $L_p$ on an embedded copy (V4.16, V4.13), pulled back by the diffeomorphism (V4.15).
A non-compact abstract manifold would need a closed embedding into Euclidean space, which Mathlib does not have.

items.title: The Euler number of an abstract manifold

milnor.label: §5, formula (3)
milnor.statement: $\chi(M) = C_0 - C_1 + C_2 - \dots \pm C_n$ for a function with isolated, non-degenerate critical points on a compact manifold, where $\chi$ is the Euler characteristic of p. 28, defined from the Betti numbers.

lean.statement: For a manifold $M$ modelled on $E$, $\chi(M) = \sum_{\lambda=0}^{\dim E} (-1)^\lambda C_\lambda(f)$ for one Morse function $f$ on $M$ chosen once and for all, and $\chi(M) = 0$ if $M$ has no Morse function.

diff: Defined through critical points, not homology. The value must not depend on the choice of $f$, which is V4.19 for compact Hausdorff $M$; there it equals $\sum_i (-1)^i \dim H_i(M; F)$ for every field $F$ (V3.38).

items.title: Formula (3) and Application 2 on a compact manifold

milnor.label: §6, Application 2
milnor.statement: On a compact $M$ some vector field has index sum $\chi(M)$ over its critical points: for a differentiable $f$, $\chi(M) = \sum (-1)^\lambda C_\lambda$, and $\mathrm{grad} f$ has index $(-1)^\lambda$ where $f$ has index $\lambda$. Since the index sum is a topological invariant (Steenrod, §39.7), every vector field on $M$ has index sum $\chi(M)$.

lean.statement: Let $M$ be a compact Hausdorff smooth manifold without boundary modelled on a finite-dimensional real normed space. (i) Every Morse function $f$ on $M$ has $\sum_{\lambda=0}^{\dim M} (-1)^\lambda C_\lambda(f) = \chi(M)$; in dimension $0$ both sides are the number of points of $M$. (ii) If $\dim M = d + 1 \ge 1$ and $N \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}$, $K \ge 1$, is a compact non-empty slice submanifold modelled on $\mathbb R^{d+1}$ and diffeomorphic to $M$, every Euler number of $N$ (V3.17) equals $\chi(M)$, so the Poincaré–Hopf integer does not depend on the embedding. (iii) $\chi$ is invariant under diffeomorphisms between compact Hausdorff manifolds. (iv) If $M$ is non-empty of dimension $d + 1$, it is diffeomorphic to a compact $N \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}$ on which every smooth tangent field with finitely many zeros has index sum $\chi(M)$.

chips: vector fields on an embedded copy
diff: Vector fields and their indices are defined in the Milnor project only for submanifolds of Euclidean space, so Application 2 is stated on an embedded copy; the topological invariance that Milnor quotes from Steenrod is replaced by the Poincaré–Hopf theorem and invariance under diffeomorphisms.
$\chi(M)$ is the integer of V4.18; it equals the Poincaré–Hopf integer of every embedded copy and, by V3.38, the homological Euler characteristic.
“Any differentiable function” must be a Morse function, and Hausdorffness is assumed.

items.title: The generic linear perturbation

milnor.label: §6, proof of Corollary 6.8
milnor.statement: Not in this form. Milnor's proof of Corollary 6.8 uses $L_p$ on an embedding $h : M \to \mathbb R^n$ whose first coordinate is the given function $f$, with $p$ close to $(-c, 0, \dots, 0)$ for a large $c$.

lean.statement: For every slice submanifold $M \subseteq \mathbb R^n$, every smooth $f : M \to \mathbb R$ and every Haar measure on $\mathbb R^n$: for almost every $a \in \mathbb R^n$, $f + \langle a, \cdot\rangle$ is a Morse function on $M$, and such $a$ exist in every non-empty open set. For $f = \frac12\|x\|^2$ this is Theorem 6.6, since $\frac12\|x\|^2 + \langle a, x\rangle = \frac12 L_{-a}(x) - \frac12\|a\|^2$.

diff: The standard linear perturbation, used in place of Milnor's construction. The proof is that of Theorem 6.6 with $L_p$ replaced by $f + \langle a, \cdot\rangle$ and $E$ by $E_\Gamma$, $\Gamma = -\nabla F$ for a local extension $F$ of $f$: a degenerate critical point $q$ makes $(q, a + \nabla F(q))$ a critical point of $E_\Gamma$ with value $a$ (V4.8), and Sard's theorem (V4.3) on countably many pieces of $N$ finishes.

items.title: Corollary 6.8 on a submanifold of $\mathbb R^n$

milnor.label: §6, Corollary 6.8
milnor.statement: A bounded smooth $f : M \to \mathbb R$ is a uniform limit of smooth functions $g$ without degenerate critical points, and $g$ may be chosen so that, on a given compact set $K$, its derivatives of every order $i \le k$ are uniformly close to those of $f$.

lean.statement: Let $M \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be any slice submanifold, $f : M \to \mathbb R$ smooth, bounded or not, $\varepsilon > 0$, $r \in \mathbb N$, and finitely many smooth coordinate systems $y_j$ on open subsets of $M$, with values in $\mathbb R^k$, with compact sets $K_j$ inside their ranges. There is a Morse function $g$ on $M$ with $|g - f| < \varepsilon$ on all of $M$ and $\|D^i((g - f) \circ y_j^{-1})(u)\| < \varepsilon$ for every $j$, every $i \le r$ and every $u \in K_j$. One can take $g = f + \langle a, \beta(\cdot)\rangle$ with $a$ small, where $\beta(y) = y/\sqrt{1 + \|y\|^2}$ is the diffeomorphism of $\mathbb R^n$ onto its open unit ball; for compact $M$ also $g = f + \langle a, \cdot\rangle$.

diff: No boundedness hypothesis on $f$: the perturbation $\langle a, \beta(\cdot)\rangle$ is bounded by $\|a\|$, whatever $f$ is. $M$ need not be compact; it is a submanifold of $\mathbb R^n$, and abstract compact $M$ is V4.22.
Derivatives on a manifold exist only in coordinates, so the approximation on $K$ is read in fixed coordinate systems covering $K$; finitely many suffice.

Milnor's embedding with bounded image and first coordinate $f$ is not constructed; the proof is V4.20 applied to the submanifold $\beta(M)$ and $f \circ \beta^{-1}$, the Morse property carried back along $\beta$.

items.title: Corollary 6.8 on a compact manifold

milnor.label: §6, Corollary 6.8
milnor.statement: Any bounded smooth function on $M$ is a uniform limit of smooth functions without degenerate critical points, which can be chosen so that their derivatives of order at most $k$ on a given compact set approximate those of $f$.

lean.statement: (i) Let $M$ be a smooth manifold without boundary modelled on a finite-dimensional real normed space, $e : M \to \mathbb R^n$ smooth, a topological embedding with injective derivative, and $f : M \to \mathbb R$ smooth. Then $f + \langle a, e(\cdot)\rangle$ is a Morse function for almost every $a$, for any Haar measure. (ii) If $M$ is compact and Hausdorff, then for every smooth $f$, $\varepsilon > 0$, $r \in \mathbb N$, and finitely many smooth coordinate systems $y_j$, with values in a real normed space, with compact sets $K_j$ inside their ranges, there is a Morse function $g$ with $|g - f| < \varepsilon$ on $M$ and every derivative of order at most $r$ of $(g - f) \circ y_j^{-1}$ of norm $< \varepsilon$ on $K_j$; one can take $g = f + \langle a, e(\cdot)\rangle$, $e$ Mathlib's Whitney embedding.

diff: (ii) is for compact Hausdorff $M$ only, where Milnor's boundedness of $f$ is automatic; non-compact abstract manifolds would need a closed embedding into Euclidean space.
The perturbation is $\langle a, e(\cdot)\rangle$ along an embedding, not Milnor's $L_p$ on an embedding with first coordinate $f$.

items.title: Lemma 6.9: the index of $L_p$

milnor.label: §6, Lemma 6.9
milnor.statement: At a non-degenerate critical point $\vec q$ of $L_{\vec p}$, the index is the number of focal points of $(M, \vec q)$ on the segment from $\vec q$ to $\vec p$, counted with multiplicity. The proof (p. 38): the index of $2(g_{ij} - t\,\vec v \cdot \vec\ell_{ij})$ is its number of negative eigenvalues, which, for $(g_{ij})$ the identity, is the number of eigenvalues of $(\vec v \cdot \vec\ell_{ij})$ that are $\ge 1/t$; compare Lemma 6.3.
milnor.note: Milnor adds that an analogous statement in Part III, the Morse index theorem, will be of fundamental importance.

lean.statement: (i) The index of $g - \ell_v$ is the number of principal curvatures in the direction $v$, counted with multiplicity, that are greater than $1$. (ii) At a critical point $q$ of $L_p$, the index of $L_p$ is the number of principal curvatures of $M$ at $q$ in the direction $p - q$ that are greater than $1$. (iii) If $k + w = n$ and $q$ is a non-degenerate critical point of $L_p$, the index of $L_p$ at $q$ is $\sum_{t \in [0, 1]} \mathrm{mult}_q(q + t(p - q))$, all but finitely many terms vanishing: the number of focal points of $(M, q)$ on the segment from $q$ to $p$, each counted with its multiplicity.

diff: The eigenvalues to count are those $> 1/t$, not $\ge 1/t$ as printed: equality would make $p$ a focal point of $(M, q)$, that is, $q$ degenerate (V4.11), and this is where non-degeneracy enters.

The direction $p - q$ is not normalized: if $p - q = tv$ with $\|v\| = 1$, the curvatures in the direction $p - q$ are $t$ times those in the direction $v$, so “greater than $1$” is Milnor's “greater than $1/t$”. For $p = q$ the index is $0$ and the segment holds no focal point.
The proof is Sylvester's law of inertia in an orthonormal eigenbasis of $S_v$, in which $g - \ell_v$ is $\sum_i (1 - \kappa_i)c_i^2$.

items.title: Reeb's theorem on a compact manifold

milnor.label: §4, Theorem 4.1 (Reeb)
milnor.statement: A compact manifold carrying a differentiable function with only two critical points, both non-degenerate, is homeomorphic to a sphere.

lean.statement: Let $M$ be a compact Hausdorff smooth manifold without boundary modelled on a real normed space of finite dimension $n$, and $f : M \to \mathbb R$ smooth with exactly two critical points, both non-degenerate. Then $M$ is homeomorphic to the unit sphere $S^n \subseteq \mathbb R^{n+1}$.

diff: This is Theorem 4.1 in Milnor's own setting of an abstract compact manifold. It sits in this chapter because its proof goes through the Whitney embedding (V4.16): V3.6 applies to an embedded copy, the critical points and their non-degeneracy being carried over by V4.15.
Hausdorffness, tacit in the book, is needed for the embedding; “only two” is read as exactly two, and $M$ has no boundary.

items.title: Milnor's form $Q'$, and multiplication by $i$

milnor.label: §7, p. 39
milnor.statement: Writing $z^h = x^h + iy^h$ in a complex quadratic form $Q(z) = \sum b_{hj}z^hz^j$ of $k$ variables and taking real parts gives a real quadratic form $Q'$ in $2k$ variables. Since $Q(iz) = -Q(z)$, an orthogonal change of variables turns $Q'$ into $-Q'$.

lean.statement: For a complex vector space $V$ and a continuous complex-bilinear $B : V \times V \to \mathbb C$, $\mathrm{Re}\,B$ is a real bilinear form; for $B(z, z') = \sum b_{hj}z^hz'^j$ on $\mathbb C^k$ its quadratic form is Milnor's $Q'$. Multiplication by $i$ is a real-linear isomorphism $J$ with $J^2 = -1$ (inverse $-J$), and $\mathrm{Re}\,B(iv, iw) = -\mathrm{Re}\,B(v, w)$ for all $v$, $w$. On a complex inner product space the real inner product $\mathrm{Re}\langle v, w\rangle$, the Euclidean inner product of $\mathbb R^{2k}$ when $V = \mathbb C^k$, satisfies $\mathrm{Re}\langle iv, iw\rangle = \mathrm{Re}\langle v, w\rangle$: $J$ is orthogonal.

chips: the sign change for the bilinear form
diff: The sign change is proved for the bilinear form $\mathrm{Re}\,B$, not only for the quadratic form $Q'$.
Mathlib's Hermitian product is conjugate-linear in the first slot, Milnor's $\sum_\alpha a_\alpha\bar b_\alpha$ in the second; their real parts agree, and only real parts occur.

items.title: Assertion 1

milnor.label: §7, Assertion 1
milnor.statement: The eigenvalues of $Q'$ come in opposite pairs: with $e$, of multiplicity $\mu$, $-e$ is an eigenvalue of the same multiplicity. Milnor says this clearly follows from the orthogonal change of variables carrying $Q'$ into $-Q'$.

lean.statement: Let $V$ be a complex inner product space, $B$ a continuous complex-bilinear form on $V$ and $e \in \mathbb R$. Then $\mathrm{Re}\,B - e\,\mathrm{Re}\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ and $\mathrm{Re}\,B + e\,\mathrm{Re}\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ have the same nullity. If $A$ is a real-linear operator on $V$ with $\mathrm{Re}\langle Au, w\rangle = \mathrm{Re}\,B(u, w)$ for all $u$, $w$ (the matrix of $Q'$ in orthonormal real coordinates), then the $e$-eigenspace of $A$ is the null space of $\mathrm{Re}\,B - e\,\mathrm{Re}\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$, and the $e$- and $(-e)$-eigenspaces of $A$ have the same dimension.

diff: The step left to “clearly” is made explicit: $J$, orthogonal with $\mathrm{Re}\,B(Ju, Jw) = -\mathrm{Re}\,B(u, w)$, carries $\mathrm{Re}\,B - e\,\mathrm{Re}\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ into $-(\mathrm{Re}\,B + e\,\mathrm{Re}\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)$, and a linear change of variables does not change the nullity.

items.title: Assertion 1 relative to an invariant form

milnor.label: §7, p. 40
milnor.statement: Not stated. Assertion 1 concerns the eigenvalues of $Q'$ for the coordinate inner product of $\mathbb R^{2k}$; on p. 40 Milnor passes from it to focal points, which by Assertion 6.4 are governed by the second fundamental form relative to the first fundamental form $(g_{ij})$, not relative to the identity.

lean.statement: Let $E$ be a real normed space, $J$ a continuous real-linear map with $J^2 = -1$, $G$ a bilinear form with $G(Jv, Jw) = G(v, w)$ and $L$ a bilinear form with $L(Jv, Jw) = -L(v, w)$, for all $v$, $w$. Then for every real $t$ the forms $G - tL$ and $G + tL$ have the same nullity, and for every real $e$ the forms $L - eG$ and $L + eG$ have the same nullity.

diff: With $G = (g_{ij})$, which is $J$-invariant by the Cauchy–Riemann equations, and $L$ the second fundamental form in a normal direction $v$, the nullities of $G \mp tL$ are the multiplicities of $q \pm tv$ as focal points (Assertion 6.4).
Assertion 1 gives the same conclusion only when the real coordinates are orthonormal at $q$, an assumption Milnor makes in §6 (p. 34) but not on p. 40. This is Assertion 1a of the exposition.

items.title: Real orthogonality to a complex subspace

milnor.label: §7, proof of Assertion 2
milnor.statement: Expanding the Hermitian product $\sum_\alpha w_\alpha(z)\bar v_\alpha$ in holomorphic coordinates as a constant plus a homogeneous quadratic $Q(z)$ plus higher terms, Milnor notes in a parenthesis that the linear terms vanish since $v$ is orthogonal to $M$.

lean.statement: Let $T$ be a complex linear subspace of a complex inner product space and $v$ a vector with $\mathrm{Re}\langle a, v\rangle = 0$ for every $a \in T$. Then $\langle a, v\rangle = 0$ for every $a \in T$.

diff: The tangent space is a complex subspace and orthogonality is meant in the real sense; the lemma is what turns real orthogonality into the vanishing of the Hermitian products, which is the content of the parenthesis.
It is stated and proved but not used: the formal route (V5.6–V5.11) avoids power series.

items.title: The Hessian of $L_p$ in holomorphic coordinates

milnor.label: §7, proof of Assertion 2
milnor.statement: With $z^1, \dots, z^k$ complex coordinates for $M$ near $q$, $w_\alpha(z)$ the coordinates of the inclusion $M \to \mathbb C^n$ and $v$ a unit normal, the real inner product $w \cdot v = \mathrm{Re}\sum_\alpha w_\alpha\bar v_\alpha$ has the real expansion $\text{const} + Q'(x, y) + \text{higher terms}$, and clearly, Milnor says, the quadratic terms $Q'$ determine the second fundamental form of $M$ at $q$ in the normal direction $v$.

lean.statement: Let $V$ be a complex normed space, $F$ a complex inner product space, $w : V \to F$ complex $C^2$ on a neighbourhood of $q$ (in particular holomorphic there), and $p \in F$. Then the real Hessian at $q$ of $z \mapsto \|w(z) - p\|^2$ is $(\xi, \xi') \mapsto 2(\mathrm{Re}\langle dw_q\xi, dw_q\xi'\rangle + \mathrm{Re}\langle w(q) - p, d^2w_q(\xi, \xi')\rangle)$, where $dw_q$ and $d^2w_q$ are the complex first and second derivatives. The first term is unchanged by $(\xi, \xi') \mapsto (i\xi, i\xi')$, being the first fundamental form of $w$; the second changes sign, being the real part of a complex bilinear form.

diff: Milnor's remark is replaced by an explicit formula for the whole Hessian of $L_p$ in the chart. For $p = w(q) + tv$, $v$ a unit normal, the second inner product is $-2t\,Q'(\xi)$ on the diagonal, $Q$ being Milnor's quadratic part of $\sum_\alpha w_\alpha\bar v_\alpha$.

items.title: Assertion 2, in a holomorphic chart

milnor.label: §7, Assertion 2
milnor.statement: On every normal line the focal points of $(M, q)$ come in pairs placed symmetrically about $q$: with $q + tv$, the point $q - tv$ is a focal point too, of the same multiplicity. The proof: the quadratic terms $Q'$ of $w \cdot v$ determine the second fundamental form in the direction $v$, and by Assertion 1 its eigenvalues occur in equal and opposite pairs.

lean.statement: With $V$, $F$, $w$, $q$ as in V5.6, for every $n \in F$ and every real $t$, the Hessians at $q$ of $\|w(\cdot) - (w(q) + tn)\|^2$ and of $\|w(\cdot) - (w(q) - tn)\|^2$ have the same nullity. $n$ need be neither normal nor a unit vector, and $q$ need not be critical.

diff: The statement concerns Hessians in a holomorphic chart. For a unit normal $n$ these nullities are the multiplicities of $w(q) \pm tn$ as focal points, by Assertion 6.4 and the Hessian formula of p. 36, which are formalized for real submanifolds of $\mathbb R^n$ (V4.9, V4.10); but a holomorphic chart of a complex submanifold is not identified with a chart of that real submanifold, so the passage to focal points is not verified.
The proof: $J = i\cdot$ carries one Hessian into the other (V5.6), as in V5.4. Milnor's route through the eigenvalues of $Q'$ is not used.

items.title: The Andreotti–Frankel identity

milnor.label: §7, p. 41
milnor.statement: Not in Milnor's text. On p. 41 he bounds the index of $L_p$ at a critical point $q$ by counting focal points: by Lemma 6.9 it is the number of focal points of $(M, q)$ between $p$ and $q$; there are at most $2k$ on the whole normal line, distributed symmetrically about $q$ by Assertion 2, so at most $k$ between $p$ and $q$. The proof of §7 is credited to Andreotti and Frankel.

lean.statement: Let $G$, $L$, $H$ be bilinear forms on a real normed space and $J$ any map of it such that, for all $v$, $H(v, v) = G(v, v) - L(v, v)$, $G(Jv, Jv) = G(v, v)$ and $L(Jv, Jv) = -L(v, v)$. Then $H(Jv, Jv) = 2G(v, v) - H(v, v)$. On a complex vector space with $J = i\cdot$ and $L = \mathrm{Re}\,B$, $B$ complex bilinear, the condition on $L$ is automatic; on a complex inner product space with $G(v, v) = \|v\|^2$ it reads $H(iv, iv) = 2\|v\|^2 - H(v, v)$.

chips: replaces the count of focal points
diff: Together with V5.9 it replaces Milnor's count of focal points on p. 41, which needs Lemmas 6.3 and 6.9 and Assertion 2 in its focal-point form.

items.title: The index bound

milnor.label: §7, p. 41
milnor.statement: Not stated; it is the abstract form of the conclusion of p. 41, that the index of $L_p$ at $q$ is at most $k$.

lean.statement: Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real normed space, $H$ a bilinear form and $J$ an injective real-linear map of $E$ with $H(v, v) + H(Jv, Jv) \ge 0$ for all $v$. Then $2 \cdot \mathrm{index}\,H \le \dim_{\mathbb R} E$. On a finite-dimensional complex vector space $V$, if $H(v, v) + H(iv, iv) \ge 0$ for all $v$, then $\mathrm{index}\,H \le \dim_{\mathbb C} V$.

diff: If $H$ is negative definite on $W$, then $W \cap JW = 0$, since a non-zero $Jw \in W$ would make both $H(w, w)$ and $H(Jw, Jw)$ negative; so $2\dim W \le \dim E$.

items.title: The index bound for forms of Milnor's shape

milnor.label: §7, p. 41
milnor.statement: The index of $L_p$ at a critical point $q$ is at most $k$, $M$ having complex dimension $k$.

lean.statement: Let $V$ be a complex vector space of finite dimension $k$, $G$ a bilinear form with $G(v, v) \ge 0$ and $G(iv, iv) = G(v, v)$, $B$ a continuous complex-bilinear form, and $H$ a bilinear form with $H(v, v) = G(v, v) - \mathrm{Re}\,B(v, v)$ for all $v$. Then $\mathrm{index}\,H \le k$. In particular, on a complex inner product space every form with quadratic form $\|v\|^2 - \mathrm{Re}\,B(v, v)$ has index at most $k$; and for any $f : V \to \mathbb R$ and $q \in V$ whose Hessian has, on the diagonal, the form $G - \mathrm{Re}\,B$, the Hessian has index at most $k$.

chips: only the shape of the Hessian
diff: Neither criticality, nor non-degeneracy, nor any smoothness of $f$ is assumed; only the shape of the Hessian matters.
The proof is V5.8 and V5.9: if $H(v, v) < 0$ then $H(iv, iv) = 2G(v, v) - H(v, v) > 0$. Milnor's count of focal points is not used.

items.title: The index of $L_p$ is at most $k$, in a holomorphic chart

milnor.label: §7, proof of Theorem 7.2
milnor.statement: Choose $p \in \mathbb C^n$ so that $L_p : M \to \mathbb R$ has no degenerate critical points; since $M$ is a closed subset of $\mathbb C^n$, each $M^a$ is compact. By Lemma 6.9 and Assertion 2 the index of $L_p$ at a critical point $q$ is at most $k$, so $M$ has the homotopy type of a CW-complex of dimension at most $k$.

lean.statement: Let $V$ be a complex vector space of finite dimension $k$, $F$ a complex inner product space, $w : V \to F$ complex $C^2$ on a neighbourhood of $q$, and $p \in F$. Then the Hessian at $q$ of $z \mapsto \|w(z) - p\|^2$ has index at most $k$.

diff: $q$ need not be a critical point, the Hessian need not be non-degenerate, and $dw_q$ need not be injective.

The statement is about the Hessian in a holomorphic chart. When $w$ parametrizes $M$ near a critical point $w(q)$ of $L_p|M$, this Hessian is that of $L_p|M$ in the real coordinates $(x, y)$, and its index is the index of $L_p$ at $w(q)$ by the chart independence of §2 (V1.5); that identification needs $M$ as a real slice submanifold with $w^{-1}$ among its charts, which is not formalized.
The proof: by V5.6 the Hessian $H$ satisfies $H(\xi, \xi) + H(i\xi, i\xi) = 4\|dw_q\xi\|^2 \ge 0$; then V5.9.

items.title: Tangent spaces, the projection $P_q$, and vector fields

milnor.label: §8, pp. 43–44
milnor.statement: Milnor works on an abstract smooth manifold $M$, with tangent spaces $TM_p$, vector fields $X$, and directional derivatives $X_pf$ of real functions $f$ in the direction of a tangent vector $X_p$.

lean.statement: In the embedded setting, $V$ is a finite-dimensional real inner product space and $N \subseteq V$ a slice submanifold, closed or not, with the induced metric. $T_qN \subseteq V$ is the range of the derivative at $q$ of the inclusion $N \to V$, and $P_q$ is the orthogonal projection of $V$ onto $T_qN$. For $F : N \to E$ into a normed space, the linear map $dN\,F\,q : V \to E$ is the derivative of $F$ at $q$ read on ambient vectors: on $v \in T_qN$ it is $dF_q(v)$, and if $F = G$ on $N$ near $q$ for some $G : V \to E$ differentiable at $q$, then $dN\,F\,q\,v = dG_q(v)$ for $v \in T_qN$. A vector field is a map $X : N \to V$ with $X(q) \in T_qN$ for every $q$, smooth if it is smooth as a map $N \to V$. The map $q \mapsto P_q$ is smooth, so every tangent vector $u$ at a point extends to the smooth vector field $q \mapsto P_qu$.

diff: The substance of §§8–9 is verified for submanifolds of a Euclidean space with the induced metric. Every Riemannian manifold is isometric to such an $N$ by Nash's embedding theorem, which is neither in Mathlib nor proved here, so these are statements about embedded manifolds.

That every tangent vector extends to a smooth vector field on all of $N$, which arguments chart by chart take for granted, is proved: in a slice chart with parametrization $x$, $P_{x(u)} = A(A^{\mathsf T}A)^{-1}A^{\mathsf T}$ with $A = dx_u$ injective, which is smooth in $A$.

items.title: Affine connections on an abstract manifold

milnor.label: §8, pp. 43–44
milnor.statement: An affine connection at $p$ is a rule giving, for a tangent vector $X_p$ and a vector field $Y$, a tangent vector $X_p \vdash Y$ at $p$, the covariant derivative of $Y$ along $X_p$; it is bilinear and satisfies $X_p \vdash (fY) = (X_pf)Y_p + f(p)\,X_p \vdash Y$. A global connection is such a rule at every point subject to the smoothness condition (1); it then satisfies (2) bilinearity, (3) $(fX) \vdash Y = f(X \vdash Y)$ and (4) $X \vdash (fY) = (Xf)Y + f(X \vdash Y)$, and (1)–(4) may serve as the definition.
milnor.note: A footnote identifies $X \vdash Y$ with Nomizu's $\nabla_XY$.

lean.statement: Let $M$ be a smooth manifold in Mathlib's sense, modelled on a real normed space, and $\nabla$ a Mathlib covariant derivative on its tangent bundle, $X_p \vdash Y$ being the value at $X_p$ of the linear map $\nabla Y(p) : T_pM \to T_pM$. Then Milnor's (3), $(fX) \vdash Y = f(X \vdash Y)$, holds at every point; (2), additivity in $Y$, holds at every point where both summands are differentiable; and (4), $X \vdash (fY) = (Xf)Y + f(X \vdash Y)$, holds at every point where $f$ and $Y$ are differentiable. Dependence on $X_p$ only, and linearity in $X_p$, are part of the definition.

diff: Milnor's connection is Mathlib's `CovariantDerivative` on the tangent bundle, and his smoothness condition (1) is the separate class `ContMDiffCovariantDerivative`.
Mathlib's object is defined on all sections and is unconstrained on sections not differentiable at the point, so (2) and (4) hold where the sections involved are differentiable.

items.title: The connection of the induced metric, and rules (1)–(4)

milnor.label: §8, p. 44
milnor.statement: A global affine connection satisfies (1) $X \vdash Y$ is smooth when $X$ and $Y$ are smooth vector fields; (2) $X \vdash Y$ is bilinear in $X$ and $Y$; (3) $(fX) \vdash Y = f(X \vdash Y)$; (4) $X \vdash (fY) = (Xf)Y + f(X \vdash Y)$. In local coordinates it is determined by its Christoffel symbols, $\partial_i \vdash \partial_j = \sum_k \Gamma^k_{ij}\partial_k$.

lean.statement: In the embedded setting put $v \vdash Y = P_q(dY_q(v))$ for $v \in T_qN$ and $Y : N \to V$, and $(X \vdash Y)(q) = P_q(dY_q(X(q)))$. Then $X \vdash Y$ is tangent to $N$ at every point, and: (1) $X \vdash Y$ is smooth when $X$ is a smooth vector field and $Y$ is smooth; (2) it is additive in $X$, and additive in $Y$ at every point where both summands are differentiable; (3) $(fX) \vdash Y = f(X \vdash Y)$ for every function $f$; (4) at $q$, $X \vdash (fY) = (Xf)Y + f(X \vdash Y)$ with $Xf = df_q(X(q))$, when $f$ and $Y$ are differentiable at $q$ and $X(q)$, $Y(q)$ are tangent.

diff: Only the connection $P(dY(X))$ of a submanifold with the induced metric is constructed; it is given by one global formula, with no Christoffel symbols and no patching of charts.
Additivity in $Y$ and the rule (4) need differentiability at the point, which for Milnor's smooth fields is automatic.

items.title: Covariant derivative along a curve

milnor.label: §8, pp. 45–46
milnor.statement: A vector field $V$ along a parametrized curve $c$ assigns to each $t$ a tangent vector $V_t \in TM_{c(t)}$, smoothly; the velocity field is $dc/dt = c_*(d/dt)$. Given a connection, the covariant derivative $V \mapsto DV/dt$ is characterized by three axioms: (a) $D(V + W)/dt = DV/dt + DW/dt$; (b) $D(fV)/dt = (df/dt)V + f\,DV/dt$ for a smooth real function $f$ on $\mathbb R$; (c) if $V$ is induced by a vector field $Y$, $V_t = Y_{c(t)}$, then $DV/dt$ is the covariant derivative of $Y$ in the direction of the velocity vector of $c$.

lean.statement: For a curve $c : \mathbb R \to N$, a vector field along $c$ is a map $X : \mathbb R \to V$ with $X(t) \in T_{c(t)}N$ for all $t$; the velocity $c'(t)$ is tangent when $c$ is smooth; and $DX/dt\,(t) = P_{c(t)}(X'(t))$. Then (a) $D(X + Y)/dt = DX/dt + DY/dt$ at $t$ when $X$, $Y$ are differentiable at $t$; (b) $D(fX)/dt = f'X + f\,DX/dt$ at $t$ when $f$, $X$ are differentiable at $t$ and $X(t)$ is tangent; (c) if $c$ is smooth and $Y : N \to V$ is differentiable at $c(t)$, then $D(Y \circ c)/dt\,(t) = c'(t) \vdash Y$.

diff: Only for the induced connection of a submanifold, where the covariant derivative along a curve is the projection of the ordinary derivative. Milnor's fields along curves are smooth by definition; the formal axioms need only differentiability at $t$.

items.title: Lemma 8.1

milnor.label: §8, Lemma 8.1
milnor.statement: Exactly one operation $V \mapsto DV/dt$ satisfies (a), (b) and (c). The proof writes $V = \sum_j v^j\partial_j$ in a local coordinate system and derives $DV/dt = \sum_k (dv^k/dt + \sum_{i,j} (du^i/dt)\Gamma^k_{ij}v^j)\partial_k$; conversely, defining $DV/dt$ by this formula, (a), (b) and (c) are not difficult to verify.

lean.statement: Let $c$ be a smooth curve in $N$. Call an operation $D$ on maps $\mathbb R \to V$ admissible if it satisfies (a) for smooth fields along $c$, (b) for smooth $f$ and smooth fields along $c$, and (c) for smooth vector fields $Y$ on $N$. Then $X \mapsto P(X')$ of V6.5 is admissible, and every admissible $D$ agrees with it on every smooth field along $c$.

chips: an ambient frame, not a chart
diff: Only for the induced connection of a submanifold.

Instead of a chart, a field along $c$ is expanded as $X = \sum_i \langle e_i, X\rangle\,(E_i \circ c)$ in the smooth fields $E_i(q) = P_qe_i$, $e_i$ an orthonormal basis of $V$, and (a)–(c) determine $DX/dt$. This avoids what the coordinate proof leaves implicit: locality in $t$, and the extension of the coordinate fields to all of $M$.

items.title: Global solutions of linear equations

milnor.label: §8, proof of Lemma 8.2
milnor.statement: The differential equations $dv^k/dt + \sum_{i,j} (du^i/dt)\Gamma^k_{ij}v^j = 0$ have solutions uniquely determined by their initial values; since the equations are linear, Milnor says, the solutions can be defined for all relevant values of $t$, citing Graves.

lean.statement: Let $A : \mathbb R \to \mathrm{End}(E)$ be continuous. (i) On a real normed space $E$, two solutions of $x' = A(t)x$ on an open interval, or on $\mathbb R$, that agree at one time agree everywhere. (ii) If $E$ is a complete real inner product space and $\langle A(t)x, x\rangle = 0$ for all $t$ and $x$, then for every $t_0$ and $x_0$ there is a solution on all of $\mathbb R$ with $x(t_0) = x_0$.

diff: Mathlib has local existence (Picard–Lindelöf) and Grönwall uniqueness only. Global existence is proved only for skew-adjoint coefficients, the case parallel transport needs: their solutions have constant norm, so the equation may be truncated outside a ball and solved on any compact interval, and solutions on nested intervals are glued by (i).

items.title: Lemma 8.2: parallel fields

milnor.label: §8, Lemma 8.2
milnor.statement: Along a curve $c$, every tangent vector $V_0$ at $c(0)$ extends to exactly one parallel vector field $V$, parallel meaning that $DV/dt$ vanishes identically; $V_t$ is then said to come from $V_0$ by parallel translation along $c$.

lean.statement: A field $X$ along $c$ is parallel if it is differentiable and $DX/dt = 0$ at every $t$. For a smooth curve $c$ in $N$, every $t_0 \in \mathbb R$ and every $v \in T_{c(t_0)}N$ there is exactly one parallel field $X$ along $c$ with $X(t_0) = v$; it is defined on all of $\mathbb R$, and it is smooth.

diff: Only for the induced connection of a submanifold; for it, any initial time is allowed, and uniqueness holds among differentiable fields, not only smooth ones.

A tangent field is parallel iff $X' = P'X$, where $P(t) = P_{c(t)}$, and uniqueness is V6.7 (i). That equation has no a priori bound, so existence solves instead $X' = (P'P - PP')X$, whose coefficient is skew-adjoint; since $PP'P = 0$, a solution that starts tangent stays tangent, and is then parallel.
On an abstract manifold the coordinate equations would also have to be patched from chart to chart along the curve; here there is one equation in $V$.

items.title: Parallel translation is a linear isometry

milnor.label: §8, p. 47
milnor.statement: After naming parallel translation, Milnor calls a connection on a Riemannian manifold compatible with the metric when parallel translation preserves inner products, that is, when $\langle P, P'\rangle$ is constant along $c$ for any two parallel fields $P$, $P'$ along any curve $c$.

lean.statement: For parallel fields $X$, $Y$ along any curve $c$ in $N$, $\langle X(t), Y(t)\rangle$ does not depend on $t$: the induced connection is compatible with the metric in Milnor's sense. For a smooth curve $c$ and times $t_0$, $t_1$, the map sending $v \in T_{c(t_0)}N$ to the value at $t_1$ of the parallel field through $v$ at $t_0$ is a linear isometry of $T_{c(t_0)}N$ onto $T_{c(t_1)}N$; it is the identity when $t_1 = t_0$, and translating from $t_0$ to $t_1$ and then to $t_2$ is translating from $t_0$ to $t_2$.

diff: Compatibility, a definition in the book, is proved for the induced connection.
Linearity, surjectivity and transitivity of parallel translation are stated and proved; the book uses them without comment.

items.title: Lemma 8.3

milnor.label: §8, Lemma 8.3
milnor.statement: For a connection compatible with the metric and any two vector fields $V$, $W$ along $c$, $\frac{d}{dt}\langle V, W\rangle = \langle DV/dt, W\rangle + \langle V, DW/dt\rangle$. The proof expands $V$ and $W$ in parallel fields $P_1, \dots, P_n$ along $c$ which are orthonormal at one point, and hence at every point.

lean.statement: For any curve $c$ in $N$ and fields $X$, $Y$ along $c$ differentiable at $t$, the derivative of $\langle X, Y\rangle$ at $t$ is $\langle DX/dt, Y\rangle + \langle X, DY/dt\rangle$.

diff: Only for the induced connection. Milnor's proof needs Lemma 8.2 for $n$ initial vectors and the smoothness of the coefficients $\langle V, P_i\rangle$; here the product rule in $V$ and $\langle PX', Y\rangle = \langle X', Y\rangle$ for tangent $Y$ suffice, so Lemma 8.3 comes before Lemma 8.2.

items.title: Corollary 8.4

milnor.label: §8, Corollary 8.4
milnor.statement: For vector fields $Y$, $Y'$ on $M$ and a tangent vector $X_p$, $X_p\langle Y, Y'\rangle = \langle X_p \vdash Y, Y'_p\rangle + \langle Y_p, X_p \vdash Y'\rangle$, by Lemma 8.3 along a curve with velocity $X_p$ at $t = 0$.

lean.statement: Embedded: if $Y$, $Y'$ are differentiable at $q$ with $Y(q)$, $Y'(q)$ tangent, and $v \in T_qN$, then $v\langle Y, Y'\rangle = \langle v \vdash Y, Y'(q)\rangle + \langle Y(q), v \vdash Y'\rangle$. Abstract: on a manifold whose tangent bundle carries a Riemannian metric (Mathlib's `RiemannianBundle`), a covariant derivative is called compatible if Milnor's identity holds at every point for all vector fields differentiable there; for a finite-dimensional model space and a $C^1$ metric this is Mathlib's `IsMetricCompatible`.

diff: Milnor's definition of compatibility, that parallel translation preserves inner products, cannot be stated for Mathlib's connections, which have no parallel transport; on an abstract manifold Corollary 8.4 is taken as the definition instead, and shown to agree with Mathlib's metric compatibility.
In the embedded setting it is proved, at points where the fields are differentiable.

items.title: The second fundamental form

milnor.label: §6, p. 33
milnor.statement: Not in §§8–9. Milnor meets the second fundamental form in §6, as the normal component of $\partial^2\vec x/\partial u^i\partial u^j$ in a fixed coordinate system, without an invariant definition.

lean.statement: For $v \in T_qN$ let $D_v$ be the derivative of $q \mapsto P_q$ in the direction $v$, and $\mathrm{II}_q(v, w) = D_vw$. For every vector field $W$ differentiable at $q$, $\mathrm{II}_q(v, W(q)) = dW_q(v) - P_q(dW_q(v))$, the normal part of $dW_q(v)$, which therefore depends only on $v$ and $W(q)$. For $v, w \in T_qN$, $\mathrm{II}_q(v, w)$ is normal to $N$ and $\mathrm{II}_q(v, w) = \mathrm{II}_q(w, v)$; and $\langle \mathrm{II}_q(v, x), y\rangle = \langle x, \mathrm{II}_q(v, y)\rangle$ for all $x, y \in V$: $D_v$ is self-adjoint, maps $T_qN$ to normal vectors and normal vectors to $T_qN$.

chips: the tool for symmetry and curvature
diff: No counterpart in §§8–9: it is what makes the symmetry of the connection, the tensor property of $R$ and Lemma 9.3 short consequences in the embedded setting.

The symmetry is proved in a slice chart $\sigma$: $T_xN$ is the kernel of $d(\sigma_2)_x$, so $d(\sigma_2)_x \circ P_x = 0$ on $N$, and differentiating along $N$ gives $d(\sigma_2)_q(\mathrm{II}(v, w)) = -d^2(\sigma_2)_q(v, w)$, symmetric in $v$ and $w$.

items.title: Definition 8.5: symmetric connections

milnor.label: §8, Definition 8.5
milnor.statement: A connection is symmetric when $(X \vdash Y) - (Y \vdash X) = [X, Y]$, the bracket being the Poisson bracket $[X, Y]f = X(Yf) - Y(Xf)$. For coordinate fields this says $\Gamma^k_{ij} = \Gamma^k_{ji}$, and Milnor notes the converse.

lean.statement: Abstract: a covariant derivative is symmetric if $X \vdash Y - Y \vdash X = [X, Y]$ at every point where $X$ and $Y$ are differentiable, $[X, Y]$ being Mathlib's Lie bracket of vector fields, which has Milnor's sign; for a finite-dimensional model space this is “the torsion is zero”. Embedded: the bracket of two maps $X, Y : N \to V$ is $[X, Y](q) = dY_q(X(q)) - dX_q(Y(q))$. For vector fields differentiable at $q$ it is tangent to $N$ at $q$; for smooth $f$ and smooth vector fields, $X(Yf) - Y(Xf) = [X, Y]f$, where $Xf = df(X)$; and the induced connection is symmetric: $X \vdash Y - Y \vdash X = [X, Y]$ at $q$ for vector fields differentiable at $q$.

diff: In the embedded setting, that the ambient formula for the bracket is tangent and acts on functions as Milnor's bracket is not automatic: the normal part of $[X, Y]$ is $\mathrm{II}(X, Y) - \mathrm{II}(Y, X)$, which vanishes by the symmetry of $\mathrm{II}$ (V6.12), and the action on functions uses the symmetry of second derivatives.
The converse “if $\Gamma^k_{ij} = \Gamma^k_{ji}$ then the connection is symmetric” is not formalized, there being no Christoffel symbols.

items.title: Lemma 8.6: the fundamental lemma of Riemannian geometry

milnor.label: §8, Lemma 8.6
milnor.statement: On a Riemannian manifold there is exactly one symmetric connection compatible with the metric.
