Uniqueness: Corollary 8.4 applied to $\partial_i$, $\partial_j$, $\partial_k$ gives three linear equations, whose solution is the first Christoffel identity, and multiplying by $(g^{k\ell})$ gives the second. Conversely, defining $\Gamma^\ell_{ij}$ by this formula, one can verify that the connection is symmetric and compatible with the metric.

lean.statement: Embedded: call an operation $D$ on maps $N \to V$ symmetric and compatible if, on smooth vector fields, $D(X, Y)$ is tangent, $D(X, Y) - D(Y, X) = [X, Y]$, and $X\langle Y, Y'\rangle = \langle D(X, Y), Y'\rangle + \langle Y, D(X, Y')\rangle$. The induced connection $P(dY(X))$ is such an operation (existence); every such operation satisfies the Koszul formula $2\langle D(X, Y), Z\rangle = X\langle Y, Z\rangle + Y\langle X, Z\rangle - Z\langle X, Y\rangle + \langle [X, Y], Z\rangle - \langle [X, Z], Y\rangle - \langle [Y, Z], X\rangle$ on smooth vector fields; and every such operation agrees with $P(dY(X))$ on smooth vector fields at every point (uniqueness). Abstract: for a manifold with a Riemannian metric on its tangent bundle, two covariant derivatives that are both symmetric and compatible (V6.11, V6.13) satisfy the Koszul formula and agree on every vector field differentiable at the point; with Mathlib's predicates, two torsion-free metric connections agree on such fields, for a finite-dimensional model space and a $C^1$ metric.

diff: Existence is proved only in the embedded setting, where the induced connection is the one; on an abstract manifold only uniqueness is proved, and only on sections differentiable at the point, a Mathlib covariant derivative being unconstrained elsewhere.

The embedded uniqueness assumes no linearity or tensoriality of $D$, only the three properties on smooth fields; it applies the Koszul formula with $Z$ the field $x \mapsto P_x(D(X, Y)(q) - (X \vdash Y)(q))$.

The Koszul formula, the coordinate-free form of the first Christoffel identity, replaces Milnor's linear system on p. 49, whose list of three unknowns contains $\langle \partial_i \vdash \partial_j, \partial_k\rangle$ twice by the symmetry he quotes, a misprint. His existence half needs a converse of Lemma 8.3, which he does not state, and a patching of the local connections.

items.title: Lemma 8.7

milnor.label: §8, Lemma 8.7
milnor.statement: On a parametrized surface $s : \mathbb R^2 \to M$, $DV/\partial x$ is the covariant derivative of $V$ along the curves $x \mapsto s(x, y_0)$. For a symmetric connection, $\frac{D}{\partial x}\frac{\partial s}{\partial y} = \frac{D}{\partial y}\frac{\partial s}{\partial x}$; the proof is a computation in local coordinates.

lean.statement: For a smooth surface $s : \mathbb R^2 \to N$ the velocity fields $\partial s/\partial x$, $\partial s/\partial y$ are tangent, and $DW/\partial x$ is defined, as in Milnor, as the covariant derivative of $x \mapsto W(x, y_0)$ along the curve $x \mapsto s(x, y_0)$, and similarly $DW/\partial y$; at a point $p$ where $W$ is differentiable it equals $P_{s(p)}(\partial W/\partial x\,(p))$. Then $\frac{D}{\partial x}\frac{\partial s}{\partial y} = \frac{D}{\partial y}\frac{\partial s}{\partial x}$ at every point.

diff: Only for the induced connection, which is symmetric (V6.13); both sides equal $P(\partial^2 s/\partial x\,\partial y)$.
The joint smoothness of $DW/\partial x$ in $(x, y)$, which the definition one curve at a time leaves open, is visible from the formula.

items.title: The curvature tensor and its sign

milnor.label: §9, p. 51
milnor.statement: The curvature tensor of an affine connection measures how far the second covariant derivative $\partial_i \vdash (\partial_j \vdash Z)$ is from being symmetric in $i$ and $j$; it is defined by $R(X, Y)Z = -X \vdash (Y \vdash Z) + Y \vdash (X \vdash Z) + [X, Y] \vdash Z$. A footnote says that Nomizu gives $R$ the opposite sign, and that Milnor's convention makes $\langle R(\partial_h, \partial_i)\partial_j, \partial_k\rangle$ the classical symbol $R_{hijk}$.

lean.statement:
For a covariant derivative on an abstract manifold, Milnor's curvature of vector fields is $R(X, Y)Z = -X \vdash (Y \vdash Z) + Y \vdash (X \vdash Z) + [X, Y] \vdash Z$; it is the negative of Nomizu's, and Kobayashi–Nomizu's, $
abla_X
abla_YZ - 
abla_Y
abla_XZ - 
abla_{[X, Y]}Z$, and $R(Y, X)Z = -R(X, Y)Z$. In the embedded setting the same formula, with the induced connection and the bracket of V6.13, defines $R(X, Y)Z$ for maps $N 	o V$. Mathlib defines no curvature, so there is no Mathlib sign to compare with.

items.title: Lemma 9.1: the curvature is a tensor

milnor.label: §9, Lemma 9.1
milnor.statement: $R(X, Y)Z$ at $p$ is determined by $X_p$, $Y_p$, $Z_p$ alone, whatever the fields do near $p$, and depends trilinearly on them; in short, $R$ is a tensor. The proof checks $R(fX, Y)Z = fR(X, Y)Z$ and leaves the analogous identities for $Y$ and $Z$ to similar computations, which Milnor calls easy.

lean.statement: In the embedded setting, for smooth vector fields $X$, $Y$, $Z$ and every $q$, $R(X, Y)Z\,(q) = \mathrm{II}_q(Y_q, \mathrm{II}_q(X_q, Z_q)) - \mathrm{II}_q(X_q, \mathrm{II}_q(Y_q, Z_q))$, that is, $R(X, Y) = D_YD_X - D_XD_Y$ on $T_qN$. Consequently $R(X, Y)Z$ at $q$ depends only on $X_q$, $Y_q$, $Z_q$, and it is the value of a trilinear map $T_qN \times T_qN \times T_qN \to T_qN$, the curvature tensor of $N$ at $q$.

diff: Only for the induced connection of a submanifold, but with more than Milnor states: an explicit formula for $R$ through the second fundamental form.

Milnor treats $X$ explicitly and leaves $Y$ and $Z$ to similar computations; for $Z$ the computation is a different one. Here, with a smooth ambient representative $G$ of $Z$, $Y \vdash (X \vdash Z)$ at $q$ is $D_YD_XZ$ plus terms that cancel by the symmetry of $d^2G$ and against $[X, Y] \vdash Z$.

items.title: The Gauss equation

milnor.statement: The book has no such formula: Milnor never relates the curvature tensor of a submanifold to its second fundamental form.

lean.statement: For all $x, y, z, w \in V$, $\langle D_yD_xz - D_xD_yz, w\rangle = \langle \mathrm{II}(x, z), \mathrm{II}(y, w)\rangle - \langle \mathrm{II}(x, w), \mathrm{II}(y, z)\rangle$ at $q$; hence, for smooth vector fields $X$, $Y$, $Z$ and any $W : N \to V$, $\langle R(X, Y)Z, W\rangle = \langle \mathrm{II}(X, Z), \mathrm{II}(Y, W)\rangle - \langle \mathrm{II}(X, W), \mathrm{II}(Y, Z)\rangle$ at every point, with Milnor's sign of $R$. With $Z = X$, $W = Y$ and the symmetry of $\mathrm{II}$ this gives $\langle R(X, Y)X, Y\rangle = \langle \mathrm{II}(X, X), \mathrm{II}(Y, Y)\rangle - \|\mathrm{II}(X, Y)\|^2$, Gauss's curvature for a surface in $\mathbb R^3$.

chips: computes the curvature of the sphere
diff: No counterpart in the book; it is how curvature is computed in the embedded setting, for instance for the round sphere (V6.25), and its sign confirms Milnor's convention against Gauss's classical formula.

items.title: Lemma 9.2

milnor.label: §9, Lemma 9.2
milnor.statement: For a parametrized surface $s : \mathbb R^2 \to M$ and any vector field $V$ along $s$, $\frac{D}{\partial y}\frac{D}{\partial x}V - \frac{D}{\partial x}\frac{D}{\partial y}V = R(\frac{\partial s}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial s}{\partial y})V$. Proof: express both sides in a local coordinate system and compute, using $\partial_j \vdash (\partial_i \vdash \partial_k) - \partial_i \vdash (\partial_j \vdash \partial_k) = R(\partial_i, \partial_j)\partial_k$.

lean.statement: For a smooth surface $s : \mathbb R^2 \to N$ and a smooth map $W : \mathbb R^2 \to V$ with $W(p) \in T_{s(p)}N$ for all $p$, $\frac{D}{\partial y}\frac{D}{\partial x}W - \frac{D}{\partial x}\frac{D}{\partial y}W = R(\frac{\partial s}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial s}{\partial y})W$ at every point, with $R(x, y) = D_yD_x - D_xD_y$ the curvature of V6.17.

chips: no symmetry of the connection used
diff: Only for the induced connection. The proof uses $W = PW$, $PD_vP = 0$, and the fact that $D_v$ maps normal vectors to tangent ones; no symmetry of the connection and no coordinates are used.
The joint smoothness of the covariant derivatives in $(x, y)$, which the definition one curve at a time leaves open, is again visible from the formula.

items.title: Lemma 9.3, symmetries (1)–(3)

milnor.label: §9, Lemma 9.3
milnor.statement: The curvature tensor of a Riemannian manifold satisfies (1) $R(X, Y)Z + R(Y, X)Z = 0$, (2) $R(X, Y)Z + R(Y, Z)X + R(Z, X)Y = 0$, (3) $\langle R(X, Y)Z, W\rangle + \langle R(X, Y)W, Z\rangle = 0$. (1) is immediate from the definition; (2) and (3) are proved for fields whose brackets vanish, which suffices since all terms are tensors, (3) being reduced to $\langle R(X, Y)Z, Z\rangle = 0$, clearly an equivalent assertion.

lean.statement: A trilinear map $R$ on a real inner product space is called a curvature tensor if it satisfies (1) $R(X, Y)Z + R(Y, X)Z = 0$, (2) $R(X, Y)Z + R(Y, Z)X + R(Z, X)Y = 0$ and (3) $\langle R(X, Y)Z, W\rangle + \langle R(X, Y)W, Z\rangle = 0$. For a linear map $T$, $\langle TZ, W\rangle$ is skew in $Z$, $W$ iff $\langle TZ, Z\rangle = 0$ for all $Z$. The curvature tensor of $N$ at each point (V6.17) satisfies (1)–(3). For maps $X$, $Y$, $Z$ of $N$ into $V$, (1) holds with no hypothesis; for smooth vector fields, (2) and (3) hold at every point.

diff: Only for the induced connection of a submanifold.

Milnor proves (2) and (3) for extensions with vanishing brackets, which must be constructed (coordinate fields cut off by a bump function). Here no extensions are needed: (2) is the symmetry of $\mathrm{II}$, and (3) the self-adjointness of $D_v$.

items.title: Lemma 9.3, symmetry (4): the octahedron

milnor.label: §9, Lemma 9.3
milnor.statement: (4) $\langle R(X, Y)Z, W\rangle = \langle R(Z, W)X, Y\rangle$, proved from (1), (2) and (3) with the octahedron of p. 54: by (2), with the help of (1) and (3), the quantities at the vertices of each shaded triangle sum to zero, and adding the identities for the top two shaded triangles and subtracting those for the bottom ones leaves twice the top vertex minus twice the bottom vertex.

lean.statement: Let $T(X, Y, Z, W)$ be any real function of four arguments that is skew in $(X, Y)$, skew in $(Z, W)$, and satisfies $T(X, Y, Z, W) + T(Y, Z, X, W) + T(Z, X, Y, W) = 0$. Then $T(X, Y, Z, W) = T(Z, W, X, Y)$. Hence every curvature tensor (V6.20) satisfies (4), $\langle R(X, Y)Z, W\rangle = \langle R(Z, W)X, Y\rangle$, and so does $R$ on smooth vector fields of $N$.

chips: the signs of the triangles written out
diff: No linearity of $T$ is used: the octahedron argument is pure combinatorics of the three symmetries.
The four triangle identities, whose signs Milnor leaves to the reader, are written out.

items.title: Sectional curvature

milnor.label: §19, Remark after Lemma 19.1
milnor.statement: For orthogonal unit vectors $A$, $B$ at $p$, Milnor calls $\langle R(A, B)A, B\rangle$ the sectional curvature determined by $A$ and $B$, and notes that it is the Gaussian curvature of the surface formed by the geodesics through $p$ whose velocities lie in the plane of $A$ and $B$.

lean.statement: For a trilinear map $R$ and vectors $X$, $Y$, put $K(X, Y) = \langle R(X, Y)X, Y\rangle / (\|X\|^2\|Y\|^2 - \langle X, Y\rangle^2)$, which is $0$ when $X$, $Y$ are dependent; for an orthonormal pair it is Milnor's $\langle R(A, B)A, B\rangle$. If $R$ satisfies (1)–(3), $K$ depends only on the plane: $K(aX + bY, cX + dY) = K(X, Y)$ whenever $ad - bc \ne 0$. With the standard sign, $-R$ also satisfies (1)–(3), and $\langle (-R)(X, Y)Y, X\rangle = \langle R(X, Y)X, Y\rangle$: the sectional curvature is the same number in both conventions.

chips: the same in both sign conventions
diff: Defined for any independent pair, and shown to depend only on the plane they span, which the book does not state.
The identification with the Gaussian curvature of a surface of geodesics is not formalized here; it needs the exponential map (Chapter 11).

items.title: Constant curvature

milnor.statement: The book defines the sectional curvature (p. 100) but does not state that a curvature tensor all of whose sectional curvatures equal $\kappa$ is $\kappa$ times a standard one.

lean.statement: $R_1(X, Y)Z = \langle X, Z\rangle Y - \langle Y, Z\rangle X$ is a curvature tensor, and $\kappa R_1$ has sectional curvature $\kappa$ on every independent pair. Conversely, if a curvature tensor $R$ has $\langle R(A, B)A, B\rangle = \kappa$ for all orthonormal $A$, $B$, or $K(X, Y) = \kappa$ for all independent $X$, $Y$, then $R(X, Y)Z = \kappa(\langle X, Z\rangle Y - \langle Y, Z\rangle X)$; with the standard sign this is $\kappa(\langle Y, Z\rangle X - \langle X, Z\rangle Y)$. Behind it: $6\langle R(X, Y)Z, W\rangle$ is an explicit combination of the values $\langle R(A, B)A, B\rangle$ at sums of $X$, $Y$, $Z$, $W$, so a curvature tensor is determined by its sectional curvatures.

diff: No counterpart in the book: Lemma 7.2 and Corollary 7.3 of the exposition, the polarization formula and its consequence for constant curvature.

items.title: The round sphere

milnor.statement: No counterpart in §§8–9: the book does not compute a curvature tensor there.

lean.statement: For the unit sphere $S^n \subseteq \mathbb R^{n+1}$, a slice submanifold of the companion project, with the induced metric: $P_qv = v - \langle q, v\rangle q$; $\mathrm{II}_q(v, w) = -\langle v, w\rangle q$ for tangent $v$, $w$; the curvature tensor is $R(x, y)z = \langle x, z\rangle y - \langle y, z\rangle x$ with Milnor's sign; so $S^n$ has sectional curvature $1$, both as $K(x, y) = 1$ for independent tangent $x$, $y$ and as $\langle R(A, B)A, B\rangle = 1$ for orthonormal $A$, $B$.

diff: A computation the book does not make in §§8–9, done coordinate-free from the Gauss equation (V6.18); it is the curvature of the sphere used in later chapters of this edition.

items.title: $\mathbb CP^n$ and Milnor's coordinates

milnor.label: §4, p. 26
milnor.statement: $\mathbb CP_n$ is the set of equivalence classes of $(n + 1)$-tuples $(z_0, \dots, z_n)$ of complex numbers with $\sum|z_j|^2 = 1$. On the set $U_0$ where $z_0 \neq 0$, set $|z_0|\,z_j/z_0 = x_j + iy_j$; then $x_1, y_1, \dots, x_n, y_n$ "are the required coordinate functions, mapping $U_0$ diffeomorphically onto the open unit ball in $\mathbb R^{2n}$".

lean.statement:
Here $\mathbb CP^n$ is the set of Hermitian projections of trace $1$ in the space $M_{n+1}(\mathbb C)$ of complex matrices (the Grassmannian of V14.16 with $m = 1$). Every point of it is $P = zz^*$, that is $P_{ab} = z_a ar z_b$, for a unit vector $z \in \mathbb C^{n+1}$. For $0 \le k \le n$ let $U_k$ be the set of $P$ with $\operatorname{Re}P_{kk} > 0$; every point of $\mathbb CP^n$ lies in some $U_k$. On $\mathbb R^{2n} = \mathbb C^n$, with coordinates $z_j = x_j + iy_j$ ($j 
eq k$), put $\operatorname{param}_k(z) = vv^*$, where $v_k = \sqrt{1 - |z|^2}$ and $v_j = z_j$ for $j 
eq k$; and for a matrix $P$ put $\operatorname{coord}_k(P) = (P_{jk}/\sqrt{\operatorname{Re}P_{kk}})_{j 
eq k}$. Then $\operatorname{coord}_k(\operatorname{param}_k(z)) = z$ for $|z| < 1$, and for $P \in \mathbb CP^n \cap U_k$, $|\operatorname{coord}_k(P)| < 1$ and $\operatorname{param}_k(\operatorname{coord}_k(P)) = P$. $\mathbb CP^n$ is a compact slice submanifold of $M_{n+1}(\mathbb C)$ of dimension $2n$, and at every $x \in \mathbb CP^n \cap U_k$ it has a slice chart whose parametrization is $z \mapsto \operatorname{param}_k(\operatorname{coord}_k(x) + z)$ near $0$.

diff: $\mathbb CP^n$ is the compact submanifold of Hermitian projections of trace $1$ in $M_{n+1}(\mathbb C)$, with the induced smooth structure; Milnor's coordinates are $P_{jk}/\sqrt{P_{kk}}$, independent of the representative, and they are the coordinates of slice charts.
"Diffeomorphically" presupposes a smooth structure on $\mathbb CP_n$, which the book does not describe.

items.title: Milnor's function on $\mathbb CP^n$: critical points and indices

milnor.label: §4, pp. 26–27
milnor.statement: $f(z_0 : z_1 : \dots : z_n) = \sum c_j|z_j|^2$, with distinct real constants $c_j$. In the coordinates of $U_0$, $f = c_0 + \sum_{j=1}^n(c_j - c_0)(x_j^2 + y_j^2)$; so the only critical point within $U_0$ is the centre $p_0$, non-degenerate, of index twice the number of $j$ with $c_j < c_0$. Similarly at $p_1, \dots, p_n$. "Every possible even index between $0$ and $2n$ occurs exactly once."
milnor.note: The scan of p. 26 prints the definition as $f = c_j|z_j|$; the display that follows it confirms $\sum c_j|z_j|^2$.

lean.statement: For real numbers $c_0, \dots, c_n$ let $f(P) = \sum_j c_j\operatorname{Re}P_{jj}$ on $\mathbb CP^n$, so that $f(zz^*) = \sum_j c_j|z_j|^2$. In the coordinates of V3.41, $f(\operatorname{param}_k(z)) = c_k + \sum_{j \neq k}(c_j - c_k)(x_j^2 + y_j^2)$ for $|z| \le 1$. Suppose the $c_j$ are distinct. Then the critical points of $f$ are exactly the $n + 1$ points $p_k = \operatorname{param}_k(0)$ (the projections onto the coordinate axes); $p_k$ is non-degenerate, of index $2\,\#\{j : c_j < c_k\}$; so $f$ is a Morse function. The map $k \mapsto \#\{j : c_j < c_k\}$ is a bijection of $\{0, \dots, n\}$, and so the number $C_\lambda$ of critical points of index $\lambda$ is $1$ for $\lambda = 0, 2, \dots, 2n$ and $0$ for every other $\lambda$.

chips: one critical point of each even index
diff: The critical points, their non-degeneracy and their indices are read in the slice parametrizations of V3.41. That each even index occurs once is the bijectivity of $k \mapsto \#\{j : c_j < c_k\}$, Milnor's tacit renumbering $c_0 < \dots < c_n$.

items.title: The cells and the homology of $\mathbb CP^n$

milnor.label: §4, p. 27
milnor.statement: By Theorem 3.5, $\mathbb CP_n$ has the homotopy type of a CW-complex of the form $e^0 \cup e^2 \cup e^4 \cup \dots \cup e^{2n}$. It follows that the integral homology groups of $\mathbb CP_n$ are $\mathbb Z$ for $i = 0, 2, 4, \dots, 2n$ and $0$ for other values of $i$.

lean.statement: $\mathbb CP^n$ has the homotopy type of a space built from the empty set by attaching cells one after another (V2.12), exactly one of each dimension $0, 2, \dots, 2n$. For every field $\mathbb k$, $\dim H_\lambda(\mathbb CP^n; \mathbb k) = 1$ if $\lambda$ is even and $\lambda \le 2n$, and $0$ otherwise.

chips: homology over fields, not over $\mathbb Z$
diff: One cell in each dimension $0, 2, \dots, 2n$, attached along arbitrary maps (V2.12). The Betti numbers over every field come from the lacunary principle (V3.37, V3.39); the integral groups are not derived.

items.title: The index of $L_p$ on a complex submanifold

milnor.label: §7, proof of Theorem 7.2, pp. 39–41
milnor.statement: For a complex manifold $M$ of complex dimension $k$, bianalytically embedded in $\mathbb C^n$, the index of $L_p$ at a non-degenerate critical point is $\le k$: the focal points of $(M, q)$ along a normal line come in pairs symmetric about $q$ (Assertions 1 and 2), and Lemma 6.9 counts those between $p$ and $q$.

lean.statement: Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and $J$ an orthogonal linear map of $V$ with $J^2 = -1$ (for $V = \mathbb C^m = \mathbb R^{2m}$: multiplication by $i$). A slice submanifold $N \subseteq V$ is called a *complex submanifold* (for $J$) if $J$ maps every tangent space $T_xN$ into itself. For such an $N$, every $p \in V$ and every critical point $q$ of $L_p = \|\cdot - p\|^2$ on $N$, degenerate or not, twice the index of $L_p$ at $q$ is at most $\dim_{\mathbb R}N$; so if $\dim_{\mathbb R}N = 2k$, the index is at most $k$.

chips: every critical point, degenerate or not
diff: "Complex submanifold" is a slice submanifold of $\mathbb R^{2m}$ whose tangent spaces are invariant under $J$; a bianalytically embedded complex manifold is one, and nothing else is used.

The bound is for the Hessian of $L_p$ on the real submanifold, in a slice chart: with $J'$ the complex structure read in the chart, $H(J'\xi, J'\xi) = 4\|dx\,\xi\|^2 - H(\xi, \xi)$, so a negative definite subspace meets its image under $J'$ only in $0$. This is the bridge that V5.7 and V5.11 lacked.

items.title: The homology of a slab without critical points of a given index

milnor.label: §§3, 5; used on pp. 39, 42
milnor.statement: §7 applies Theorems 3.1 and 3.2 to $L_p$ on $M$ and to $1/L_p$ on $V$, whose sublevel sets need not be compact.

lean.statement: Let $N$ be a slice submanifold of a finite-dimensional real inner product space, $F$ a smooth function on the ambient space, $f = F|N$, and $\mathbb k$ a field. Let $a \le b \le a_0$ be such that $f^{-1}(-\infty, a_0]$ is compact (or only the slab $f^{-1}[\ell, a_0]$, for some $\ell \le a$), every critical point of $f$ in it is non-degenerate, and $a$ and $b$ are not critical values. If no critical point $q$ with $a < f(q) < b$ has index $j$, then $H_j(N^b, N^a; \mathbb k) = 0$, where $N^c = f^{-1}(-\infty, c]$. A Morse function on $N$ which is bounded below by $0$ and has compact sublevel sets has regular values $a_0 < 0 \le a_1 \le a_2 \le \dots$ tending to infinity.

diff: If no critical point between two regular levels has index $j$, then $H_j(N^b, N^a) = 0$ over a field, by induction on the critical values, from Theorems 3.1, 3.2 and Remark 3.3 with the exact sequences of triples. Only the slab between the levels need be compact, which is what $-L_p$ requires.

items.title: Theorem 7.2

milnor.label: §7, Theorem 7.2
milnor.statement: A complex manifold of complex dimension $k$, bianalytically embedded as a closed subset of $\mathbb C^n$, has the homotopy type of a $k$-dimensional CW-complex.

lean.statement: Let $M \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be a slice submanifold of dimension $2k$ which is closed in $\mathbb R^n$ and complex for an orthogonal $J$ with $J^2 = -1$ (V5.13). Then $M$ has the homotopy type of a countable cell complex (VA.18) all of whose cells have dimension at most $k$.

diff: For a closed slice submanifold of $\mathbb R^n$ of dimension $2k$ with complex tangent spaces. "$k$-dimensional" is "of dimension at most $k$". The complex is the countable tower of cell attachments of VA.18, with arbitrary attaching maps.
$L_p$ is a Morse function for almost every $p$ (V4.12), with compact sublevel sets because $M$ is closed, and its critical points have index $\le k$ (V5.13).

items.title: Theorem 7.1 (Andreotti and Frankel), over a field

milnor.label: §7, Theorem 7.1
milnor.statement: If $M \subset \mathbb C^n$ is a non-singular affine algebraic variety of real dimension $2k$, then $H_i(M; \mathbb Z) = 0$ for $i > k$.

lean.statement: Under the hypotheses of V5.15, $H_i(M; \mathbb k) = 0$ for every field $\mathbb k$ and every $i > k$.

diff: Over every field, for the submanifolds of V5.15; that a non-singular affine variety is one is not formalized. The proof uses the filtration by sublevel sets, not cellular homology.

items.title: Hyperplane sections, for an abstract pair

milnor.label: §7, pp. 41–42
milnor.statement: Corollary 7.3 is proved from the exact sequence of the pair $(V, V \cap P)$, Lefschetz duality, and Theorem 7.1 for $V - (V \cap P)$. Theorem 7.4 is proved from "the hypothesis that some neighborhood $U$ of $V \cap P$ can be deformed into $V \cap P$ within $V$".

lean.statement: Let $X$ be a compact space, $A \subseteq X$ closed, $M$ as in V5.15, and $e$ a homeomorphism of $M$ onto $X \setminus A$ such that $\|e^{-1}(y)\| \to \infty$ as $y \to A$. *Hypothesis (N)* for $A$ in $X$: there are an open $U \supseteq A$ and a homotopy $H : [0, 1] \times U \to X$ with $H_0$ the inclusion, $H_1(U) \subseteq A$, and $H_t(a) = a$ for all $t$ and all $a \in A$. Under Hypothesis (N), for every field $\mathbb k$: $H_r(X, A; \mathbb k) = 0$ for $r < k$; hence the map $H_r(A; \mathbb k) \to H_r(X; \mathbb k)$ induced by the inclusion is bijective for $r + 1 < k$ and surjective for $r < k$. On the way: at a non-degenerate critical point of $L_p$ on $M$, the function $-L_p$ has index at least $k$.

diff: For $X$ compact, $A$ closed, and $X \setminus A$ a closed complex submanifold of $\mathbb C^n$ going to infinity at $A$: under Hypothesis (N), $H_r(X, A) = 0$ for $r < k$, so $H_r(A) \to H_r(X)$ is bijective for $r < k - 1$ and onto for $r = k - 1$.

Instead of duality: a neighbourhood $V_R$ of $A$ deforms into $A$, and $H_r(X, V_R)$ vanishes by excision and Morse theory for $-L_p$ on a compact slab, whose critical points have index $\ge k$. The deformation must keep $A$ pointwise fixed, which Milnor does not say.

items.title: Corollary 7.3 (Lefschetz), over a field

milnor.label: §7, Corollary 7.3
milnor.statement: Let $V$ be an algebraic variety of complex dimension $k$ in $\mathbb CP_n$ and $P$ a hyperplane containing the singular points of $V$. Then the inclusion $V \cap P \to V$ induces isomorphisms of homology groups in dimensions less than $k - 1$, and is onto in dimension $k - 1$.

lean.statement: Let $V \subseteq \mathbb CP^n$ (V3.41) be closed and $P$ the hyperplane $z_0 = 0$, the set of projections $Q$ with $Q_{00} = 0$. The *affine part* of $V$ is the set of $u \in \mathbb C^n = \mathbb R^{2n}$ for which the projection onto the line of $(1, u)$ belongs to $V$; it is homeomorphic to $V \setminus P$, and its points go to infinity as their images approach $V \cap P$. Suppose the affine part is a slice submanifold of $\mathbb R^{2n}$ of dimension $2k$, complex for multiplication by $i$, and suppose Hypothesis (N) for $V \cap P$ in $V$ (V5.17). Then for every field $\mathbb k$ the map $H_r(V \cap P; \mathbb k) \to H_r(V; \mathbb k)$ induced by the inclusion is bijective for $r < k - 1$ and surjective for $r = k - 1$.

diff: For a closed $V \subseteq \mathbb CP^n$ whose affine part is a complex submanifold of $\mathbb C^n$ of complex dimension $k$: this replaces "algebraic variety with singular points in $P$" and includes pure dimension, which Milnor omits and the statement needs.
Hypothesis (N), which Milnor draws from triangulability, is assumed. Another hyperplane is brought to $z_0 = 0$ by a unitary change of coordinates, not formalized.

items.title: Theorem 7.4 (Lefschetz)

milnor.label: §7, Theorem 7.4, pp. 41–42
milnor.statement: Under the same hypotheses, the relative homotopy group $\pi_r(V, V \cap P)$ is zero for $r < k$. The proof uses $f = 0$ on $V \cap P$ and $f = 1/L_p$ elsewhere, whose critical points have index $\ge k$, and a neighbourhood of $V \cap P$ that deforms into $V \cap P$ (from the triangulability of algebraic varieties).

lean.statement: Under the hypotheses of V5.18: for $r < k$, every continuous map $h : I^r \to V$ is homotopic, relative to $h^{-1}(V \cap P)$, to a map into $V \cap P$; the same holds for maps from any compact space that admits a continuous injection into a real vector space of dimension $< k$, and for the abstract pair $(X, A)$ of V5.17. Consequently, for every $x \in V \cap P$, the map $\pi_i(V \cap P, x) \to \pi_i(V, x)$ induced by the inclusion is bijective for $i + 1 < k$ and surjective for $i < k$.

diff: Relative homotopy groups are not in Mathlib; the statement is that every map $I^r \to V$, $r < k$, is homotopic, relative to the preimage of $V \cap P$, to a map into $V \cap P$. It gives $\pi_i(V \cap P) \to \pi_i(V)$ bijective for $i < k - 1$ and onto for $i = k - 1$.
Milnor's $1/L_p$ is infinite at $p$; $1/(1 + L_p)$ is used. The maps are pushed past the critical levels by the lemma of Chapter 13 (V13.13) on a compact slab.

notFormalized.title: The torus: the intermediate sublevel sets and the cell attachments
notFormalized.label: §1, pp. 1–3
notFormalized.book: For $f(p) < a < f(q)$, $f(q) < a < f(r)$ and $f(r) < a < f(s)$, $M^a$ is homeomorphic to a 2-cell, to a cylinder and to a compact genus-one surface bounded by a circle; up to homotopy type, passing $p$, $q$, $r$, $s$ attaches a 0-cell, a 1-cell, a 1-cell and a 2-cell (p. 2).
notFormalized.instead: **What is proved is the frame, not the pictures.** The torus of revolution is a compact surface whose height function has exactly four critical points, non-degenerate, of indices $0, 1, 1, 2$ (V3.22, V3.23); $T^a$ is empty below $0$ and all of $T$ from $2R + 2\rho$ on, and between critical values Theorem 3.1 holds (V3.24). The homeomorphism types of (2)–(4) would need explicit homeomorphisms, and Theorem 3.2 on submanifolds (V2.8), which would give the cell attachments up to homotopy, has not been applied to the torus. Morse theory with the height function gives only $b_0 \le 1$, $b_1 \le 2$, $b_2 \le 1$ and $b_0 - b_1 + b_2 = 0$; the Betti numbers $1, 2, 1$ are not derived.

notFormalized.title: Regular sublevel sets are manifolds with boundary
notFormalized.label: §2, p. 4
notFormalized.book: If $a$ is not a critical value of $f$, the implicit function theorem makes $M^a$ a smooth manifold-with-boundary, whose boundary $f^{-1}(a)$ is a smooth submanifold of $M$.
notFormalized.instead: **Not restated.** It is the companion project's Lemma 3 (`Milnor.isHalfSliceSubmanifold_of_regularValue`) applied to $a - f$. Theorems 3.1 and 3.2 are stated here for sublevel sets as topological subspaces, without a structure of manifold with boundary.

notFormalized.title: The intrinsic Hessian
notFormalized.label: §2, pp. 4–5
notFormalized.book: $f_{**}(v, w) = \tilde v_p(\tilde w(f))$ for vector fields $\tilde v$, $\tilde w$ extending $v$, $w$; it is symmetric because $[\tilde v, \tilde w]_p(f) = 0$ at a critical point, and therefore independent of both extensions.
notFormalized.instead: **The coordinate formula instead.** The formal Hessian is the second derivative read in the preferred chart, Milnor's matrix of second partial derivatives (V1.4), and its independence of the extensions is replaced by its independence of the chart (V1.5).

notFormalized.title: Example (b), and the submanifold claims of (d) and (e)
notFormalized.label: §2, pp. 8–9
notFormalized.book: (b) $F(x) = e^{-1/x^2}\sin^2(1/x)$ has a degenerate, non-isolated critical point at the origin; in (d) the critical set is a submanifold of $\mathbb R^2$, and in (e) it is not even a submanifold.
notFormalized.instead: **Not done.** The smoothness of (b) at $0$ needs the flatness of $e^{-1/x^2}$ against the growth of the derivatives of $\sin^2(1/x)$. The critical sets of (d) and (e) are computed and shown to be degenerate (V1.12), but whether they are submanifolds is not formalized.

notFormalized.title: Lemma 2.4 on a manifold
notFormalized.label: §2, Lemma 2.4
notFormalized.book: A smooth vector field on a manifold $M$ which vanishes outside a compact set generates a unique 1-parameter group of diffeomorphisms of $M$.
notFormalized.instead: **Vector spaces only.** Lemma 2.4, and the smooth dependence of the flow on the initial point, are proved on a Banach space (V1.14, V1.15); Mathlib has no smooth dependence on initial conditions on manifolds. On submanifolds of $\mathbb R^K$, which is where flows are needed, Chapter 2 uses instead the ambient flow of a compactly supported field tangent to the submanifold, which preserves it (V2.3).

notFormalized.title: Compact support cannot be omitted
notFormalized.label: §2, Remark, p. 11
notFormalized.book: Without compact support Lemma 2.4 fails: the standard vector field $d/dt$ on the open interval $(0, 1)$ generates no 1-parameter group of diffeomorphisms.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized.** The example plays no role later; the analogous remark on Theorem 3.1, p. 13, is formalized (V2.5).

notFormalized.title: Theorem 3.1 on a non-compact abstract manifold
notFormalized.label: §3, Theorem 3.1
notFormalized.book: For a smooth $f$ on any manifold $M$, with $f^{-1}[a, b]$ compact and free of critical points, $M^a$ is diffeomorphic to $M^b$ and is a deformation retract of it.
notFormalized.instead: **Three classes of spaces, not all manifolds.** Proved on $\mathbb R^n$ (V2.2), on submanifolds of $\mathbb R^K$, closed or not (V2.3), and on compact Hausdorff manifolds through Mathlib's Whitney embedding (V2.4). A non-compact abstract manifold would need either a closed embedding into Euclidean space or flows of vector fields on manifolds, and Mathlib has neither.

notFormalized.title: Theorems 3.2 and 3.5, Remarks 3.3 and 3.4, on abstract manifolds
notFormalized.label: §3, pp. 14–24
notFormalized.book: Each is stated for a function on an abstract manifold.
notFormalized.instead: **Not transferred.** Theorem 3.1 is carried to compact abstract manifolds through the Whitney embedding (V2.4), but the cell-attaching statements are proved only on $\mathbb R^n$ (V2.6, V2.10) and for $f = F|N$ on submanifolds of a Euclidean space (V2.8, V2.9, V2.12, V2.15). The transfer, along the lines of V2.4 and V4.24, has not been made.

notFormalized.title: Remark 3.4 on submanifolds, and the Remark of p. 24 at a critical value
notFormalized.label: §3, pp. 20 and 24
notFormalized.book: $M^c$ is a deformation retract of $M^{c+\epsilon}$, and $M^{c-\epsilon} \cup e^\lambda$ one of $M^c$; hence each $M^a$ has the homotopy type of a finite CW-complex with one cell for each critical point in $M^a$, even if $a$ is a critical value.
notFormalized.instead: **Only on $\mathbb R^n$, and at regular values.** Remark 3.4 is proved on $\mathbb R^n$ (V2.10); on submanifolds it is not, so the Remark of p. 24 is proved only for $a$ not a critical value (V2.15).

notFormalized.title: The CW structure in Theorem 3.5
notFormalized.label: §3, Theorem 3.5
notFormalized.book: $M$ has the homotopy type of a CW-complex, the attaching maps being made cellular by cellular approximation (p. 23).
notFormalized.instead: **An iterated adjunction space instead.** The formal Theorem 3.5 produces a space built from the empty space by attaching cells one at a time along arbitrary continuous maps, with exactly $C_\lambda$ cells of dimension $\lambda$ (V2.11, V2.12). Mathlib has no cellular approximation theorem, so the attaching maps are not made cellular and the result is not shown to be a CW-complex.

notFormalized.title: Theorem 3.5 for a non-compact manifold
notFormalized.label: §3, proof of Theorem 3.5
notFormalized.book: If $M$ is not compact but all critical points lie in one compact $M^a$, then $M^a$ is a deformation retract of $M$; with infinitely many critical points, the union of the complexes $K_i$ with the direct limit topology and Whitehead's theorem give a homotopy equivalence $M \to K$ (pp. 23–24).
notFormalized.instead: **Compact submanifolds only.** With finitely many critical points the non-compact case needs a deformation of $M$ onto some $M^a$ obtained by patching flows; with infinitely many it needs Whitehead's theorem and the fact that a manifold is dominated by a CW-complex, neither of which Mathlib provides.

notFormalized.title: Smale's handles
notFormalized.label: §3, Remark, p. 17
notFormalized.book: In Smale's terminology $M^{c-\epsilon} \cup H$ is $M^{c-\epsilon}$ with a handle attached, and by Theorem 3.1 the manifold-with-boundary $M^{c-\epsilon} \cup H$ is diffeomorphic to $M^{c+\epsilon}$.
notFormalized.instead: **Not recorded.** It is Theorem 3.1 applied to $F$, which the proof of Theorem 3.2 uses (Assertion 3, as a strong deformation retraction), but the diffeomorphism itself is not stated.

notFormalized.title: Reeb's theorem with degenerate critical points
notFormalized.label: §4, Remark 1
notFormalized.book: The theorem remains true even if the critical points are degenerate, but the proof is more difficult; Milnor cites his own paper and one of R. Rosen.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized.** A proof needs M. Brown's monotone union theorem, which is not in Mathlib; a proof by that route is written out in the exposition, Chapter 3, §1.

notFormalized.title: Exotic spheres
notFormalized.label: §4, Remark 2
notFormalized.book: The theorem gives no diffeomorphism with the standard $S^n$, and none need exist: the 7-sphere with an exotic differentiable structure of Milnor's 1956 paper is shown to be homeomorphic to $S^7$ by means of a function with two non-degenerate critical points.
notFormalized.instead: **Out of scope.** It needs characteristic classes and the signature theorem. The formal proof of Reeb's theorem shows where smoothness is lost: Alexander's cone is not differentiable at the centre (V3.5).

notFormalized.title: Manifolds with three critical points
notFormalized.label: §4, p. 26
notFormalized.book: If an $n$-manifold carries a differentiable function with only three critical points, these have index $0$, $n$ and $n/2$ (by Poincaré duality), and the manifold has the homotopy type of an $n/2$-sphere with an $n$-cell attached; such functions exist on the real and complex projective planes.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized.** Singular homology with its exact sequences is available (V3.26–V3.31), but Poincaré duality, needed mod 2 since $\mathbb RP^2$ is not orientable, is not; the homotopy type would also need Theorem 3.5 on abstract manifolds.

notFormalized.title: Complex projective space: what remains
notFormalized.label: §4, pp. 26–27
notFormalized.book: On $\mathbb CP_n$ the function $f(z_0 : \dots : z_n) = \sum_j c_j|z_j|^2$, with distinct constants $c_j$, has $n + 1$ critical points, every even index between $0$ and $2n$ occurring exactly once; so $\mathbb CP_n$ has the homotopy type of $e^0 \cup e^2 \cup \dots \cup e^{2n}$, and $H_i(\mathbb CP_n; \mathbb Z)$ is $\mathbb Z$ for $i = 0, 2, \dots, 2n$ and $0$ otherwise.
notFormalized.instead: **Now proved** for the submanifold of rank-one projections: the coordinates (V3.41), the critical points and indices of $f$ (V3.42), the cells and the Betti numbers over every field (V3.43). What remains: the CW-complex in the strict sense (cells are attached along arbitrary maps, V2.12) and the integral homology (next entry).

notFormalized.title: Integral homology
notFormalized.label: §4, p. 27, and §5, p. 31
notFormalized.book: The homology groups of $\mathbb CP_n$ are given with integer coefficients, and Corollary 5.4 is said to find them without Theorem 3.5.
notFormalized.instead: **Fields only.** §5 works over a field, and so do V3.32–V3.39. The integral groups, and more generally the exposition's Proposition G (in the lacunary case $H_\lambda(M; \mathbb Z)$ is free of rank $C_\lambda$), are not derived, although relative homology and the cell computations are available with integer coefficients (V3.26–V3.31).

notFormalized.title: Sard's theorem for $C^1$ maps
notFormalized.label: §6, Theorem 6.1
notFormalized.book: For a $C^1$ map between manifolds of the same dimension with countable bases, the image of the set of critical points has measure $0$.
notFormalized.instead: **Smooth maps into a vector space.** Sard's theorem is proved for smooth maps from a second countable manifold into a finite-dimensional vector space, in any dimensions (V4.3), which is every use Milnor makes of it; the Milnor project proves the Euclidean case for smooth maps only.

notFormalized.title: Corollary 6.7 for a non-compact abstract manifold
notFormalized.label: §6, Corollary 6.7
notFormalized.book: On any manifold there is a function with no degenerate critical points all of whose sublevel sets are compact, by Whitney's embedding as a closed subset of $\mathbb R^{2n+1}$.
notFormalized.instead: **Closed submanifolds and compact manifolds.** Proved for closed submanifolds of $\mathbb R^n$ (V4.13) and for compact Hausdorff manifolds (V4.17). Mathlib's Whitney embedding is for compact manifolds only, so a non-compact abstract manifold has no closed embedding into Euclidean space here; the abstract forms of Corollary 6.8 (V4.22) are limited in the same way.

notFormalized.title: Application 1: the homotopy type of a CW-complex
notFormalized.label: §6, Application 1
notFormalized.book: A differentiable manifold has the homotopy type of a CW-complex, by Corollary 6.7 and Theorem 3.5.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized.** Theorem 3.5 is proved only for compact submanifolds of Euclidean space and only as an iterated adjunction space, Mathlib having no cellular approximation (V2.11, V2.12); it has not been transferred to abstract manifolds, and the non-compact case needs Whitehead's theorem.

notFormalized.title: Application 2 as Milnor argues it
notFormalized.label: §6, Application 2
notFormalized.book: On a compact manifold the index sum of $\mathrm{grad} f$ is $\chi(M)$, and the index sum of any vector field is $\chi(M)$ because it is a topological invariant (Steenrod, §39.7).
notFormalized.instead: **Run the other way, on an embedded copy.** $\chi$ enters as the Poincaré–Hopf integer of the Milnor project (V3.17, V4.18) and is identified with $\sum_i (-1)^i \dim H_i(M; F)$ afterwards (V3.38). The topological invariance quoted from Steenrod is not formalized, and vector fields on an abstract manifold are not treated, only on an embedded copy (V4.19).

notFormalized.title: Independence of the principal curvatures
notFormalized.label: §6, p. 34
notFormalized.book: The principal curvatures are the eigenvalues of $(\vec v \cdot \vec\ell_{ij})$ in coordinates with $(g_{ij})$ the identity at $q$, tacitly independent of the coordinates chosen.
notFormalized.instead: **Not proved, and not needed.** The principal curvatures are the eigenvalues of the shape operator of the chosen slice chart (V4.6), and every statement that uses them is proved in that chart.

notFormalized.title: Theorem 7.2 for complex manifolds, and CW-complexes
notFormalized.label: §7, Theorem 7.2
notFormalized.book: A complex manifold of complex dimension $k$, embedded bianalytically as a closed subset of $\mathbb C^n$, is homotopy equivalent to a CW-complex of dimension $k$.
notFormalized.instead: **Proved for closed submanifolds with complex tangent spaces** (V5.15), as a countable cell complex with cells of dimension at most $k$. What remains: that a bianalytically embedded complex manifold is such a submanifold (holomorphic charts are not formalized as charts of the real submanifold), and a CW-complex in the strict sense, with cellular attaching maps.

notFormalized.title: Theorem 7.1 with integral coefficients
notFormalized.label: §7, Theorem 7.1
notFormalized.book: A non-singular affine algebraic variety $M \subset \mathbb C^n$ of real dimension $2k$ has $H_i(M; \mathbb Z) = 0$ in every degree $i > k$.
notFormalized.instead: **Proved over every field** (V5.16), for closed submanifolds with complex tangent spaces. What remains: integral coefficients, and that a non-singular affine algebraic variety is such a submanifold.

notFormalized.title: Assertion 2 for focal points, and the count of p. 41
notFormalized.label: §7, pp. 40–41
notFormalized.book: The focal points of $(M, q)$ along a normal line occur in symmetric pairs about $q$; there are at most $2k$ of them on the line, hence at most $k$ between $p$ and $q$, which by Lemma 6.9 bounds the index of $L_p$.
notFormalized.instead: **Replaced.** Assertion 2 is proved for Hessians in a holomorphic chart (V5.7), and the index bound by the Andreotti–Frankel identity (V5.8–V5.11), on the real submanifold in V5.13; these need neither focal points nor Lemma 6.9. The focal-point form is not formalized.

notFormalized.title: Corollary 7.3 with integral coefficients; Hypothesis (N)
notFormalized.label: §7, Corollary 7.3
notFormalized.book: For an algebraic variety $V$ of complex dimension $k$ in $\mathbb CP_n$ and a hyperplane $P$ containing its singular points, the inclusion $V \cap P \to V$ induces isomorphisms of integral homology in dimensions less than $k - 1$, and a surjection in dimension $k - 1$.
notFormalized.instead: **Proved over every field** (V5.17, V5.18), without Lefschetz duality, for a closed $V \subseteq \mathbb CP^n$ whose affine part is a complex submanifold, under Hypothesis (N). What remains: integral homology; algebraic varieties (that their affine parts satisfy the hypothesis); and Hypothesis (N) itself, the deformation of a neighbourhood of $V \cap P$ into it.

notFormalized.title: Theorem 7.4: triangulability
notFormalized.label: §7, Theorem 7.4
notFormalized.book: Under the same hypotheses the relative homotopy groups $\pi_r(V, V \cap P)$ vanish for $r < k$.
notFormalized.instead: **Proved under Hypothesis (N)** (V5.19), as the compression criterion for $\pi_r(V, V \cap P) = 0$. What remains: Hypothesis (N), which Milnor obtains from the triangulability of algebraic varieties (quoted), and relative homotopy groups as objects.

notFormalized.title: §§8–9 on an abstract Riemannian manifold
notFormalized.book: Connections, Christoffel symbols, covariant derivatives along curves, parallel translation, the Levi-Civita connection and the curvature tensor are developed on an abstract Riemannian manifold, in local coordinates.
notFormalized.instead: **Embedded manifolds instead.** The substance of §§8–9 is proved for submanifolds of a Euclidean space with the induced metric (V6.1–V6.21). On an abstract manifold only Milnor's rules for Mathlib's covariant derivatives, the definitions of compatibility and symmetry, the uniqueness half of Lemma 8.6, and the curvature formula with its sign (V6.3, V6.11, V6.13, V6.14, V6.16). Mathlib has no curvature, Christoffel symbols, covariant derivative along curves, parallel transport or Levi-Civita connection, and the embedded results reach an arbitrary Riemannian manifold only through Nash's embedding theorem, which is not proved. The induced connection is not constructed as a Mathlib covariant derivative, so the embedded existence and the abstract uniqueness are parallel results, not one theorem.

notFormalized.title: Symmetric Christoffel symbols, and the second covariant derivative
notFormalized.label: §8, p. 48
notFormalized.book: If $\Gamma^k_{ij} = \Gamma^k_{ji}$ then the connection is symmetric throughout the coordinate neighbourhood; and, in a footnote, a connection is symmetric iff the covariant second derivative $X_p(Yf) - (X_p \vdash Y)f$ is symmetric in $X_p$ and $Y_p$.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized**, there being no Christoffel symbols in either setting; the second covariant derivative of a function is not defined.

notFormalized.title: Parallel fields along a flat surface
notFormalized.label: §9, pp. 52–53
notFormalized.book: If the curvature tensor vanishes, a vector field $P$ along a parametrized surface with $DP/\partial x = DP/\partial y = 0$ and a given value at the origin can be constructed.
notFormalized.instead: **Not formalized.** Lemma 9.2, on which the construction rests, is proved for embedded manifolds (V6.19).
